Katalog Berita (Halaman 42/57)

#3160. Barrick Mining (B) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Gold and copper output held guidance while buybacks and net cash stood out.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Barrick Mining Corporation (B +4.22%) reported third quarter results that matched or exceeded the company's operational targets across its gold and copper portfolios. Management stated that safety and operational execution allowed the business to capture higher realized metal prices, leading to a 41% year-over-year increase in adjusted net earnings per share. The company reported a net cash position of $900 million and confirmed its 2026 production guidance ranges for both gold and copper. Management also indicated that the company is proceeding with a restructuring of North American assets, including an initial public offering for a new entity to hold those interests. Capital allocation remains focused on growth projects like the Lumwana expansion and returning cash to shareholders through dividends and a $3 billion buyback program.

Operator: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us, and welcome to the Barrick Third Quarter 2026 Results. [Operator Instructions] I will now hand the conference over to Emily Chieng, Senior Vice President, Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Emily Chieng: Thank you, and good morning, everyone. We hope you've had an opportunity to review the press release we issued before market opened this morning. This presentation deck is also now available to download on our website. Presenting our results today are Mark Hill, Barrick's President and CEO; Seb Bock, CEO of Barrick International, which we previously referred to as Barrick Rest of World; and Helen Cai, Senior EVP and CFO. Other members of Barrick's management team will be available after our prepared remarks for Q&A. Before we begin, please note that we will be making forward-looking statements.

This slide includes a summary of the significant risks and factors that could affect Barrick's future performance and our ability to deliver on those forward-looking statements. This material is also available on our website. I will now hand over to Mark.

Mark Hill: Thanks, Emily. We had our fourth quarter in a row with improved safety and excellent operating and financial results. Once again, we delivered against all 4 of our priorities. We continue to focus on safety, which remains our #1 priority. We delivered higher gold production than last quarter and continue to manage our costs. That allowed us to capture the benefits of higher metal prices and deliver strong financial results. We had adjusted net earnings of $0.82 per share and consolidated adjusted EBITDA of $3.5 billion, and consolidated free cash flow of $1.2 billion. As we announced last quarter, we have restructured the management of the Fourmile project and NGM which has already produced significant synergies.

On the growth projects, we continue to advance the Pueblo Viejo resettlement and tailings expansion, and the mine continues to be on track and on budget. Finally, we expect to complete the IPO of our North American gold assets by the end of this year or early next year, subject to market conditions and regulatory review. So as I said, safety is our #1 priority. Our goal is for everyone to go home safe and healthy every day. In Q3, our leaders continue to get out in the field to identify and manage risks. We conducted over 24,000 Critical Control Verifications. Our recordable injury rate decreased quarter-on-quarter from 0.77 to 0.71. We're also working hard to reduce high potential incidents.

So turning to our Q3 highlights. We delivered 816,000 ounces of gold. As we flagged last quarter, gold production was higher in Q3. The strong ramp-up of Goldrush underground and Loulo-Gounkoto more than offset the weather disruptions at Veladero and Porgera. Third quarter copper production was 50,000 tonnes, which Seb will provide more details on shortly. We continue to manage our gold costs. While we are seeing pressures in Africa from fuel, other consumable costs, and foreign exchange, we expect to remain within our full year guidance range. Our adjusted net earnings of $0.82 per share is up 41% year-over-year. Our attributable adjusted EBITDA is up over 20%, and our year-to-date capital returns of $3.2 billion are double last year's.

We're also on track to deliver full year production guidance, and we expect to further extend our track record of strong operational execution. So in North America, we had another increase in production this quarter with almost 0.5 million ounces of gold, with NGM and Pueblo Viejo generating 67% and 72% EBITDA margins, respectively. We saw record throughput at the Gold Quarry roaster. We progressed the ramp-up of Goldrush underground and mined record tonnes from Turquoise Ridge underground. Gold production from Pueblo Viejo was softer in the third quarter due to planned autoclave maintenance. Also in North America, we continue to evaluate a number of growth opportunities.

At NGM, we're assessing options to optimize infrastructure, including new processing capacity at Cortez and rail infrastructure, which could drive a step change in production over the next decade. At Cortez, we're advancing drilling along one of the most prospective corridors in Nevada down the Goldrush trend. And at Carlin, we turned our focus to drilling at Greater Leeville. We are also looking at optimizing process capacity, which could extend open pit life well beyond 2050. Turning to Pueblo Viejo, where the resettlement and advancement of the TSF construction continues on schedule. We have 99% of the resettlement packages accepted and have resettled more than 97% of the families.

We continue to advance the engineering work for the addition of a third flotation train, which will deliver improvements to recovery beyond 2030. And we expect to share more information regarding that work in Pueblo Viejo with our upcoming IPO filings. So with that, I'll turn it over to Seb to discuss the performance of Barrick International. Thanks, Seb.

Sebastiaan Bock: Thank you, Mark, and good morning, everyone. Barrick International produced 319,000 ounces in the third quarter, up 6% on Q2, with strong performance at Loulo-Gounkoto, Kibali, and Bulyanhulu more than offsetting weather disruptions at Veladero and Porgera. The increase came from 2 places. Loulo-Gounkoto continued to perform well, up 16% on higher throughput and grade, with mining and processing consistently running ahead of the original restart plan. And Kibali, up 20%, delivered its highest quarterly production since Q4 2023 as the underground brought more ore at higher grades. Moving to Tanzania. Bulyanhulu stepped up again as the Upper West development resulted in greater mining flexibility.

North Mara was up on the quarter despite an extended plant shutdown and some power instability. Veladero and Porgera were affected by El Niño weather events. Severe winter storms suspended operations at Veladero on several occasions, while drought-related water shortages at Porgera limited plant operating rates. We've seen these conditions continue into early Q4. We manage Barrick International as a portfolio, and the performance across the rest of the operations keep us on track for our full year gold production guidance. On costs, higher volumes at Kibali and Bulyanhulu brought unit costs down. Veladero, Porgera, and North Mara went the other way, with impacts from the storms adding to Veladero's costs. Royalties and fuel remain the main pressures year-to-date.

Despite that, Barrick International generated over $800 million of attributable adjusted EBITDA from the gold operations in the quarter with an adjusted EBITDA margin of 59%. Moving to copper. Production remains on track for full year guidance. We produced 50,000 tonnes in the quarter, with Lumwana completing a planned mill reline in late September, which sets us up for a clean run through the fourth quarter. Our other copper operations were flat on a combined basis, with higher grades and recoveries at Jabal Sayid offsetting lower throughput and grades at Zaldívar. Costs were higher in the quarter, driven mainly by diesel prices, local currency appreciation, higher royalties on the stronger copper price, and some additional waste stripping on top.

For the full year, we expect our copper cost to be around the top end of the range, given the same diesel and currency pressures. The Lumwana expansion will take production to 240,000 tonnes a year with a mine life of more than 30 years, and it remains on track for first copper from the expansion at the end of Q1 2028. Since the start of the project, we've spent $795 million on the expansion, and total expected project capital remains on target at $2 billion. Procurement of all major long lead equipment is complete. The mill building, which sits on our critical path, is scheduled for completion in Q4.

To close, quarter 3 shows the portfolio delivering where we control the variables and doing what we can to mitigate the external pressures on costs. We remain on track to deliver full year production in line with guidance for both gold and copper. With that, I'll hand over to Helen.

Hongyu Cai: Thank you, Seb, and good morning, everyone. We produced a strong set of financial results this quarter with solid operational execution, allowing us to capture more of the favorable gold and copper prices. This more than offset the increasing cost pressures we face. Compared to last year's Q3 results, we delivered a substantial increase in earnings, highlighting our leverage to rising prices and robust operating cash flow. Adjusted net earnings rose 37% year-on-year, and attributable adjusted EBITDA increased 22%. Operating cash flow was in line with last year, and we stepped up investments in our growth options across the portfolio. This includes executing on the Lumwana expansion project, increasing stripping at Loulo, and developing NGM optionality.

Free cash flow was strong at $1.2 billion with $154 million of additional growth-related CapEx compared to this time last year. We closed Q3 with $0.9 billion of net cash on the balance sheet, up $586 million over prior year despite higher return to shareholders, still leaving us some flexibility to invest in our future growth opportunities. A disciplined approach to capital allocation is a top priority, particularly when the business is generating significant cash. We have a clear framework for deploying capital. Our first priority is balance sheet strength. With $0.9 billion of net cash and an undrawn $3 billion revolving credit facility and no meaningful debt due until 2033, we are in a strong position.

Our second priority is sustaining the business and earnings accretive growth. Lumwana and NGM optimization are 2 clear examples where we are deploying capital into low-risk brownfield opportunities that we believe will generate superior returns. Our third priority is returning cash to shareholders. Our new dividend policy implemented earlier this year prioritizes a quarterly base dividend of $0.175 per quarter topped up at year-end to target a total payout of 50% of attributable free cash flow. This quarter, we completed $0.8 billion of share buybacks, and we continue to return excess cash to shareholders. Since 2021, Barrick has returned $10.4 billion to shareholders. And this year, we are set to deliver record annual returns with $3.2 billion returned so far.

With that, I will turn the call back over to Mark.

Mark Hill: Okay. Thank you, Helen. So for 2026, production and cost guidance remain unchanged. As we round out the year, we expect the fourth quarter gold production to be slightly higher than Q3. So in conclusion, for the fourth quarter in a row, we have improved our safety, although we acknowledge there's more work to do. We delivered on our production and cost. Mark Hill: Okay. Mark Hill: Okay. Thanks, Anita. Tim, can I hand that over to you? Can you comment on that, please?

Tim Cribb: Yes, sure. Thanks, Mark. Look, on the -- I think on PV, we will be updating it, as Mark said, when we put out the S-K 1300 reports later this month with the filing. Fahad Tariq: On the optimized Nevada Gold Mines infrastructure, can you talk about the timing of that and how we should be thinking about CapEx and whether the improvements, whether it's the Cortez processing or the rail, are they all really to optimize Fourmile or is it the other operations as well?

Mark Hill: So let me start off and then others can jump in. Look, what we're trying to do is now that everything is rolled into NGM, the idea was Tim and the team are going about optimizing the whole of the NGM asset. So we're not looking at them in isolation. So we are trying to work out what is the optimal processing route for all of the ore. I think one of the questions actually that analysts keep asking is can we provide a flow chart. So we're actually going to have that, and we'll be able to give that to you. But what it shows is it's quite complex.

So to optimize that and what new processing capacity and where we need, still that's a bit of a work in progress. And the roaster work is at its early stage. I mean we've only just awarded the engineering study to Hatch. So that will take some time. And then the rail is obviously the ability to move things around Nevada at a much lower cost, which again will optimize the total group of operations rather than just any individual operation. Tim, again, if you want to add something to that?

Tim Cribb: I think you covered most of it, Mark. Just in terms of the question around, is it just Cortez or is it more broader? Again, I'd refer you back to the presentation we gave at Denver because once you take a view of increased processing capacity at Cortez, you free up roaster capacity at Carlin. And so the exploration of Carlin, but particularly focusing in that North Leeville area as well as increasing potentially the material handling capacity through a shaft or decline there becomes important because then you're talking additional process capacity at both of the centers.

Fahad Tariq: Okay. And on the timing, these improvements all come after 2030. Is that the right way to think about it?

Mark Hill: That's the right way to think about it, yes.

Operator: Your next question comes from Brian MacArthur with Raymond James.

Brian MacArthur: Can I just follow up a little bit on the last question? So in the S-1, have you had enough time? You've talked a lot about optimizing all the flows, which we've talked about for years. But do you think now you actually have had enough time to figure it out? Or should we think about the S-1 as kind of optimization 1? And then as we do more work over the next year, we do optimization 2, it changes what's out there in 2030? Because it would strike me a little bit that there's still a lot of information, as you said, from drilling you don't have yet to try and optimize everything perfectly. Is that a fair comment?

Mark Hill: So look, Brian, I think it's a very fair comment, right? So we've only just done this. And you're right. It's highlighted some gaps and things we have to drill off and for more information we have to get. But at least it's giving us a road map to actually start identifying those gaps and what we have to do to further optimize the complex. But yes, you are 100% correct.

Brian MacArthur: Great. And maybe just one other question. I noticed you highlighted the Andean portfolio, and you talked a little bit about that at El Alto, Norte Abierto, and Lama. Is -- when you talk about review of development options, is that the process to review how you're going to develop them? Or is it just a whole process that we might actually see these things hold going forward?

Sebastiaan Bock: Look, it's a process to review the assets as they stand today in the environment we are today, a lot has changed in the last 10 to 15 years. That said, that doesn't mean we would necessarily want to develop them. The point is we need to understand the assets better, how do they actually fit into -- if you were to develop them today or try and derive some kind of value from them. So if I talk about going back to South America, number one, it refers to, of course, all the exploration opportunities. The governments are a lot more business-friendly and pro-mining at the moment. The gold price and commodity prices are a lot higher.

We've now got power at Veladero, which we didn't have a decade ago, et cetera. So I think it's more realistic. It's around how do we actually get the most value from those assets and not let them just sit on our reserve and resource statements. If that answers the question.

Operator: Your next question comes from Bob Brackett with Bernstein.

Bob Brackett: Could we get an update on the starter dam permitting for Pueblo Viejo?

Mark Hill: Okay. Tim, do you want to give an update?

Tim Cribb: Yes. So the -- I assume you're referring to Naranjo, the new TSF. But in terms of that, the work is advanced. We have the initial construction of the walls occurring, and we're still depositing into El Llagal. We have approximately a 6- to 12-month buffer between that changeover when we move to Naranjo in late 2029, early 2030. But in terms of the permitting, the majority of the permits received, there are some permits around road construction and bridges, which are ongoing, but they are not impacting the schedule. And as we've done over the past 12 to 18 months, we bring them in as needed.

So I think things are on track and the budget for it also on budget, as Mark mentioned earlier.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I will now turn the call back to Emily for the closing remarks.

Emily Chieng: Thank you, everyone, for joining us today. We look forward to speaking with you again on our next results call in the new year. Please get in touch with us if you've got any further follow-up questions. Thank you.

#3159. Which Foldable Phone Has the Best Battery Life? We Put Them to the Test

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

From Apple's iPhone Duo to Samsung's and Motorola's foldables, we tested how today's most popular book-style and flip phones hold up under pressure.

For years, foldable phones haven’t exactly been praised for their battery life. However, that’s starting to change.

Because of their unique design, foldables have traditionally struggled to match the battery life of conventional slab phones. Their massive displays, space-consuming hinge mechanisms and limited room for heat dissipation all present challenges. But battery technology has improved in recent years, with some of the newest foldables benefiting from higher-energy-density silicon-carbon batteries and more power-efficient processors. Even slim phones like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 can last all day, showing that you don’t have to sacrifice practicality for a sleek, innovative design.

Still, foldable phones remain a niche category, even with a major player like Apple entering the market with the iPhone Duo. But they offer an appealing alternative for anyone looking to break away from the sameness of more traditional slab phones. And with battery life being a key consideration when choosing a new device, it’s important to know which phone can keep up with all your scrolling, streaming and snapping without constantly reaching for a charger.

We’ve dug into CNET’s extensive smartphone lab data to find out which foldable phone in 2026 delivers the best battery life. Because book-style and flip phones differ in design and screen size, we’re separating the results to provide a more accurate comparison.

Here’s how devices from Samsung, Apple, Google and Motorola stack up.

This year, CNET has reviewed and tested five book-style foldable phones: the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra, Motorola Razr Fold, Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold and the Apple iPhone Duo. These devices are phone-tablet hybrids, with designs ranging from taller, narrower builds to squatter, passport-style designs. (We didn’t include Samsung’s Galaxy Z TriFold because of its unique design.)

Apple’s $1,999 iPhone Duo may be late to the foldable game, arriving seven years after Samsung’s first Galaxy Fold ushered in the modern era of foldable phones. Still, given Apple’s strong brand loyalty and mainstream appeal, the Duo has generated considerable buzz.

And there’s another reason Apple’s first foldable deserves attention: its battery. The iPhone Duo achieved the highest average score in CNET’s testing among book-style phones. It’s a testament to its dual-cell battery design, which is standard in foldables, and the efficiency of the A20 Pro chip powering the device.

To test a phone’s battery, CNET runs a 3-hour streaming video test and a 45-minute endurance test that includes watching videos, scrolling through social media, playing a game and joining a video call. Both tests take place on the foldable phone’s inner screen, starting with a full charge and while connected to Wi-Fi.

The iPhone Duo had the highest remaining charge after the 45-minute endurance test, finishing with 99%. It ended the 3-hour streaming test with 84%, placing it just below the Razr Fold, Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Z Fold 8 Ultra in that category. That average gives the Duo, which has a 4,883-mAh battery, the number-one place in our foldable battery tests.

Not far behind is the Razr Fold, Motorola’s first book-style foldable. This phone has a whopping 6,000-mAh silicon-carbon battery, which helped it earn one of the top spots in our battery testing.

Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, which is the company’s first palm-size foldable phone, just barely tops the more standard-size Z Fold 8 Ultra. Both phones are the thinnest in this ranking, which makes their results even more impressive. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 measures 4.5mm thick when unfolded and 9.7mm when folded, and has a 4,800-mAh silicon-carbon battery. The Z Fold 8 Ultra is 4.1mm thick when open and 8.9mm when closed, and it has a 5,000-mAh silicon-carbon battery.

Close behind the competition is Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which has a 4,806-mAh battery. Like the other phones, including the iPhone Duo, it performed relatively better in the endurance test than in the streaming test. That suggests these devices handle shorter bursts of use well but can take a more noticeable battery hit during prolonged activities like video streaming. Even so, they should easily power through a full day of mixed use, whether you’re watching movies, scrolling through social media or taking photos.

Overall, every book-style foldable we tested demonstrated strong battery results. Beyond the numbers, our hands-on experience suggests you can get through most days without constantly worrying about your phone’s battery level. Be sure to check out CNET’s in-depth reviews for more on the everyday experience using each of these phones.

Some people may prefer the more nostalgic design of a flip phone. Motorola revived its iconic Razr brand for the smartphone era, and now has a handful of devices at varying price points to choose from. Samsung’s Galaxy Z Flip 8 is another pocket-friendly choice.

These clamshell devices have less space for a battery than larger foldable and slab phones. Still, Motorola’s and Samsung’s battery specs are nothing to sniff at.

This year’s $800 Motorola Razr has a 4,800-mAh battery, the $1,100 Razr Plus has a 4,500-mAh battery and the $1,500 Razr Ultra has a 5,000-mAh battery. Meanwhile, the $1,200 Z Flip 8 has a 4,300-mAh battery. Every one of these phones uses a silicon-carbon battery to squeeze more power into a smaller design.

Impressively, the baseline Motorola Razr got the best average score in our battery testing of clamshell phones. It also had the highest result in CNET’s 3-hour streaming test among its peers and tied with the much pricier Razr Ultra in our battery endurance test. The Razr Ultra, Galaxy Z Flip 8 and Razr Plus are in close succession.

Interestingly, the flip phones aren’t that far behind their book-style counterparts in our testing. One key advantage is that their smaller cover and inner displays require less power, helping them keep pace with larger foldables.

The results are also a testament to how battery technology is progressing, with the mobile industry increasingly shifting toward high-density silicon-carbon batteries, which can pack more capacity into tighter dimensions. This means that regardless of whether you choose a book-style or clamshell foldable, you can be assured that your battery won’t leave you in the lurch as you go about your day.

From the newest foldables like the iPhone Duo and Pixel 11 Pro Fold to flip phones from Motorola and Samsung, you no longer have to sacrifice battery life for a more versatile mobile design. Today’s devices can comfortably get you through a full day of swiping, scrolling and snapping photos, even with larger screens to power.

In fact, when ranked among all the phones CNET tested this year, including non-folding options, the iPhone Duo sits among the top five performers, with the iPhone 18 Pro Max taking the top overall spot.

That’s especially important given that a major part of a foldable phone’s appeal is the ability to switch between two displays. You can quickly send a text on a smaller screen, then move to a larger one to watch a movie, for example. That versatility requires a battery capable of handling more intensive tasks like streaming and gaming, as well as extended activities like browsing and working across multiple displays.

And while the iPhone Duo and Motorola Razr topped CNET’s foldable battery tests, the other phones we evaluated weren’t far behind, highlighting just how competitive battery life has become across the leading brands. Ultimately, choosing the right foldable will come down to other factors, including camera performance, design and price.

Our testing data, combined with real-world experiences shared in our in-depth reviews, illustrates just how far foldable phones have evolved. They’re no longer just a novelty; they’ve become increasingly practical devices in their own right.

#3157. Thinking Machines’ new model takes the lead in western open-weight AI

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Another competitive model developed outside of China could change the open-weight landscape.

Thinking Machines Lab, a small AI startup from ex-OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, has released its latest model, Inkling 2 Small — and according to third-party tester Artificial Analysis, it’s set to give Chinese models a run for their lead. It’s technically proprietary until now, but Thinking Machines said it will release its weights next week.

Also: Open weights vs. closed: An AI civil war’s afoot

Chinese companies have led the pack on open models over the last few years. Models from DeepSeek and Moonshot regularly top leaderboards and rival the capabilities of much more expensive, closed models from OpenAI and Anthropic.

Since DeepSeek’s R1 performed similarly to OpenAI’s o1 in January 2025, Chinese open models have given investors and high-paying enterprise customers reasons to rethink their expensive contracts with US-based labs. Western labs creating more competitive open models changes the landscape.

Thinking Machines’ latest model has 594 billion parameters and supports image inputs but outputs only text. The company noted its web and game design capabilities and that it evaluated the model’s approach to coding problems alongside the code it generated during testing.

“The result is a model that is both stronger at coding and easier to use inside real agent loops,” the company said.

Also: Nvidia takes another step forward for US open-weight AI

Inkling 2 Small scored a 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, a composite test “for tracking progress toward artificial general intelligence” that combines benchmark scores spanning coding, science, and general categories. A score of 31 is above average for models in its class and is tied with Gemini 3.8 Flash. For context, Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 top the index at 60 and 59, respectively.

Thinking Machines said it will release the model’s weights next week, a practice that is becoming customary. Given the heightened security concerns around AI in general, AI companies spend a few weeks testing the to-be-open model with cybersecurity teams and safety reviewers before releasing the weights, rather than leading with the weights out of the gate.

French AI lab Mistral recently released its Le Chonk model via the same staggered process — it now keeps pace with OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Terra in coding abilities, which is rare for western-made open models.

Also: Mistral’s Le Chonk is now a top open model for coding

“[Thinking Machines’] plan to release its weights would make it the highest-scoring open weights model developed outside China based on current rankings,” Artificial Analysis said.

“Inkling 2 Small is amongst the leading models in intelligence and reasonably priced when comparing to other models of similar price. It’s also notably slow per task and very verbose,” Artificial Analysis said. The organization also called Inkling 2 Small’s pricing “somewhat expensive” at $0.30 per one million input tokens, since the median cost for its class is $0.24.

Still, the model’s progress over its predecessor stands out to Artificial Analysis reviewers: Inkling 2 Small jumped 41% in automation capabilities and 20% in coding abilities. However, most models excel in certain areas or on specific benchmarks, making it hard to deem one or another the outright best coding model overall.

Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a local AI stack that’s completely free

Inkling 2 Small also made some gains in accuracy, Artificial Analysis said.

“On AA-Omniscience v1.1, the hallucination rate falls from Inkling Small’s 61% to 27%, while accuracy rises from 32% to 34% and the attempt rate falls from 77% to 53%,” its review reported.

#3156. Google’s AI Mode Will Soon Show Ads Even in Your Follow-Up Questions

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Ads will start appearing in AI Mode’s follow-up answers in the US as Google expands AI Mode ads to more countries.

Sponsored results will soon appear in responses to follow-up questions in Google’s AI Mode in the US. Google announced the change, along with plans to show ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode to more people, after reporting that AI Mode searches generate less revenue than traditional searches.

The company says sponsored product listings in AI Mode already get clicked about as often as organic results. For publishers, the change adds paid competition inside AI answers, which a Pew Research Center study last year found already make people less likely to click through to websites.

You’ve probably seen how this works: Type a question into Google, and an AI-generated summary often appears at the top of the page. That can mean fewer clicks on the ads below, which underpin Google’s core revenue.

Now, the tech giant is expanding how and where we see ads when using AI Mode during searches. Google is scaling ads in AI Mode to 10 new countries (including Australia, Canada, India, Kenya and Singapore), with plans to launch in Brazil, Mexico and the UK later this year.

In the US, Google is launching what it calls “multiturn ads,” allowing ads to appear directly within follow-up queries in AI Mode when a search or conversation has “commercial relevance.” Take, for example, if you start a search with “How does a smart fridge work,” and follow up with “What are the best-selling smart fridges?” You could then see refrigerator ads in sections labeled “sponsored.”

Google said that “multiturn ads” can better target what a user wants in a product because AI Mode gathers more information during a back-and-forth conversation. Ads can also appear on initial AI Mode queries, not just after follow-up questions, and sometimes ads won’t appear at all if there doesn’t appear to be purchase intent, according to Google.

But as Google relies more on AI Mode and AI Overview, there’ll be less reason to click on content links “below the fold,” meaning content that sits out of view until a reader scrolls down a web page.

Lily Ray, a well-known SEO expert and founder of Algorythmic, told CNET that it’s going to become harder to use Google to find articles from preferred publishers and articles you want to read directly from a website. “You’ll have to dig deeper and look outside of Google’s products,” Ray said via email.

According to Ray, Google’s AI tools aren’t designed to give you the exact link you’re looking for. Still, you don’t have to rely on AI Mode or AI Overviews to get search results. You can also scroll down to the search results the old-fashioned way or use a web filter to use Google as a list of links. She also recommends setting up your favorite publications as “preferred sources” (instructions here) so you can see more of those pages cited in your personalized results.

“Unless you’re satisfied with AI answers directly on Google, you’re going to need to start evolving your own search behavior to find the websites you’re looking for,” Ray said.

Google is still the largest search engine in the world, accounting for nearly 90% of the global search engine market. In fact, the company said its year-over-year query volume growth in the third quarter was the fastest over the past five years.

But beginning with the launch of AI Overviews in May 2024, Google’s reliance on AI has slowed advertising.

The impact has been even more devastating for online publishers — ranging from major newspapers and digital media sites to brands and trade associations — driving an unprecedented decline in website traffic. AI Overviews now appear on nearly half of Google search queries, with a corresponding 61% drop in raw traffic volume to other pages. Google is effectively scraping publisher information, summarizing it and satisfying the user before they leave the search results page. That’s why it’s often referred to as the “zero-click” crisis.

“AI Mode and AI Overviews answer questions directly in Google’s interface, so there’s less reason for people to click on publishers,” Ray said.

AI Overviews are summary boxes at the top of a traditional search results page, while AI Mode is a conversational interface designed for ongoing dialogue and research. You can access AI Mode directly by selecting the AI Mode button at the far right of the search bar on the Google home page, or by selecting AI Mode in the horizontal menu near the top of other Google pages.

When you use AI Mode, you won’t get an AI Overview or a long list of links to other websites offering more information. Instead, AI Mode provides “more advanced reasoning and ways of interacting” with a conversational approach. For instance, if I use AI Mode and ask, “Where can I see the northern lights?” I get a map and a list of various locations with pros and cons for each. In regular search mode, I get an AI Overview at the top and, below that, pages of links to websites related to my query.

Ray said that with more ads, there’s going to be an even greater decline in organic click-through rates — in publishing speak, that’s the percentage of people who actually click on a natural, nonpaid search engine result, out of the total number of people who simply saw the headline on the page. Not only will the AI text answer your question, but Google will now aggressively route you toward advertisers rather than publisher links.

“Like many things in Google Search, it means that if you’re not participating in Google Ads, it’s going to be harder and harder to get that traffic organically,” said Ray.

#3155. Why Micron Technology Stock Gained On Monday

Micron stock is bouncing back as chip stocks recover from last week's midterm-driven sell-off, but I think the drop showed how much of the share price rests on perception. With data center opposition growing, especially at the local level, I think there's a good chance construction slows enough to matter.

Micron Technology (MU +6.25%) stock jumped 6.3% on Monday, Nov. 9, as chip stocks continue to recover after last week's mid-week sell-off.

The S&P 500 (^GSPC +2.35%) and the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +2.74%) finished up 2.4% and 2.8%, respectively.

The Democratic win in last Tuesday's midterms raised worries about the AI data-center build-out. Many successful candidates ran on promises of increased scrutiny of data center permitting or outright moratoriums on new builds, including candidates in key states like Texas and Ohio.

A slowdown in data center building could mean fewer orders for Micron's precious memory chips.

But beginning Friday and continuing into today, it appeared investors were confident the capex would keep flowing.

Micron's latest quarterly numbers were once again incredibly strong: revenue was up 379% year over year to $54.2 billion.

The business looks as strong as it's ever been, but in my mind, last week's drop shows just how much of the stock price is based on perception. The share price cannot afford a real slowdown in data center building and, despite the recovery, I think there is a good chance we'll see a meaningful impact on construction from political opposition, especially at the local level where voters are especially animated: 40 out of 41 data center measures that were on the ballot last week went the wrong way for the industry.

Johnny Rice has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Micron Technology. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3154. Android is getting my favorite iOS tracking feature – what to expect

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

'Notify when left behind' is making its way to Android - but to limited devices for now.

A much-needed update — “Notify when left behind” — is rolling out to Google’s Find My hub. The feature sends a notification when a registered device is separated from your phone, except when you leave it at your house.

Also: 7 Galaxy settings I always change to boost my battery life

According to 9to5Google, this feature was first previewed in October, with the notification available for Chipolo trackers and Moto Tag.

This feature is not yet available for other peripherals such as headphones. I tried to see if my Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones or Google Pixel Buds Pro 2 have it — they don’t. Hopefully, support is on the way. In the meantime, here’s what we know.

“Notify when left behind” is my all-time favorite device tracking feature on iOS. Any device set up on my Find My network is compatible with this feature, including my MacBook Air, AirPods Pro 3, and Apple Watch, three devices I often take out of the house — and have indeed left behind once or twice.

Also: Google’s Pixel Tag tracker has a big advantage over AirTags

If these devices are separated from my phone in an unsaved location, I’ll get a notification of which device I left and where. In iOS, you can customize which locations are “safe,” and won’t notify you if you leave them there.

On Android, this feature is currently limited to only notifying you when a device is left at a location other than the home address registered to your Google account. Hopefully, location customization is on the horizon.

#3151. Biotech stocks are surging. How investors can play the new drug innovation boom

Moderna gave investors a scare as its stock plunged on Thursday. But it's still one of the hottest biotechs this year. And it's hardly alone – the sector is on a roll and looks poised for more gains.

The iShares Biotechnology ETF (IBB) is up 24% through October 23, building on a 28% gain in 2025. Two dozen of the ETF's 233 holdings have more than doubled year-to-date. Moderna leads the pack with a 587% surge — even after an 18% decline following a leak of clinical data for its cancer vaccine (which was actually positive).

Analysts say a new biotech cycle is underway, fueled by clinical trial results, M&A activity, and promising technologies such as genomics, mRNA — and AI.

"We're in the midst of a powerful innovation cycle," said John Hall, portfolio manager of the T. Rowe Price Biotechnology ETF. "What's super exciting is we're seeing newer modalities start to make it to market." Companies "understand the disease biology better," he adds, and that could ultimately lead to more novel drugs making it to market.

Investors are excited about technologies like mRNA and genomics, along with a steady stream of new drug approvals. The FDA approved about a dozen novel biologic drugs in 2025, out of 46 approvals in total. Roughly 66 novel drugs are in the pipeline for FDA approval, including potential blockbusters like Moderna and Merck's cancer drug for melanoma, and a next-generation obesity drug from Eli Lilly.

Analysts say AI could also lead to more approvals as companies deploy the software to speed up drug development.

"Biotech is a phenomenal application for artificial intelligence and machine learning," says Piper Sandler analyst Ted Tenthoff. "You can set up exciting predictive models that, frankly, can do things that we've never been able to do in the space in terms of novel drug discovery."

Granted, the industry is recovering from a fallow period. The sector's last strong performance was during the Covid era when ultra-low interest rates encouraged investment in early-stage drug developers, and mRNA vaccines fueled a revenue surge for companies like Moderna, Pfizer and Biontech.

The sector then went cold as many early-stage companies fizzled. Demand for Covid vaccines evaporated, and surging interest rates put a chill in IPOs and M&A.

The risks haven't evaporated – this is still a sector whose products take years to develop, resulting in far more failures than successes. But analysts say the outlook is healthier now. While that's reflected in strong performance and richer valuations, there's still good reason to invest.

Recent clinical trial results are stoking excitement that novel drugs in the works could tackle some of the toughest problems in medicine.

Moderna and Merck's melanoma drug, for instance, uses mRNA to trigger an immune response in patients, targeting tumors that have been surgically removed and genetically analyzed. It's not a preventive vaccine, but it uses a similar immunology mechanism and showed a 42% reduction in cancer recurrence or death (used in conjunction with Merck's cancer drug Keytruda).

While the Phase 3 results disappointed Wall Street, oncologists say the outcomes were still highly positive. And they see the technology as a potential game changer, ushering in an era of personalized treatments for cancers. Moderna and Merck have said they aim to submit the drug for FDA approval and get it launched in 2027.

Inflammation treatment is another promising area. AstraZeneca and Amgen recently released positive Phase 3 results for another use for their drug Tezspire, an injectable approved for nasal polyps and asthma. In clinical trials, it showed that it successfully relieved swallowing symptoms and healed microscopic and visual tissue damage in patients with severe throat inflammation.

Roche, meanwhile, notched a win after the FDA approved its drug Enspryng, a therapy to treat rare inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. It became the first and only at-home injection for adults with thyroid eye disease.

Obesity drugs are also advancing beyond the first generation of GLP-1s. Eli Lilly's retatrutide, a "triple agonist" targeting three different hormone receptors, cleared two more clinical trials over the summer. The drug produced 28%-30% weight loss at the highest doses in the study, Lilly said. The company plans to submit the drug for FDA approval in the first quarter of 2027.

Much of the innovation isn't just happening in drug-making – it's also in areas like gene sequencing, mRNA, and high-tech instruments.

Illumina has more than doubled this year. The DNA and gene sequencing company is seeing accelerating demand for its NovaSeq X high-end sequencing platform. Pharmaceutical companies including Bristol-Myers Squibb, Merck and Kura are working with Illumina to develop precision oncology solutions.

Another big winner is 10x Genomics, up more than 300%. The biotech firm offers its lab instruments to help scientists research cancer, immunology and neuroscience. The company's Atera platform is helping produce data sets to train AI models, a process that helps accelerate personalized therapies.

On the AI front, companies are using the technology for more efficient drug discovery, says Shreefāl Mehta, president of Guidant BioTherapeutics. Using AI, "you can now bring a drug to clinical trials with less capital. More investment is also going into companies that are demonstrating that," he said.

Global AI in drug discovery will grow from a $20 billion market in 2025 to more than $160 billion by 2035, according to forecasts by Towards Health, a research and consulting firm.

One other catalyst for the sector could be M&A. Dealmaking for biopharma hit $134 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $112 billion for all of 2025, notes Jeet Mukherjee, biotech analyst at BTIG. That's a positive signal, indicating more drugs in development are showing clinical promise.

It also helps that Big Pharma has a "patent cliff" ahead. Products representing $180 billion of revenue will lose exclusivity by 2030, according to research firm RTW Institute. Companies with looming expiries "are looking for novel products and innovative products to put into their pipeline," Mehta says.

GLP-1 blockbusters have also left some companies flush with cash for acquisitions. Eli Lilly alone has completed 10 acquisition deals in 2026 worth $25 billion.

ETFs can capture the investing theme, though they aren't all alike. The iShares Biotech ETF is one of the lower cost funds. It tracks a market-cap weighted index of biotech stocks, led by companies like Gilead Sciences, Amgen, Vertex Pharmaceuticals, and Moderna.

The State Street SPDR S&P Biotech ETF holds stocks in equal weight, offering more exposure to small- and mid-cap names. Its top holdings are Moderna, Natera, Twist Bioscience and Halozyme Therapeutics.

Piper Sandler calls Illumina and 10x Genomics the "primary infrastructure plays" in the life science arena, saying their technologies are "driving the next generation of precision medicine."

Piper analyst David Westenberg has a buy rating and $305 target on Illumina, implying 14% gains from recent prices around $267. He has a hold rating on 10X with an $80 target, above recent prices around $70.

Twist Bioscience is another name to consider. The company makes customized synthetic DNA and sells DNA sequencing tools. Twist has partnered with Eli Lilly's AI and machine-learning platform and linked up with Anthropic in August to start testing its AI model, Claude, for protein development.

Twist isn't expected to turn an EPS profit until 2029, according to consensus forecasts. But revenue is expected to go from $572 million in 2027 to $833 million in 2029. Analysts have an average target of $168 on the stock, implying 21% returns from recent prices around $138.

In the small-cap space, Piper Sandler's Tenthoff likes Monte Rosa Therapeutics, a pioneer in protein degradation that selectively destroys disease-causing proteins.

The firm has partnered with Novartis to develop a drug for inflammatory conditions and autoimmune diseases. The companies announced a Phase 2 clinical study in September for an autoimmune disease treatment, which has been "triggering milestones to Monte Rosa," Tenthoff said.

Tenthoff has a buy rating and $37 target on the stock, which recently traded around $10.70.

Also in the small-cap arena, BTIG's Mukherjee recommends Faeth Therapeutics.

The biotech is developing a novel two-drug regimen to treat breast cancer and other tumors. The regimen "has the potential to address safety and dosing limitations of another recently approved drug for breast cancer," he says. And it could become "a mainstay of the future breast cancer treatment paradigm and other cancers."

Faeth is a clinical-stage company that has yet to bring a drug to market. Yet the stock is up 93% year-to-date on positive clinical trial results, trading around $18. Mukherjee has a $55 target on it.

Kymera Therapeutics is worth considering too. The company is developing an oral version of the blockbuster drug Dupixent (made and co-developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals and Sanofi). Dupixent is an injectable, however, and oral agents "are frequently preferred by patients," Mukherjee says. "The drug has the potential to not only take share from patients taking Dupixent for numerous immunological diseases but also expanding the market to those not taking systemic biologic drugs," he tells CNBC.

Kymera has said it doesn't expect a patent fight over Dupixent because its drug is distinct, not a biosimilar or biologic copy.

T. Rowe's Hall also likes Kymera for its potential "to unlock disease targets that have been classically considered un-druggable." The stock is the second largest holding in T. Rowe's Biotech ETF, accounting for 4.2% of the portfolio.

#3150. Prediction: This Will Be the Price of Bitcoin by the End of 2030

Even if Bitcoin's annual growth rate slows, it could still hit a price of $150,000 in four years.

If you're a Bitcoin (BTC -0.12%) investor, it may be time to tamp down your expectations. The days of triple-digit annual growth may be over, and that means it could be time to put those spectacular $1 million price predictions for Bitcoin on the shelf.

As Bitcoin becomes increasingly mainstream, it's starting to behave more like a traditional financial asset. If that's the case, then the price of Bitcoin by the end of 2030 should stay below $150,000. Here's the math behind that prediction.

Given Bitcoin's steep 40% decline over the past 12 months, it's easy to see why investors, analysts, and crypto insiders are now ratcheting down their future price targets for Bitcoin. Even Michael Saylor of Strategy (MSTR -2.59%) -- arguably the biggest Bitcoin bull on the planet -- is now suggesting that the world's most popular cryptocurrency may face difficulties getting back to $100,000.

For now, the best prediction about where Bitcoin is headed next comes from JPMorgan Chase. According to the base case scenario from JPMorgan Asset Management, Bitcoin will grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 10% over the next 10 years. In a bull-case scenario, Bitcoin will "only" grow at a 17% CAGR.

That might sound modest compared to Bitcoin's historic boom-and-bust cycles, but don't let the calmer numbers fool you. Here's the thing: That 10% growth rate is far better than stocks, bonds, or gold will deliver over the next decade. In fact, JPMorgan Chase predicts that Bitcoin will be the top-performing asset class over the next decade.

Unfortunately, that performance comes at a steep cost: extreme volatility. These won't be steady 10% returns, cranked out year after year. Instead, due to Bitcoin's highly cyclical nature, there could be some years when Bitcoin skyrockets in value and others when it collapses.

So let's run the numbers. If Bitcoin ends the year at its current price (roughly $75,000), then a 10% annualized growth rate will only take Bitcoin to $110,000 in four years. However, if Bitcoin grows according to JPMorgan Asset Management's bull case scenario, then Bitcoin could soar even higher.

I'm inclined to favor the higher 17% growth rate in the bull case scenario. Historically, Bitcoin reaches a new all-time high every new four-year cycle, and that means it's likely headed higher than its current all-time high of $126,000.

If Bitcoin can make it back to $80,000 by the end of this year, then a 17% annualized growth rate will take it to $150,000. Sentiment in the crypto industry can turn on a dime, and I'm fully expecting crypto investors to return as soon as Bitcoin begins to move higher.

JPMorgan Chase is an advertising partner of Motley Fool Money. Dominic Basulto has positions in Bitcoin. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Bitcoin and JPMorgan Chase. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3149. Alpine Linux and OpenSSH patch flaw that’s as bad as it can get

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

This dangerous Linux security hole must be patched as soon as possible.

The perfect nightmare scenario for a Linux server is when all an attacker needs to do is reach the server’s Secure Shell (SSH) port, waltz right in, and take it over. That’s what happened to Alpine Linux, the popular, lightweight Linux server. Adding insult to injury, this happened only days after Alpine Linux dodged a security hole-sized bullet to its GitLab implementation.

Also: Linux Mint 27 arrives next month, and I like it already: What to expect

How bad is it? As bad as it can get. Alpine Linux explained in its security advisory that if an attacker can reach a vulnerable server’s SSH port, they can get in “with one connection,” and the attack “works every time, and needs no retries.”

As security engineer Gregory Bryant explained in his LinkedIn post:

Most authentication bypasses come from complex logic chains, but yesterday’s Alpine Linux OpenSSH vulnerability (CVE-2026-123158) comes down to a single character: *.”

If you run Alpine Linux (or another musl-based distro) with the default openssh-server package (no Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM)) and PasswordAuthentication enabled, an attacker can log into password-disabled, or key-only accounts simply by sending a password between 257 and 1024 bytes long.

Alpine Linux isn’t the only operating system that uses musl, a lightweight version of the standard C library (libc). Other operating systems that use musl and are potentially vulnerable include Adélie Linux; Void Linux; Sabotage Linux; OpenWrt, an Android variant,  and the Yocto Project, which is used to build embedded Linux distributions.

Also: This clever banking scam keeps phishing by faking its own demise

Wind River, which produces the commercial embedded Linux distro, Wind River Linux, is also looking into the issue. A company representative told me, “Wind River takes security seriously. We are actively reviewing the reported vulnerability and assessing its potential impact. We will take appropriate action as needed.”

Behind the scenes, when OpenSSH is built without PAM, it verifies passwords by hashing the password attempt using the C library’s crypt() function. It then compares the result to the account’s stored password field. So far, so good.

But when a key is longer than 256 bytes, musl’s crypt() function returns the string * as an error indicator. That is also what the password field holds for any account with no password, such as a key-only account. Thus, the “hash” matches and the login succeeds, and the attacker walks in.

Also: The new Cutefish Linux distro might be the best MacOS clone around

To exploit it, an attacker only needs the name of such an account. The attacker also needs at least one other account on the machine with a 5 or 6 password hash, and then to send a password of 257 to 1,024 bytes. According to Alpine, one user with a password is enough to make every passwordless account accessible.

In Linux systems that use glibc’s crypt(), which is almost all of them, the same attempt would return NULL on error, which sshd already rejects, so Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, etc., aren’t affected.

According to *sshole, the group that uncovered the problem, this is a side effect that has been hiding since 2016.

Alpine said every release it checked is affected: 3.21 through 3.24, edge, and the older 3.16 to 3.20 branches. Exposure requires the following:

Root is not directly exposed in most cases. It has shipped as root:* in the base image since about Alpine 3.16, but OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password blocks it. Another account that can become root, for example through doas, still gives an attacker a route to root.

Alpine singled out its official tiny-cloud images, versions 3.18.11 through 3.24.3, as especially vulnerable. These ship with an alpine user with a * password field and passwordless doas. They are safe on first boot but become exploitable once any 6 hash exists on the machine. That can happen when an administrator sets a console password or when user data adds a user with a hashed password, which means, essentially, all of them.

Alpine released 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 on Thursday, with the OpenSSH fix among the security changes. It also published fixed packages for each release back to 3.16. Alpine 3.21 reached end of support on Nov. 1.

The just-released OpenSSH 10.6p2 avoids the problem in sshd. Alpine’s stable branches carry a patch for the same problem. You should run apk upgrade -U -a and then restart the daemon with rc-service sshd restart. Alpine stressed that upgrading the package does not replace the running daemon. Anyone who cannot update should set PasswordAuthentication no and restart sshd, after confirming that key login works.

Also: Maze Linux is the best security-focused distro I’ve ever tested

To check for an attack, Alpine told administrators to search /var/log/messages for “Accepted password for” lines that name an account with no password. It also advised reviewing dedicated OpenBSD application subexecutor (doas) use and recently created users, files, and authorized keys. “If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised.” Just what you wanted for your weekend, I know, but here we are.

#3148. Uber Parking Lets You Book a Spot Directly in the App. Here’s How

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The new feature is launching in 15 cities before expanding across the US and Canada. It follows Uber's acquisition of SpotHero earlier this year.

Uber is adding a parking reservation option directly within its app.

The rollout of Uber Parking, announced on Monday, comes after the ride-hailing platform’s acquisition of SpotHero earlier this year. Now, you can reserve a parking spot from the Uber app homepage, alongside existing options to book a ride, rent a car or order a meal.

Uber says its acquisition of SpotHero is bringing more than 13,000 garages, lots and valet options across more than 400 cities onto Uber’s platform. The SpotHero brand and app won’t go away, though customers might see branding for SpotHero by Uber on garage signage, for example.

At launch, Uber Parking is available in 15 cities, including Chicago, Nashville, San Francisco, Atlanta, Austin, Boston, Dallas, Denver, Los Angeles, Miami, New York City, Philadelphia, San Diego, Seattle and Washington, DC.

“Our mission is to help people get around, and this seemed like a very natural thing for us to solve, given how painful parking is today,” Amit Fulay, vice president of product at Uber, said in an interview. “If we can bring that ease that we have for rides into the app, it fits with helping people move. It felt like a very natural extension.”

Uber One members will get 10% back in credits on eligible completed parking reservations, which they can use on future rides and Uber Eats orders. (Uber One costs $10 per month.)

To reserve a spot with Uber Parking, open the Uber app and tap the new Parking icon on the home screen. Enter your destination, and choose a date and time. You’ll then be able to see available nearby parking options via an interactive map, which will show pricing upfront.

You can filter for options like self-parking or valet, as well as a garage or surface lot. You can also select amenities such as on-site staff or re-entry capability.

Fill out your vehicle information, including make, model and license plate number. As with booking a ride, you’ll be able to pay using a payment method in your Uber Wallet.

You’ll then be able to access your “Parking pass” in the Uber app. Depending on where you park, you’ll either scan a QR code or use license plate recognition to get in. You can extend your reservation in the app if you end up staying longer than expected.

Uber says that with most parking options, you can cancel your booking for free before the start time.

Over the coming weeks and months, Uber Parking will expand from 15 launch cities to over 400 across the US and Canada, according to the company.

Uber Parking is the latest example of how the ride-hailing company aims to be known for much more than just that. Uber now has options for everything from car and bike rentals to hotel reservations to food delivery through Uber Eats. The addition of Uber Parking gives people another reason to open the app and, importantly, give more of their dollars to Uber.

The Uber One subscription service is another way the company has worked to entice customers. It includes no delivery fee on food and grocery orders, 5% back on rides and 10% back on hotel bookings, among other perks. Uber says it has over 55 million Uber One members across 47 countries.

Uber’s new parking venture feeds into another area the company is heavily investing in: autonomous vehicles. With more than 30 AV partners, Uber says it plans to “explore leveraging parking spots as staging and waiting locations for AVs, which can reduce deadheading, congestion and vehicle wear while improving fleet efficiency.”

Fulay notes that this network can also be useful for delivery drivers working in areas where parking is difficult to find, or for those with downtime who need a convenient place to stop for a while in dense urban areas.

“Once we have this infrastructure, those are the next set of things we’ll look to explore,” Fulay said.

Ultimately, offering a service within an app consumers likely already have on their phones could make them more inclined to stick with a single company. Uber appears to be betting on just that.

#3143. Samsung’s new SmartTag 3 debuts with next-gen Bluetooth – and one big problem

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The Galaxy SmartTag 3 supports emerging Bluetooth tracking tech, but it's not a match for Samsung's OS exclusivity.

Samsung’s Galaxy SmartTag 3 is now available for purchase in the US, promising a smaller, lighter design than previous generations, compatibility with iOS devices, 550 days of battery life, an NFC-powered Lost Mode, Left Behind Alerts, and an IP67 dust- and water-resistant rating.

Though the Galaxy SmartTag 3 is compatible with iOS devices, the features available to Apple fans are limited, with Ring Phone, Left Behind Alerts, and Compass View reserved for Galaxy users. Compass View is enabled by Bluetooth Channel Sounding, an upgraded Bluetooth distance-finding technology. Despite Samsung embracing a low-cost boost to device tracking, Channel Sounding is locked inside the Galaxy ecosystem, a blow to the technology’s intended purpose.

Also: 3 ways Bluetooth 7 upgrades your devices beyond lossless audio

Channel Sounding is also Google’s Pixel Tag and Motorola’s Moto Tag 2, but these manufacturers open the technology to all compatible Android phones. However, Samsung’s SmartTag 3 doesn’t rely on Android’s vast but fragmented Find My Device network; instead, Samsung’s take on Channel Sounding will rely exclusively on the Galaxy Find Network. If a semi-closed ecosystem can help make evolving Bluetooth tech more reliable, does it matter that its implementation is counterproductive?

Samsung is the Goldilocks of device ecosystems. It’s not considered a walled garden like Apple, but it’s not as open to full third-party interoperability as Google. Many of Samsung’s most useful features are reserved for use within its Galaxy ecosystem. However, Samsung’s OS is built on top of Android, allowing for more flexibility than iOS, but still offering OS-exclusive features and, more importantly, feature reliability.

Full access to Samsung’s Galaxy Find Network is exclusive to Galaxy devices, similar to how full access to Apple’s Find My tracking features is reserved for Apple devices. On the other hand, Google’s Find Hub can accommodate Android phones from several manufacturers, including Samsung.

Also: Android is getting my favorite iOS tracking feature – what to expect

According to a press release, nearly 900 million Galaxy devices exist on the Galaxy Find Network. Each one’s constant Bluetooth signals contribute to an expansive network of crowdsourced data, extending the Galaxy FindTag 3’s reach and surfacing location data faster.

Google’s Find Hub’s greatest benefit is its scale: it can work with headphones, earbuds, Bluetooth trackers, smartphones, and smartwatches from multiple manufacturers.

However, different ecosystems limit tracking features to basic functionality, showing only where a device was last seen before it was powered off, or emitting a chime if you lose it. Live location data and accurate direction and distance finding from your smartphone aren’t possible.

Also: Apple has a Bluetooth problem, and Android is taking advantage

Implementing Bluetooth Channel Sounding aims to break down ecosystem-specific barriers, especially in a device-tracking context. If your smartphone, headphones, and smartwatch all support Channel Sounding, you could access fine-ranging tracking on all of them, regardless of device manufacturer.

Despite Samsung’s ecosystem providing it a device-tracking advantage, it defeats the purpose of Bluetooth: democratization. Basic Bluetooth connectivity allows any Bluetooth-compatible device to connect to another; that’s why you can wirelessly pair a pair of AirPods with a Lenovo laptop.

Also: Google’s Pixel Tag tracker has a big advantage over AirTags

Channel Sounding’s goal is no different in that it aims to bring more accurate distance awareness to Bluetooth-enabled devices, allowing you to finely track a pair of Sony headphones with an iPhone — that’s the goal, but not yet reality.

Samsung instead adopted Channel Sounding for its first consumer-ready endpoint within the boundaries of its ecosystem. Only Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy S26 Ultra, and Galaxy S26 Plus users can unlock the Galaxy SmartTag 3’s Channel Sounding capabilities when engaging its Compass View feature.

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

All of these phones support Bluetooth 6.0 and Channel Sounding, but the Galaxy SmartTag 3’s Channel Sounding abilities will only be available to them and future Galaxy phones with Channel Sounding.

Conversely, Google’s Pixel Tag offers Channel Sounding to all Android phones that support it, including Galaxy phones. The result is that the Galaxy SmartTag 3 will operate just like any other Bluetooth tracker when paired with a base-model flagship phone, an older Galaxy phone, or an iPhone.

During this year’s WWDC, Apple announced Channel Sounding support for iPhones with its N1 networking chip and third-party Bluetooth 6.3 devices. Bluetooth 6.3 devices aren’t on the market yet and won’t be for a few years.

I assume Apple’s announcement of faraway future support is to give itself time to decide how Channel Sounding will fit into its walled garden, similar to Samsung’s implementation in the Galaxy SmartTag 3.

Also: How to tell if a hidden AirTag is tracking you – and disable it ASAP

Sure, Google’s Find Hub still needs some maturing; just last year, Google boosted the opt-in opportunities to add more devices for crowdsourced data, Find People is coming to Wear OS, and Find Hub is getting “Notify when left behind” alerts soon.

Apple’s and Samsung’s device location networks may be more feature-rich thanks to their closed ecosystems, but Google is working toward a truly open, easy-to-use network of devices powered by Channel Sounding. Which one is more important to you is for you to decide when it’s time to make a purchase.

#3141. 3 High-Yield Dividend Stocks to Buy Now and 2 to Avoid Despite the Yield

Three consumer stocks yield up to 4.4% and keep raising the payout. Two others yield more, and that is exactly the problem.

A high dividend yield is either a gift or a warning, and the number itself will not tell you which. Yield is just the payout divided by the share price, so it can go up for two very different reasons: either because a company keeps raising the dividend or because investors keep selling the stock. The first kind of yield is earned. The second kind is a value trap wearing a nice suit.

The way to tell them apart is to look past the percentage at what the company is doing. Is it growing earnings faster than the dividend, launching products, winning customers? Or is it holding the payout flat and hoping nobody notices the business shrinking underneath it? Three consumer companies below pass that test. Two do not.

PepsiCo (PEP +0.38%) yields about 4.4% at a share price near $141, the highest it has been in years, and it has raised its dividend for 54 consecutive years. This 50+ year increase makes this company a Dividend King. The payout is $1.48 a quarter, up 4% this year. What makes the yield earned rather than suspicious is what the company did in October: It renewed its beverage deal with Taco Bell for another 11 years, days after losing KFC's fountains to Coca-Cola (KO +0.38%), which told you how hard PepsiCo will fight for the accounts it still has. Third-quarter revenue grew 5.6% to $25.3 billion, and management said it will take "additional structural cost reduction actions" to fund growth.

Best Buy (BBY +6.68%) pays $0.96 a quarter, has raised the dividend for 21 straight years, and yields close to 4%. The reason to own this company now is that the business turned a corner this summer. Q2 comparable sales rose 4.1% against a company forecast of about 1%, and Best Buy raised its full-year sales and earnings outlook. Newer categories like AI-powered glasses and trading cards more than doubled, per Bloomberg. In October, the company launched Best Buy Gamers, a dedicated gaming hub, ahead of a holiday season with Grand Theft Auto VI on the calendar.

Philip Morris International (PM -2.40%) yields about 3.2%, lower than the other two, but it just raised the dividend 8.8% to $1.60 a quarter, its 17th straight annual increase. That raise is funded by a company that reported record quarterly revenue, gross profit, and operating income in October. The smoke-free business, built on IQOS heated tobacco and ZYN nicotine pouches, now accounts for more than 40% of revenue, and operating income grew 14%. The payout ratio is high at around 90% of reported earnings, which would be a worry if profits were flat. They are not: Operating income grew 14% last quarter and adjusted earnings rose 5%.

Kraft Heinz (KHC -0.77%) yields about 6.5%, and on a screen it looks like the best deal on this list. It is not. The quarterly dividend has been $0.40 since the company cut it in 2019, seven years without a raise. Q3 net sales fell 2% and adjusted operating income fell 15%. The plan to split the company in two, announced last year, was put on pause in February. The yield is high because the stock has fallen to about $24 while the payout sat still. That is the second kind of yield, and the only thing it tells you is that the market expects less from this business, not more.

Universal Corp. (UVV -1.78%) is the world's largest supplier of leaf tobacco, and it yields about 8.4% after 56 straight years of dividend increases, which is why it shows up on so many income lists. (Incidentally, its record of dividend increases makes Universal Corp. a Dividend King.) The first quarter of its fiscal year told a different story: Revenue fell 12%, the company posted a net loss, and management blamed an oversupply of tobacco that has customers delaying purchases. The dividend now costs several times what the company earned over the past year. A 56-year streak is impressive, but a streak does not pay the dividend. Earnings do, and right now there are not enough of them.

Micah Zimmerman has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Best Buy. The Motley Fool recommends Kraft Heinz and Philip Morris International. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3140. Bluetooth Core 7.0 Speeds Are Set to Quadruple in 2027, Especially for Audio

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The Bluetooth Group has announced a new standard. Here's how it works and when you can expect to benefit from it.

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Wireless tech is about to get a whole lot snappier. On Thursday, the Bluetooth Special Interest Group, the trade association that oversees Bluetooth, officially unveiled Bluetooth High Data Throughput, a flagship upgrade set to arrive as part of the Bluetooth Core 7.0 standard. The revision supercharges Bluetooth Low Energy by pushing maximum bit rates to 7.5Mbps, effectively quadrupling the throughput of the existing LE 2M technology. Compatible devices are slated to hit store shelves starting in 2027.

That’s good news for phone users, tablet havers, laptop groupies, smart speaker stans and more. Bluetooth is still the most popular medium-to-short-range wireless standard for connecting devices. But this is a big rollout, and the changes will start with premium wireless, such as earbuds, with other applications following.

Those other applications could include spatial computing, exchanging AI-related info with local devices, connecting to health wearables and a host of smart home applications, like playing Spotify through an Amazon Echo Studio or dimming a smart bulb.

“In practical terms, a smartwatch could sync hours of sensor-rich training data to a phone in seconds. A smart home product could complete a firmware update with little visible downtime,” Damon Barnes, Director of Technical Marketing at the Bluetooth Special Interest Group, told CNET. “Smart glasses and other AI-enabled devices could exchange more data with a companion device or the cloud. And in audio, the additional capacity can support richer experiences, including high-resolution, lossless, surround, and spatial audio.”

A representative from the Bluetooth Special Interest Group didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The biggest change in this update is a new physical layer for Bluetooth. Layers are like different sections of the Bluetooth protocol, and the physical layer is the bedrock of the standard, the foundational layer involved in transmitting and receiving data signals.

Improvements in the physical layer can have very significant effects on all Bluetooth communications. In this case, new modulation schemes let the physical layer handle data more efficiently and transmit more data at once, which is why the speed increases are so significant.

These improvements also make the new standard more efficient, saving battery life in many applications. So your smart lock may last longer before you need to exchange the AA batteries, earbuds won’t need to go back in the case as fast, and so on.

We know the first flagship devices are expected to appear with the technology in early 2027, but don’t have an exact date.

Barnes also told use that since the update is starting with wireless audio, the first devices to see it will be headphones, earbuds and speakers.

With protocol changes like this, it can take some time for new products to reach the market, and manufacturers may take a long time, even years, to adopt it.

The requirements have changed little since last year, aside from the new minimum software requirement. The new instructions for wired Android Auto support are straightforward: Phones must be running Android 11 (Red Velvet Cake) or newer, have an active data plan, and be supported by a compatible car. Google also recommends a quality USB cable.

Android Auto is integrated into compatible phones, so you do not need to download it. Android Auto isn’t available on devices that run Android (Go edition).
