Travis Hoium: Matt, how do you think about this with the whole industry? Because it seems like three years ago, it seems like Nvidia is going to win everything related to artificial intelligence. It doesn't appear that that's going to be the case, whether that's something like TPUs, which is getting attention. But also these custom chips, I think that's really going to be interesting over the next year or two from OpenAI. Then you have the big choke point, which is TSMC. TSMC doesn't just want to be Nvidia shop. If Nvidia chips are undersupplied, that could partly be because TSMC wants to allocate to Broadcom and to Google and to OpenAI and all these other companies.

Matt Frankel: You just said some of this was out of necessity. It's not just the strategy of being an agnostic player. It's necessity. There aren't enough chips to go around. If you're sticking to Nvidia chips, it really limits how fast you can build your data centers out. Oracle’s edge is being able to build their data centers fast and deliver on that backlog that everyone’s so worried about. Being chip-agnostic, it widens their customer pool. Like you said, it reduces their dependence on any one supplier. It also deepens that relationship with OpenAI, which is half of their backlog. By using their chips, you're making them happy. Making a company happy who is committed to paying you $300 billion for your services is a pretty smart strategic move.

Travis Hoium: Lou, if you're an Nvidia shareholder right now, what are you thinking about news like this?

Lou Whiteman: Again, I think we're in this weird state where the best growth days related to AI are over, but that doesn't mean the music has stopped. I think we actually have seen this in the last few quarters, just the market's reaction. The sense is that I think Nvidia can sustain these elevated numbers that we've seen, but maybe we're not going to see them keep growing the same way. That's not ideal for a shareholder, but it's fine. I can deal with that. As long as it's not falling off a cliff, I think they'll be fine.

Travis Hoium: Are we starting to see the shape of what this market will actually look like in the future? It seems like a few years ago, it was just all Gaga growth, buy Nvidia chips as fast as you can. Now, it seems like companies are starting to think about, where do we want to be strategically long term? What Cloud infrastructure companies do we want to have as our counterparties? What chips do we want to be using? It seems like it's much more of a we talked about maturation in relation to Robinhood, but it seems like this is a more mature decisions on the part of all these AI players diversifying, commoditizing your complements. If you have the power, you can do those kinds of things.

Lou Whiteman: I don't know if we're mature yet. I think we are still in a land grab, but the land grab is shifting. I think the big thing that this comes back to is that there is a focus now on efficiency, overall spending. Like how can we spend smart versus just get anything out there before? Yes, the market is evolving. I think I'd be surprised if we are at its solid state yet. I think we still have evolutions to go, but that's where we are now.

Matt Frankel: I would agree with that and I would also point out that, with Oracle, one, their Investor Day is today. We got a lot of clarity on their chip strategy and things like that. We don't know their financial strategy, which is really to tie it back into what you were saying. That's the part that we don't know where it's not mature. We don't know what the financing is going to look like. These companies are going to have to find more capital-light ways to do what they're doing in a lot of cases. You can't just exponentially grow your borrowing, even if you're a Google or a Microsoft or whatever. I think we're not at maturity yet. There's a lot of unknowns, maybe not as many as two years ago. But in terms of how all this is being paid for, I think we're still in the very early stages of answering that question.

Travis Hoium: We are going to learn more even after the market closes today when Microsoft reports earnings. We'll talk about their recent layoffs in a month.

Travis Hoium: Welcome back to the show. Matt Frankel: The 60,000 number, take that with a big grain of salt. That's who's eligible for this voluntary exit offer. It's not going to be nearly that many. I would expect the actual number to be a fraction of that 60,000. That would represent 27% of their workforce. They don't want 27% of their workforce to leave at the same time. The real thing here is at one AI is replacing some work, so there's that narrative that we need fewer people. A lot of companies, Block has done layoffs and blamed it on that recently On the other hand, companies like Microsoft and I talked about this in the last segment are going to have to figure out how to pay for all their AI build-out. They don't want to just grow their debt forever and ever. They don't want to dilute shareholders forever and ever. Reducing headcount is a way to free up capital to pay for the AI build-out. It serves two purposes. I'm curious as to what the real number is going to be, but it's a sign that big tech has to find ways to pay for this.

Travis Hoium: This is a strategy that Oracle has also deployed to a company that we just talked about.

Lou Whiteman: As Matt said, this isn't a layoff. Maybe it's like Gwyneth Paltrow. It's a conscious uncoupling or something like that. We need better words for this, but we need to underline what Matt said, because, yes, they are offering this to 60,000 people. There is no way in heck they want anything near there. You offer this broadly so you get some. It's going to be well short of that. I think that needs to be said. These are always interesting, though, buyouts, because you tend to sometimes lose the people you want to keep, so you have to be careful there, like the ones who are confident enough to get another job. Sometimes the first one's out the door, but it is just a way to thin the headcount. I'll say, too, I don't know what to think. But even if all 60,000 leave, Microsoft would still have a higher headcount than they did in 2019. There was a lot of bloat during the pandemic. We've talked about this forever, but to some extent, this is using AI to reverse that bloat, and all of these layoffs have been. I don't think we can say this proves that they are seeing efficiency up. I certainly don't think that's true of the overall economy. There was just an apographic out that yes, revenue per worker is up at the Mag 7 since 2022. But adjusted for inflation. The S&P 493, the rest, they have not seen any revenue per worker gains since pre-COVID. Maybe it's coming, but I think it's much too early to say, oh, this is relevant or this is signal as far as how AI is doing. I just don't think we know yet.

#3137. Ready for a Siri AI agent? Apple under pressure to upgrade its assistant faster

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Smart Home > Smart Assistants

Apple's public-facing satisfaction with the Siri AI launch obscures internal pressures and tensions.

Apple’s recently appointed CEO, John Ternus, is allegedly pushing the company internally to ramp up its AI strategy — including making Siri an AI agent.

Also: My 5 favorite Siri AI ‘onscreen awareness’ tricks

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the CEO is publicly pleased with the Siri AI launch, but privately encouraging Craig Federighi, Apple’s SVP of software engineering, to move faster.

“Desiring more and frustrated by what he sees as a reluctance to embrace AI with the same urgency as competitors, Ternus pushed his software chief to accelerate the company’s road map and move quickly beyond merely making necessary improvements to Siri,” Gurman wrote. He added that the tension stems from Federighi’s reputation as an AI skeptic.

The revamped Siri AI is now a much better voice assistant with some helpful features. Gurman noted he thinks Siri AI’s ability to automatically fix your weak passwords is already somewhat agentic behavior, though AI-generated passwords have their own issues.

But Siri AI isn’t yet on par with increasingly autonomous agents from AI-first companies that aim to proactively organize your tasks, use your computer, and write advanced code. Still, those rival agents deliver a patchwork of capabilities: while some, like OpenClaw and Anthropic’s Claude Code, are highly functional, others, like Google’s Gemini Spark, aren’t quite there yet.

Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a free local AI stack

Regardless, the issue here is time. Despite developing powerful hardware perfectly suited for running local AI models, Apple has remained slower than competitors on the AI software front. Competitors have demonstrated they can make promised agent features a reality, some quicker than others.

On the other hand, the fact that Apple hyped Siri AI for two years only to release an improved voice assistant (rather than a groundbreaking AI product) may mean users are ready for more advanced features.

In addition, AI companies are working on their own hardware. “If they can combine that software with AI-native devices designed from the ground up around assistants that see, remember and act, Apple’s longstanding advantages could begin to matter less,” Gurman wrote.

An agentic Siri would most likely build on what users already like about the new version.

The on-screen awareness feature, for example, is currently limited to what’s visible on your screen in that moment, meaning only the part of a long email that you’ve actively scrolled to. An agentic Siri could ideally scroll all the way through an email on its own and surface the insights you’re looking for.

Also: The iPhone made Apple a giant – but the Mac could help it win the AI era

But in the short term, Ternus’ push will likely just deliver on existing promises. Gurman also pointed out that Siri AI still lacks advanced in-app actions, which Apple initially announced in 2024 and would let third-party apps create plug-ins for and pathways through Siri.

“This functionality would let Siri tap into both in-house and third-party applications with more precision,” Gurman wrote. “This past week, as part of the first beta version of iOS 27.3, Apple finally began talking about the feature again.”

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Plus, if we’re talking about agents specifically, newcomers like OpenAI’s Dot and Anthropic’s Duet aren’t competitive themselves yet: ZDNET’s AI vetter-in-residence David Gewirtz found both to be “a little odd” and not “quite ready for prime time”.

Also: I tested OpenAI Dot and Anthropic Duet for weeks – and all I got was one helpful notification

For users who appreciate the subtlety of Siri AI, though, anything similar to ChatGPT or Claude on their devices might not land, unless each feature is opt-in.

#3136. How to Use AI Tools Like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude to Prep for a Job Interview

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

AI makes it easy to rehearse a job interview as many times as you need, with feedback after every answer.

ChatGPT’s voice mode lets you run a spoken mock interview and hear follow-up questions in real time.

For job seekers, the job interview can feel like an endurance test of their skills and personality.

It’s enough to make a person yearn for the simpler days of newspaper ads and in-person handshakes. But alas, we find ourselves immersed in the era of smart homes and Bluetooth-enabled blueberry mint vapes. But AI offers one practical advantage: a way to rehearse before the real thing.

A chatbot can play the role of a hiring manager, ask questions likely to come up for a specific job and tell you — bluntly, if you want — where your answers fall flat. That makes AI chatbots some of the more practical interview prep tools available, especially since you can rehearse as many times as you need without leaning on a friend’s patience. These chatbots can also help you research the company, prepare stories that answer common behavioral questions and get a rough sense of what the role should pay.

Here are a couple of ways you can leverage AI tools to ace your next job interview.

Read more: The New Age of Hiring: AI Is Changing the Game for Job Seekers

How you look in a job interview matters. Even if you’re sitting at home pantsless and just woke up from a nap, you gotta look the part on Zoom.

You can ask ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude to generate Zoom backgrounds that showcase your understanding of and affinity for the company culture.

Gemini created these backgrounds for my theoretical job interviews with Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, Apple, Google, Netflix and more.

Some of them turned out a little better than others, but you get the idea.

Some states, like California, have made it all but mandatory for employers to post the salary range for jobs they post as vacant. Even if you might know the salary range of the job going into the interview, the topic of compensation is always best approached with as much information as possible.

I asked Google’s Gemini AI to reference Glassdoor listings, public earnings, expenditure announcements, shareholder communications, and online media results for the salary ranges of the CEOs at Meta, Amazon, Apple, Microsoft, Netflix, and Alphabet and to provide me with salary ranges for mid-level marketing professionals at those companies.

Gemini then gave me a five-year growth schedule, where it laid out how I could begin to make more money by leveraging my sign-on bonus in the first year, my vesting stock in the second, a raise in the third, a title change in the fourth and a big promotion in the fifth (very idealistic, but it could happen).

Gemini also provided more information on how each of those companies typically structures your compensation — whether it’s an all-cash salary, one with built-in bonuses, or employee stock options. It’s important to have this information when you’re asked about the salary you expect.

Most guides on how to land a gig suggest that job seekers research the company, its culture and what the role entails. But honestly, job seekers are already investing a tremendous amount of time applying to open positions and going through multiple rounds of interviews.

What’s more important is your ability to effectively explain why you’re perfect for the job.

For my hypothetical marketing role, I used Claude to research the CMOs at those companies, including their social posts and their teams’ major priorities. I asked the AI tool to give me some one-word anchors for interview talking points, cross-referenced to elements of my resume that would be directly applicable.

It gave me some keywords to bring up, and how to relate them back to my own resume, listed out CEOs’ vision and products, told me which company could be my biggest opportunity and best fit and why — and how to express that in an interview:

Nerves are normal in a high-stakes communication like a job interview. You’re trying to appear interested but not desperate, competent but not cocky, and decide on a salary requirement you won’t live to regret.

One way to get your mind right for the job interview and take the edge off could be using an AI tool to run through some sample interview questions with you.

Several online platforms offer features that let you run a trial before your interview, including Final Round AI, which offers real-time interview transcription and support, mock interviews and resume building. Another platform, Yoodli, focuses on AI-powered communication coaching to improve both verbal and nonverbal delivery and offers AI roleplays. You can also talk with Gemini Live and get real-time responses.

In my case, I asked ChatGPT via the voice chat feature to pretend it was the hiring manager for a job at a fictitious company that sells subscription dog-sitting services, and to act as if it was unimpressed by my resume to give me a challenge and desensitize me to the worst-case scenario.

While the text chat was more of a critique of my resume, bless its sweet little machine algorithm, ChatGPT in voice chat was way too nice to even get into character for this challenge, no matter how I prompted it.

AI tools can be effective options for job seekers who don’t feel comfortable reaching out to someone in their network to help them prepare. Always keep in mind, however, that AI tools come with pitfalls, including issues related to data collection, bias and inconsistent messaging.

Use AI to prepare, but don’t let it fake your performance. AI doesn’t replace genuine networking, and the guiding principle should be to stay authentic.

Basic economy tickets come with plenty of restrictions, but holding the right credit card is my top trick for avoiding some of them.

As airfares remain high, that basic economy fare might look more tempting than ever. Saving $100 on a round-trip domestic flight could mean more money for hotels, dining or other experiences at your destination.

I’ve flown my fair share of basic economy flights, which come with restrictions like being unable to select a seat, earning no award miles and boarding last. You also can’t make changes or cancel your itinerary without paying a hefty fee, and — specific to United Airlines — you can’t bring a full-size carry-on on board.

But as a United frequent flyer, I have a secret to share with you: Holding the United℠ Explorer Card (annual fee: $0 intro for the first year, then $150) lets you avoid several of those basic economy restrictions.

Right now, new United℠ Explorer Card applicants can receive this welcome offer: Earn 70,000 bonus miles after you spend $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months your account is open. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles when you add an authorized user in the first 3 months your account is open.

Most major airlines no longer let you earn points or miles on basic economy fares. United is an exception, though — assuming you hold the right credit card.

Eligible cardholders, including those who have the United℠ Explorer Card, earn at least 3 miles per $1 spent on United basic economy tickets, excluding taxes and select fees. That’s half of what a standard economy ticket earns for cardholders (6 miles per $1), but it’s better than zero. If you have elite status, you’ll earn more.

Those miles are in addition to the 3 miles per $1 you earn on all United purchases when using your United℠ Explorer Card.

With the card, your miles can become more valuable. That’s because cardholders get at least 10% off award tickets that are operated by United or United Express. If you have United status, that discount gets bumped up to at least 15% off.

With the credit card, you have access to priority boarding in Group 2. That means you’ll be able to board earlier compared to the rest of the basic economy passengers in Group 6, making it more likely you’ll find space for your carry-on bag.

Now, you might be thinking: Wait a minute… Basic economy doesn’t allow you to bring a carry-on bag. Let me explain how that works.

United enforces its full-size carry-on restriction based on your boarding group. Group 6 passengers can't bring a full-size carry-on.

Because the credit card gets you Group 2 boarding, you essentially skip that restriction.

Premier members — who board in Group 2 or earlier — are also exempt from the full-size carry-on restriction when flying basic economy.

If you don’t want to deal with the hassle of a carry-on bag, you can opt to check it instead.

As long as you pay for your ticket using your United℠ Explorer Card, you’ll be able to check your first bag — and your companion’s first bag — for free when traveling on United. (If you’re booking an award ticket, make sure to use your card to pay for the taxes and fees.)

Keep in mind that if the first flight on your itinerary is operated by another airline, that airline’s baggage rules would apply and you would have to pay for your bag.

Of course, holding the right United credit card only gets you so far.

With basic economy, you’ll still need to pay a fee to change or cancel your ticket, and you won’t be able to select a seat for free.

Ultimately, whether basic economy is a good deal depends on a few factors.

If your plans might change, pay up for standard economy. Otherwise, the penalty to change or cancel will end up costing you more than you saved.

Another thing to consider is whether you’re willing to sit in a middle seat. You might be fine with it for a few hours, but what about a long-haul flight to Asia? Everyone’s threshold is different, so you’ll need to decide whether the middle-seat gamble is worth it.

If your plans are firm and you don’t mind a potential middle seat, booking a basic economy ticket can be a solid way to save money. Just book with a United card like, the United℠ Explorer Card, to avoid the biggest downsides.

#3134. NASA’s Voyager 1 to Cross Historic One Light-Day Milestone on Nov. 18

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Traveling one light-day took the space probe 49 years. it would take a human 612,015 years to walk that distance.

NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft is on track to set another historic record as its mission approaches the half-century mark. On Nov. 18 at 5:16 a.m. ET, the probe will reach a distance of one light-day from Earth, a journey of nearly five decades that places it farther from our planet than any human-made object in history.

It’s quite an accomplishment for a spacecraft built in the mid-1970s One light-day is the distance that light travels in a single day at the speed of light, which is approximately 186,282 miles per second. That translates to 25.9 billion kilometers or about 16.1 billion miles in a single day. At an average human walking speed of 3 mph, it would take a human 612,015 years to walk that distance.

Fortunately, Voyager 1 has been traveling a bit faster than that. It currently zips along the cosmos at a steady 37,763 mph, a speed it achieved in 1980 after a gravity-assisted Saturn flyby. It has been flying at that speed ever since.

The milestone comes 14 years after its previous one, when Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause, the point where the sun’s heliosphere ends, and entered interstellar space. It’s also 28 years after passing Pioneer 10 to become the human-made object that has traveled the farthest into space.

The historic milestone isn’t without its drama. Voyager 1 has been in space for nearly half a century, and in that time, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory has done everything it can to extend the life of Voyager 1. That includes troubleshooting issues, performing maintenance and shutting down various systems to save power and extend the spacecraft’s life-span.

Several of those efforts took place in 2026. The team running Voyager 1 spent weeks shutting down three devices and powering on three low-power alternatives to reduce overall power usage. This initiative, which was internally called The Big Bang, was also performed on Voyager 2. The transition was completed in early September, giving Voyager 1 more time with its dwindling power supply while also keeping it warm enough to continue operating in the frigid conditions of interstellar space.

It was a tricky maneuver that required the team to simultaneously turn multiple instruments on and off. The difficulty of the maneuver was amplified by the fact that it took almost a full day for any signal to reach Voyager and another full day for Voyager to send a signal back, with hours of downtime while the spacecraft performed the operations.

All of this took place several months after Voyager 1 experienced a sudden drop in power, which necessitated shutting off one of its three remaining instruments still in operation. Voyager 1 now has only two instruments still in operation.

Making it a whole light-day away from Earth is likely going to be Voyager 1’s final milestone while it still has enough power to communicate with Earth. Voyager 1 is powered by three radioisotope thermoelectric generators. They are essentially nuclear-powered batteries that generate energy by converting the steady heat from decaying plutonium-238.

When Voyager 1 first launched, its radioisotope thermoelectric generators produced about 470 watts of power. But plutonium-238 doesn’t last forever, and after 50 years in space, the RTGs now produce about 215 watts of power, with an average loss of about 4 watts per year. Most of that power is used to keep Voyager 1 up and running, which is why NASA has shut down eight of the 10 instruments that Voyager had when it launched.

At its current rate of usage and decay, Voyager 1 is expected to shut down its final science instrument in the 2030s and will eventually lose communication with Earth in 2036 due to insufficient power to send back a radio signal.

The same fate is expected for Voyager 2, Voyager 1’s twin, which has also spent half a century in space. While it is labeled the sequel, Voyager 2 actually launched 16 days before Voyager 1, and the two have spent nearly identical amounts of time traversing the cosmos. Thanks to its slower speed and trajectory, it likely won’t reach the one light-day distance until after its instruments shut down.

Thanks to the vastness of space, Voyager 1 will lose all of its power before it hits its next milestone, which is the beginning of the Oort Cloud, a vast, icy shell of comets at the edge of our solar system. It’ll take about 300 years for Voyager 1 to make it there.

Thanks to the near-perfect vacuum of outer space, Voyager 1 will continue to fly at its current speed even after it shuts down entirely. So it’ll still hit that milestone; it just won’t be able to phone home to tell us about it.

#3133. AMD confirms GPU driver bug is wearing out your SSD – how to stop it

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

AMD has admitted a bug within its External Events Utility is wearing out SSDs, and promises a fix.

Under normal circumstances, an SSD might go all day without needing to access or write files. But for some AMD Radeon users, anything but normal circumstances are causing drives to continuously write and re-write data. The External Events Utility (EEU) that AMD installs alongside its CPU and GPU drivers is reportedly the culprit.

Also: Nvidia RTX 50 GPUs hit with more price hikes

Fortunately, there are a few workarounds available to avert disaster while AMD works on a more permanent solution.

Reports of the issue first surfaced in July on AMD’s official PC user forum, with one user stating that the External Events Client Module and EEU were constantly writing information to their SSD after installing a Radeon 9060XT graphics card. Subsequent comments on the thread this month confirm that the issue has persisted despite several bug fixes and patch updates, with two users reporting hard numbers for data usage ranging from 0.3 MB/s to as much as 1.5 MB/s.

Also: The best laptops: Expert tested and reviewed

This week, Reddit user darklinkpower posted that the AMD Adrenaline Edition desktop application also had the EEU driver bug, using up to 1% of their drive health per month for around 16 months. That might not sound like much, but it can cause catastrophic problems if left unchecked.

AMD seems to be aware of the issue; a company official who goes by AMD_Vik on Reddit commented that it will “hopefully [be] fixed in the next [update].” While there’s little indication of how quickly a permanent, official patch will be pushed to users, there are a few ways you can protect yourself from the bug and prevent your storage drive from collapsing.

This seems to be the most consistent fix for most AMD users reporting issues, but disabling the EEU can cause its own problems, such as disabling AMD FreeSync support or introducing display glitches if you hot-swap screens while your PC is powered on.

The AMD Adrenalin Edition desktop app lets you control how your PC components communicate with one another, and it might be another facet of a complex problem. By allowing your CPU to access your graphics card’s memory, you can temporarily boost performance, but the EEU bug seems to let it and your GPU run rampant, eating up every bit of memory they can find. This is a more niche solution that carries its own risk of introducing communication issues between your CPU and GPU, so I only recommend trying this route if disabling the EEU itself doesn’t resolve the issue. AMD’s official fix may be in the works, but without a firm timeline for release, users are left twisting in the wind trying to stop their PCs from hemorrhaging storage capacity.

#3132. Apollo to buy nearly 10% stake in Abu Dhabi-backed alternative asset manager Mubadala Capital

Investing giant Apollo Global Management is finalizing a deal to buy nearly a 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager subsidiary of Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala Investment Co., according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The deal is expected to be announced later Monday morning, they said. Financial terms were not immediately known.

The transaction is significant on multiple fronts. It further advances Apollo's ambitions in Abu Dhabi often called the "capital of capital." The firm has spent the past 15 years building key strategic relationships there, with both the country's investment arm and its core leadership.

Apollo already has a multibillion-dollar partnership with Mubadala Investment Co., first established in 2022 and extended two years ago. At the time of that extension, Apollo said the agreement would strengthen the firm's Capital Solutions platform by enabling the firms to jointly source and provide customized debt and equity financing to companies worldwide.

In 2023, the institutions formed a $2.5 billion joint venture designed specifically to co-invest in global private credit opportunities over a five-year horizon.

For Mubadala Capital specifically — the region's only large-scale asset manager, advising and administering more than $755 billion in assets — the deal further advances its growth strategy under the direction of CEO Hani Barhoush, and its relevance on the global investing stage. It also marks an inflection point for the company's core alternatives business, which has grown to more than $60 billion.

John Zito, co-president of Apollo's Asset Management arm, and Barhoush have worked closely together over the past several years and, according to sources, their close-knit relationship and the success of prior partnerships led to talks of deepening ties. So did the belief that scale in the asset management business matters more than ever.

"Capital as a moat is a big thing," said one person familiar with the deal.

Importantly, the deal also continues a notable shift in the relationship between American investment firms and the Middle East. While the region, and Abu Dhabi specifically, has long been a sought-after source of capital, this deal further reverses that dynamic, with Apollo making a significant direct investment in the country and its investment vision.

Mubadala Capital's international offices include London, New York, Rio de Janeiro and San Francisco.

Apollo's investment in Mubadala Capital is similar to deals the firm has done with other asset management platforms, including Diameter Capital, Thoreau, Motive Partners and others.

Spokespersons for both firms declined to comment.

#3131. KKR (KKR) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Record fee-related earnings and a $146 billion dry powder war chest anchor a quarter of firsts.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

KKR & Co. Inc. (KKR +1.67%) reported record third-quarter results, marking a consecutive period of historic highs across its headline financial metrics. Management highlighted a significant increase in capital returned to clients, with total distributions expected to exceed $40 billion for the full year. The firm's strategic focus remains on its multi-engine business model, with record fee-related earnings driven by management fee growth and fee-related performance revenues. Leadership emphasized a disciplined capital allocation framework, prioritizing reinvestment into insurance, share buybacks, and strategic holdings to drive long-term earnings per share. Additionally, the company is set to finalize its transition to a traditional governance structure, implementing a one-share, one-vote system following the expiration of super-voting rights for its co-founders.

And as a reminder, we report our segment numbers on an adjusted share basis. This call will contain forward-looking statements, which do not guarantee future events or performance. Please refer to our earnings release and our SEC filings for cautionary factors about these statements.

So first, beginning with our results for the quarter. Once again, for the second consecutive quarter, we're reporting record results across all 3 of our headline financial metrics: fee-related earnings, total operating earnings and adjusted net income per share. Management fees in the quarter were $1.2 billion.

Looking at management fees, excluding catch-up fees in all periods, management fees grew 16% year-over-year and were up 19% looking at the first 9 months of '26 compared to '25. And visibility here remains healthy as AUM that has not yet turned on and is not yet paying management fees ended the quarter at $75 billion with a blended fee rate of approximately 90 basis points. Since the start of the year, that $75 billion figure is up 24% and 2 additional items of note just on the management fee side. First, it's worth highlighting our progress in real assets. Over the last 3 years, fee-paying AUM has increased from $108 billion to $176 billion.

That's an 18% CAGR with a blended fee rate ex catch-up fees that has increased every year alongside. And second, looking even more broadly, in 2019, we earned $1.2 billion of management fees across the full year. Given the growth and diversification across KKR, we're generating this level of management fees now in a single quarter. Back to our Q3 results. Total transaction and monitoring fees were $328 million in the quarter. Capital markets fees reached $290 million. That's our third highest quarterly result on record, and insurance-related capital markets activity picked up nicely this quarter. Fee-related performance revenues were -- $326 million and are up year-over-year, driven by our U.S. domiciled infrastructure and private equity K-Series vehicles.

As a reminder, this is the second quarter where the crystallization from private equity wealth is sitting within that FRPR line. Turning to expenses. Fee-related compensation was again at the midpoint of our guided range at 17.5% and other operating expenses for the quarter came in at $215 million. So in total, fee-related earnings were a record $1.3 billion or the $1.42 per share figure I mentioned a few moments ago. And our FRE margin came in just around 71%, also the highest we've reported in our history. Insurance segment operating earnings were $230 million. Excluding the impact of GA's annual actuarial assumption review and other related items, insurance operating earnings would have been $257 million.

As we've discussed on prior calls, insurance operating earnings do not fully capture the broader impact of GA to KKR. So Page 17 of the earnings release details the management fees under our investment management agreement, fees from Ivy-related vehicles, where we now have over $60 billion of AUM that wouldn't exist without GA as well as GA-related capital markets fees, again, which picked up in Q3. So while we've been more disciplined throughout the first half of the year, given the competitive environment, we're still seeing really attractive all-in economics. And over the LTM, that total insurance economic figure was $1.9 billion. That's net of compensation.

And that does not include, as a reminder, the impact of mark-to-market as we report our insurance investment portfolio largely based on cash outcomes. Turning now to Strategic Holdings. We delivered a strong quarter with $192 million of operating earnings, bringing the year-to-date total to $277 million. This puts us firmly on track to achieve our expectation of more than $350 million in operating earnings for full year 2026. And over the last 12 months, 84% of our total pretax segment earnings were driven by these more recurring earnings streams, which again, we feel demonstrates the durability of our model. Moving now to investing earnings. Realized performance and investment income totaled $824 million, and we had $71 million of net realized investment income in Strategic Holdings. And again, just to be clear, these results do not reflect the USI transaction, which is subject to closing.

Robert Lewin: Thanks a lot, Craig, and thank you, everyone, for joining our call this morning. This stands in sharp contrast to the muted monetization activity that we are seeing across our industry, and I think reflects both the performance of our portfolio and the benefits of our disciplined approach to linear deployment and portfolio construction. Year-to-date, we have returned $31 billion to our clients across private equity, real assets and credit and including announced transactions and activity completed since September 30. We expect that figure to reach over $40 billion in 2026, exceeding our previous annual record by more than 50%. Turning briefly to USI.

In late August, we announced the sale of the business, which was our inaugural core private equity investment. The sale is expected to deliver an approximately 6x multiple of our cost on the original 2017 investment, a 3.4x multiple on all KKR balance sheet capital, part of which was invested just last year and a roughly 33% premium to USI's unaffected valuation last quarter.

We expect Strategic Holdings to continue building on this theme.

As a reminder, Strategic Holdings represents KKR's direct ownership in companies that we believe are durable, less cyclical and well positioned to compound value over the long term. As a reminder, we have 4 key tools available to us: share buybacks, Strategic Holdings, strategic M&A and insurance. These all take full advantage of the KKR ecosystem. And as a result, we have the potential for very high ROEs. Importantly, our capital allocation approach does not assign a predetermined amount of capital spend into any one of those 4 buckets. Let me go through some examples of our recent activity here. First, as it relates to share buybacks, it is an area where we have leaned into this year.

Scott Nuttall: Thanks, Rob. Hi, everybody. Thanks for joining our call today. There's a lot being written about our industry, and most of it is not flattering. We think what's missing is a broader historical context. So I thought today, we would share our perspective through the lens of our 50 years of experience. The first thing we want to do is acknowledge all of the noise and complexity that have made it so difficult for the market to understand what's really happening.

This year alone, we've heard worries about software, private credit, private wealth, private equity monetizations, insurance affiliate issues, the impact of higher interest rates and the consequence of all of the aforementioned on overall returns and the ability to raise scale capital. There has been a lot thrown at you and no shortage of things to worry about. As you just heard, despite all of this noise and all of these questions, we continue to report record results. And it is not just this quarter and not just some metrics. And the momentum going forward is strong. So how do we square the broader private market sentiment with our performance? Herein lies the opportunity for a broader historical perspective to make sense of all of this. When you step back, we think there are 2 things going on. First, alternative asset managers have not been public companies for very long. Most of us came public around the time of the financial crisis or thereafter. So the market's ability to learn about our business model has been limited by the market environment over the last 16 years.

As we have discussed on prior calls, the first 10 of those years were a benign environment with low interest rates, low inflation and multiples expanding. It was a relatively straightforward period in which to generate returns, especially investing in levered equity. The last 6 years, however, have been more complicated with the pandemic, rising rates and inflation, 2 wars, tariffs and anxiety about both the downside and the opportunity set afforded by AI. Speaking of history and to put a finer point on it, the average 10-year Treasury yield since KKR was founded in 1976 is 5.8%. The average Treasury yield since the beginning of 2010 is 2.7%.

Said simply, today's Treasury rate at around 5% is less than the 50-year average since KKR was founded. But the market has only known our space in a public context in a 2% to 3% or lower interest rate environment until very recently. So your experience set is different than ours. We generated strong returns for our investors before 2010 and in much higher interest rate environments than the one we're in right now. But the public market has not had the benefit of experiencing that yet and uncertainty and fear tend to be very powerful emotions.

Part of why we like this period of time is that it will provide you with the opportunity to get to know us and our business better, and we can move from theory to more of a shared lived experience. Second, our strong belief is that you only know if you're good in this business once you've been able to invest through a few cycles. What makes this time particularly challenging to understand is that we have not had a normal recession or cycle in the United States, for example, for 16 years. You have to go back to the financial crisis. And the one prior to that was in 2001, around the time of the telecom bubble.

So most of the opportunity the public markets have had to get to know our space has been in an environment where we haven't had a real cycle. And everyone is learning together, both the public markets and we believe a number of the younger entrants in the private markets. In the past, we've talked about the fact that the private markets industry was about $3 trillion in size at the time of the financial crisis. That number today is in excess of $15 trillion. That sounds like a lot of growth, but it's about 12% per year.

Through our lens, what is more important to understand is the number of participants in the industry that have experienced investing through cycles. That's where the numbers get far more interesting. As best we can tell, over 65% of the participants in the private markets industry were formed after 2009. They were not even in existence at the time of the global financial crisis. Said another way, only 35% of the market participants have experienced a real recession or cycle. And if you want to go back further to the 2001 recession, less than 20% of the market participants were in business at that time.

Said simply, 65% of the firms in our industry have not experienced a real cycle and over 80% were not around at the time of the 2001 recession. That is a lot of new players. Most investors are experiential learners. What is happening now, we believe, is that many market participants, a majority are learning by doing. And some of their results will reflect the fact that they have not invested through a cycle before. We expect many of them will learn from it and like us, get better from the experience. Some will disappear. Where we are different is that we have been around for 50 years.

We've seen not only the financial crisis and the 2001 recession, but you can go back further to the early '90s real estate crisis. We've seen oil shocks. We've seen the recession of the early '80s. We've seen a 20-plus percent prime rate. We've been able to invest and learn over the course of many cycles over the last 5 decades. And most of the firms operating in our space have not. That is a critical distinction in our view. We try to be a learning organization. A lot of the mistakes that other people are making now, we made a couple of decades ago or more.

And we changed our investment process to reflect the mistakes we made and become better all-weather through-cycle investors. That, we believe, is what is showing up in our results. So another reason we like this time is that it gives you an opportunity to see what's different about us and that benefit of experience. But there's not just an educational benefit to all of this. It's also a fundamental positive for our business momentum. The good news for us in this now K-shaped industry is that the happy part of the K is taking market share from the less happy part of the K.

We are raising more capital now than we ever have, and we are finding a significantly magnified focus by global investors on through-cycle investment acumen. The result is more concentrated commitments by our clients with firms like ours that are performing through the noise. And we anticipate this dynamic will accelerate going forward. We say all this with a lot of humility and acknowledging that we will continue to make mistakes, and we will continue to learn. We say all this acknowledging we do not get everything right, but we are working to get better at what we do. We believe we are making progress, and we are pleased to see that progress in our results.

I hope this explanation helps as you decipher all of the information coming out about our industry and all of the varied stories being written about our space. And I hope it helps to put our results in context and allows you to better understand the confidence we have in our own future. As I said last quarter, the best response to pessimism is performance. We get that. Our focus is on continuing to perform for everybody counting on us, including you, our fellow shareholders and partners. With that, we're happy to take your questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Craig Siegenthaler with Bank of America.

Craig Siegenthaler: We have a set of questions on Global Atlantic. And I heard your comments that you're leaning into growth at GA, and we saw the inflow acceleration in 3Q.
