And have you been leaning into high-yielding segments of the AI adjacency verticals like GPU financing? And sorry, just one more. I know there's a bunch here, but you have some long-term goals in place, duration extensions, reallocation to alts within GA. Where are you in that trajectory?

Robert Lewin: Great. Craig, let us start going through those one by one, probably the combination of us will tackle some of your questions. As it relates to the first one, we saw a better opportunity to invest in the quarter. And I think that came from a number of different factors. We did see the rate movement upward, and we have positioned the business to respond very quickly to that. At the same time, you would have seen some movement in fixed income spreads. And so the left-hand side of the balance sheet moved in our direction, and we didn't see competition move necessarily as quick as it relates to pricing.

And so we have spent now a number of years making sure that our liabilities and investing teams are synced up literally to the day, and we were able to respond pretty quickly to that environment. So that would be point one. As it relates to duration of our assets, you absolutely would have seen us continue to extend the duration of our assets. If I'm looking at year-to-date numbers through 2026, 93% of our liabilities 5-plus years in duration, 63%, 7-plus years in duration. Compare those numbers to 2024, 75% 5-year and only 37% 7-year. So we're extending the duration of liabilities.

And in tandem, we're continuing to modestly increase the pace at which we move the book of assets to an alternatives portfolio, roughly 2% of our portfolio today. We can see that getting closer to industry average, but that's going to happen over time. Industry average is closer to 5% to 8%. But as we've mentioned multiple times on these calls, we're going to do this in a way that's prudent and in a way that matches the extension of the duration of our liabilities, which we continue to work through. Go ahead, Scott.

Scott Nuttall: Just one other thing I would add is, I think we talked in the past about a big focus the last 12, 24 months is in having our investment teams globally source these structured alternatives deals that we think are very attractive and fit nicely with investment-grade opportunities that fit into the GA balance sheet. Some of those just take several weeks or months to actually gestate and be able to close. And so part of what's also going on is feeding what Rob is talking about is we've got a significantly increased pipeline and a magnified focus across the firm that's really taking hold.

Operator: Our next question comes from Glenn Schorr with Evercore.

Glenn Schorr: One of the conversations I get into a bunch is on quality of earnings. And people look at a quarter like this and say, okay, you have all those records, but some of the beat today is transaction fees, Strategic Holdings, FRPR performance fees, but management fee rate -- management fee, and insurance earnings are decelerating. So they don't like that mix. You've spoken to part of it, but I do want to give you a chance to respond to the aggregate. But I want to specifically focus on transaction fees. I think you were one of the first to enhance the quality and the scale of the platform.

You make a lot of money from it, but people somehow discount that as lesser class than a management fee. So maybe get your perspective on how to think about that over the next couple of years in terms of per dollar of AUM, per dollar of deployment with all your dry powder? Is there lots of white space? Like I just wanted to get your big picture thoughts on quality of earnings. So I really appreciate it.

Robert Lewin: Yes. Thanks for the question, Glenn. It's Rob. I'll start. So we have positioned our firm very much on purpose to be able to have multiple ways to positively impact the P&L. And you listed off a bunch in your response, and we think that's important. Multiple different ways for us to be able to utilize our model to be able to achieve outcomes, first and foremost, for our clients, policyholders, and shareholders. And you're seeing some of that flow through our earnings over the past couple of quarters.

As it relates specifically to your question on transaction fees, I think you're getting into capital markets fees, we look at the scale of the business we've created in capital markets and its breadth. And when I talk about breadth, I can talk about it by geography. I could talk about it by client coverage. I can also talk about it around product. And so you think about insurance-related capital markets fees on the product side, structured products can add into that. I think on the geography side, big opportunity for us in Asia Pacific.

And on the client side, we've got a very significant effort to cover both the sponsor and corporate community that we think provides just an additional layer of growth for that business. Interestingly, if you look at our capital markets business and maybe look at a decade ago, you would have seen very significant peaks and valleys. Based on what I just went through, I think we've brought up the floor in that business pretty dramatically over the years. You look at, go back in history, 2023 and 2024, the capital markets in both of those years were largely shut. You did not see a lot of leveraged finance activity.

And in each of those years, we generated $600-plus million of capital markets fees. Obviously, in a more robust capital markets environment, you're seeing us deliver much better results. But I think the key for us is, are we building a business that is both durable, can protect fees on the downside? We think the answer is yes. And then are we building a business that has multiple growth levers in front of it. We also think the answer is yes there, too. But back to where you started this question, Glenn, lots of different ways to positively impact the P&L. That is our business model, and we believe we're delivering on that.

Scott Nuttall: Glenn, it's Scott. Yes, the only thing I would add maybe just a little bit of color. As you know, with the capital markets business, we're monetizing the deal flow that we have inherent in the firm to a much greater extent. And I really do view these as recurring. And if you look at kind of the activity level across the firm, it is recurring and it is an incredibly high flow-through margin because we don't have a lot of people that are doing this. A lot of the deal work is already being done by the deal teams.

And so if you look at it, we habitually are syndicating $10 billion to $20 billion plus of equity a year. And you add on top of that the financing and refinancing across the embedded portfolio, which is always busy. Then you add on top of that the third-party business, which also feeds direct lending and other parts of our credit business, plus IPOs plus secondaries and plus on top of that, to your question about white space, Global Atlantic/insurance and these big structured alts deals. And so in any given week, we've got multiple different transactions that are kind of working their way through the capital markets business. And I do view that as highly recurring.

To Rob's point, you can see the baseline of that business continue to increase. So I really appreciate the question because I don't really think the market fully understands what I just said, and we see significant growth opportunities ahead.

Operator: Our next question comes from Alex Blostein with Goldman Sachs.

Alexander Blostein: So lots of developments in the last week or 2 related to the AI ecosystem broadly and KKR generally has been a bit more measured and kind of picking your spots as you lean into it. But it's helpful to maybe kind of mark-to-market where your sort of AI-related infrastructure exposure sits between both your credit business and your equity-related businesses. And I guess, more importantly, as you think about the forward growth and if we see moderation in deployment opportunities related to any sort of data center restrictions, how impactful could that be on your forward growth?

Scott Nuttall: Great, Alex, it's Scott. First off, congratulations. Let me start. So at the highest level, and I appreciate you asking the question, so I'm going to go high altitude because I think it's important context. Obviously, AI is a very large opportunity. We think we're really well positioned to benefit, but we're also cognizant of the risks. And like any set of developments like this, we think money will be made and money will be lost. So our thinking is grounded in 3 things. First, recognition that no one knows how this will play out. This level of spend this fast is unprecedented. And we think it's important to approach all of this with a lot of humility.

Second, we try to stay focused on what we're authentically good at. We find in moments like this, which are a mix of excitement and confusion, it's important to stay grounded in what we do well, so we don't drift. Third thing I'd say, it's important to set a goal. So our goal has been that in 10 years, we want to look back and be proud of how we protected our clients' capital and realized profit for them by leveraging what I referenced before, what we're authentically good at. So we want to be proud of the body of work regardless of how all this plays out. So through that lens, we've been doing a few things.

And I know your question is focused on data centers, but it's broader than just data centers is kind of how we thought about what's going on here. First thing you need to do when you have a disruptive technology in our experience is get out of the way of disruption. We did an inventory of what we owned 4 or 5 years ago and looked at everything through the lens of where is AI an opportunity, a threat, or a question mark. If it was a threat or a question mark, we decided to try to get out of the way. And so we sold some businesses that we are worried about.

But that's probably an important part of this. You got to make sure you don't get disrupted. We learned that from what happened with the Internet event. Second, we recognize we own some assets today that are really benefiting in an outsized way from what's going on with AI. We've been selling those in some cases. This year, Kokusai is a good example in Japan, semiconductor equipment business. CoolIT, we've talked about. We sold Kokusai for roughly 20x our investors' cost, CoolIT for 15x. Maybe if we'd held them longer, we could have done better than that, but those are pretty good outcomes. And third, to your question, we've been trying to judiciously deploy capital into new opportunities.

But trying to do that with a long-term mindset and an eye to portfolio construction, diversification, and deployment pacing. So we've done roughly $45 billion of equity investments in digital infra to date, roughly $40 billion of equity in power deals so far, but we're staying diversified. So the 7 data center platforms we have, they aggregate 6% of our infrastructure AUM. And when you take those investments plus other things we have across the firm, including in Global Atlantic, it aggregates 1% to 2% of total firm AUM. And we're trying to be appropriately careful, right? So a lot of the offtake is for cloud, not AI.

When we bought CyrusOne 5 years ago, as an example, that was predicated on cloud. AI was all upside. 90% of our long-term lease exposures are to governments or investment-grade hyperscalers. 3% are to neoclouds, just to size it for you. And then we've also been trying to think about how do we develop new capital, new approaches to this space. And we've talked in the past about Helix, which is more of a one-stop shop. It's got power data centers and equipment, all in one offering to work with hyperscalers. So as I said, our overall expectation is that money will be made and lost but we're trying to lean on our experience.

So that means get out of the way where you need to, sell a bit early, that's better than a bit late and focus on your downside and be ready to be opportunistic if some run into trouble. That's usually where some of the most interesting opportunities arise. Craig, anything you want to add?

Craig Larson: No, I think that's great. We'll go to the next question.

Operator: Our next question comes from Steven Chubak with Wolfe Research.

Steven Chubak: So I wanted to ask on the management fee outlook. Thinking through the list of upcoming fundraising campaigns, Asia infra should continue to raise early in the first half next year. You have Asia private equity and Europe, which will generate inflows through '27 and '28. But zooming out, we are entering a period beginning in '27 of lighter campaign contributions following a very active super cycle. I was hoping you could speak to the expected contribution from non-campaign fundraising ahead and how it informs your outlook for management fee growth heading into '27.

Robert Lewin: Steven, it's Rob. I'm glad you asked about management fees. Maybe taking a step back, this has been a real strength of our franchise, but I want to be clear about how we think about that strength that it is not just focused on one line item here either. If you look back in history, and we'll come to the future in a second, we've clearly had really robust management fee growth over the past several years. You look since the end of 2022, we've compounded here at roughly a 17% level. We're proud of that as a management team, but we're also proud of a few other things that I'd say go in tandem with management fee growth.

Number one is diversification. Prior to the closed transaction with Arctos, we had roughly 1/3 of our management fees coming from each one of our 3 business lines. So 1/3 from private equity, real assets and credit, and liquid strategies. Number two, we've done so while simultaneously increasing the duration of our capital. Today, 54% of our capital is now perpetual or 15-plus years in duration. We spend a lot of time talking about that. And then most importantly, as you think about management fees, we've ensured that our management fees drop to the bottom line. So 17% compounded growth since 2022. Our OpEx has compounded at 10% during that time.

And because of the shift we have made in our comp ratios, our fee-related comp has compounded at 2% during that time. So we've taken the 17% management fee growth and translated that into 22% FRE growth. That's what's really important. And I think if you take, like if you think about our business model, and we spent a lot of time on these calls talking about it, we want to be great in areas that we are already present. And to your question, we see a lot of room for growth across our platform. We have $75 billion of AUM not yet earning fees.

That's a record number for us, and that's up 24% just from the beginning of the year. But at the same time, we don't want to be all things to all people in asset management. We've said that for a while now. We're not going to start something new unless it could be really scalable, and we think we can be uniquely great at it. As a result, we're not the platform that's going to go down market for that last dollar of management fee growth. But what we do know is that our strategy is going to yield maximum efficiency as it relates to how we translate management fee growth into FRE growth.

And that's what we care the most about because we do not think our model requires a lot more operating complexity or people intensity to be able to achieve those results. And maybe lastly, on the point as we're talking about business model because I think it's important, I think it's worth remembering that this strategy has much more focus to it, and it is also much more compatible with keeping our small collaborative culture, which in turn is what we think generates a lot of our investment alpha, which in turn makes the flywheel continue to perpetuate. Hopefully, that's helpful in terms of how we think about it big picture.

A lot of specifics that, of course, go into any 1 year, but that is how we approach this topic of management fee growth. And really, it's a translation into durable management fee growth over time and bottom line results.

Operator: Our next question comes from Benjamin Budish with Barclays.

Benjamin Budish: I wanted to ask a few follow-ups on the back of, I think, Craig's question from earlier on the insurance side. I guess you talked about the allocation to alts. I'm curious if you could also spend a bit of time talking about your allocation to investment-grade private credit on the fixed income side. And then you guys mentioned earlier that the capital markets fees related to GA had kind of stepped up this quarter. Just curious if you could unpack that a bit -- a little bit. I know that's been sort of part of the thesis, sort of another place that KKR can benefit more broadly. But what did you see in Q3?

How can we think about that scaling up over time as well?

Craig Larson: Ben, it's Craig. Why don't I start? So I think, look at the starting point here, I think I'd even take it up a level as it relates to ratings and capital position. So looking across the 4 agencies, GA has been affirmed or upgraded by all 4 of these agencies over the last 18 months. Capital position remains really strong, ahead of its RBC range, lots of liquidity. And so I think when we look at GA's portfolio as a whole, diversified by asset class, industry sector, geography issuer, quality of the portfolio remains high, 94% NAIC 1 or 2. Now to your question, we do get asked a lot about GA's exposure to private originated fixed income.

So you may have seen on GA's website as it relates to where you see the bondholder presentations, we've actually added quite a bit of disclosure. I think to summarize some of that disclosure of GA's adjusted investment assets, around 4% of that is invested in senior secured direct lending. And if someone is more narrowly focused on the non-IG-rated portion of that piece of the pie, the number is lower. So the non-investment-grade rated portion of that is around 1% of adjusted invested assets. So again, it's a small piece.

And I think if you look back more holistically, when you look at where we've chosen to invest in risk assets, it's really been this first lien senior secured risk. We've been less focused on the equity bucket, for instance. So I think, again, looking at the portfolio as a whole, GA would have more limited equity exposure relative to peers. So I think as it relates to the overall investment portfolio and on this topic, those are some of the things that give us comfort.

Robert Lewin: Ben, let me follow up real quickly on your question on capital markets. We've talked about it being a very significant opportunity for our business model. In the quarter, we generated plus or minus $50 million of revenue in insurance-related capital markets fees. As Scott mentioned, we started to see some of those structured alts come to fruition. I think that, in particular, is a big opportunity for the broader platform, inclusive of capital market syndication.

Scott Nuttall: Yes. We've shared in the past, we expect that to be several hundred million of capital markets revenues a year. That continues to be our expectation.

Operator: Our next question comes from Michael Cyprys with Morgan Stanley.

Michael Cyprys: Just wanted to circle back to capital allocation and the $3.3 billion of USI sale proceeds. I heard you outline 4 areas for potential allocation of capital there. Just curious how you're weighing those different opportunities where incrementally you're seeing at the margin, more attractive opportunities of maybe buybacks most immediately. And just curious what's the time frame for putting that capital back to work? And with the recent Strategic Holdings investments, how should we think about the contribution of dividends from holdings into '27 and '28 given the newer investments you've made?

Robert Lewin: Great. Thanks, Mike. Listen, it's a dialogue that we are having absolutely all the time, right, as it relates to capital allocation. We have no fixed dollar amount or percentage to go to any, against any one of our 4 buckets of capital allocation. It is really all about how we take that marginal dollar of free cash flow and deploy it in a way that generates the most amount of earnings per share that are both durable and growth oriented. That's our goal and variables are going to be changing all the time.

As we talked through as an example, we saw variables shift a little bit in the quarter on insurance, and we started to allocate more capital there. Share buybacks, obviously, an area where we've allocated real capital in the quarter and for the year. And our expectation is that could be an interesting and compelling opportunity for our shareholders going forward. As it relates to your question on Strategic Holdings and USI, so we've already announced 3 new investments. I touched on those in my prepared remarks. One has already closed in Q4. Taken together, we would expect these 3 investments to generate roughly half of USI's anticipated operating earnings by 2028 and nearly match it by 2030.

So in short, we've not even closed on USI yet, and we already have investments that would largely replace the 2030 earnings that we were expecting from USI by deploying less capital than what USI will return. So I feel good about the body of work in Strategic Holdings. And as I said, we'll continue to keep you updated on capital allocation, but the one constant that you will hear from us as a management team is consistency in approach. And that can, how we allocate our capital as a result can shift depending on how variables evolve across any number of things in our business.

Scott Nuttall: Yes, Mike, it's Scott. Just one thing I'd add. If you go back to April '24 when we had our Investor Day, one of the things we shared is that we saw a path to $15-plus per share of ANI in 10 years or less. So call that 2034 or earlier. And so what we're really doing as we look at these capital allocation questions is thinking about where can we generate the biggest impact on that $15-plus outcome. And the good news is right now, buybacks are accretive and look good. Strategic Holdings are accretive and look good and insurance is accretive and looks good.

So we're able to have a pretty good debate around how and where to allocate amongst those 3, but they all look quite attractive. Some are more attractive immediately, some are more attractive longer term, but it falls in the good problem category.

Operator: Our next question comes from Mike Brown with UBS.

Michael Brown: So KKR is returning more than $40 billion to clients in 2026, and so you're exceeding your prior annual record. How deep is the remaining monetization pipeline here? And as we look out to 2027, is the 20%-plus level that consensus is baking in for realized performance revenues achievable given the current market conditions? And then just given you've given a view into 4Q, can you maybe help frame the monetization level that you're expecting to see for the fourth quarter based on what you know currently?

Robert Lewin: Yes. Sure, Mike. Let me take those questions. So as we look forward to our monetization visibility, obviously, that number is quite robust with USI, $3.5-plus billion over the next couple of quarters. That would be split roughly 75% realized investment income, 25% realized performance revenue. Ex USI number is about $600 million. About 85% of that $600 million is going to be realized investment income or other forms of revenue that have a similar comp load, so a high flow-through to that $600 million. And on a look-forward basis, there's no predictions as it relates to 2027, lots of different things that can impact where we are.

But our embedded gains across our platform today at 9/30 stand at $18 billion. That is up around 60% over the past 3 years. And that has happened while I think it's fair to say that we have outpaced the industry on monetizations, which clearly have a negative drag to that $18 billion. So I feel good about how we're positioned heading into 2027. And we'll, of course, see how the market performs and where it makes sense to monetize on behalf of our clients.

Operator: Our next question comes from Dan Fannon with Jefferies.

Daniel Fannon: So I was hoping to get an update on your outlook for private wealth and your K-Series suite of products. And just where you are in the distribution rollout and as we think about more products into next year, other things that are in the pipeline or planned at this point?

Craig Larson: Dan, why don't -- it's Craig. Why don't I start? Look, I think in terms of the progress, in some ways, we think the statistics speak for themselves. So AUM was $45 billion at September 30. That's up 55% relative to a year ago on a year-to-date basis, up over 30%. And that's, we think those are pretty positive numbers. Like think of all the volatility, all the angst, all the headlines on wealth and AUM over the first 9 months of the year is up a pretty healthy amount. 6 of our 8 strategies, if you look more recently, had positive flows in the quarter.

And for the 2 that were negative, one has, was negative $4 million and the second was negative $15 million. So again, I think all of those statistics speak very positively about our franchise, about the brand, about the distribution, about the investments we've made, about this being a global opportunity. And to your point on new products, we're not done yet. So we don't have anything to announce at the moment in terms of incremental products and strategies, but stay tuned. And I think the wealth platforms themselves remain very interested in the engagement that we have as it relates to this very topic and opportunities that we see to continue to expand the K-Series into additional directions.

Operator: Our next question comes from Bart Dziarski with RBC Capital Markets.

Bart Dziarski: I wanted to ask around in an incrementally higher rate environment, how you're evolving or adapting the value creation plans to ensure performance in private equity is maintained. You talked about a through-the-cycle acumen and you've got operational DNA. So just wanted to see how you're thinking about that in the current environment for private equity.

Scott Nuttall: Bart, it's Scott. I'll take a shot. So first thing I would say is back to the prepared remarks, we don't view this as a kind of a strange environment with rates where they are. We kind of view this as more of a return to normalcy. If you kind of put on a chart, the 10-year Treasury yield back to 1976, you'll see what I mean. The strange period was the 10-plus years where it was kind of really low, close to 0. So we don't think we need to meaningfully evolve our value creation tools. We keep adding more clearly.

But what you tend to also find in a period of time like this where rates are a little bit higher than maybe they've been is your entry multiple probably on the margin can be a bit lower. So what happens when you think about buying a business or an asset when rates are really low, you probably need to think about whether rates are going to be higher when you exit. And the answer is probably yes. So you're probably assuming you're going to have multiple contraction over the course of your ownership period. In a period of time like this, maybe that's less the case.

But our ability to kind of invest in good assets and companies and make them great is something that we have been systematically developing over the course of the 3-plus decades I've been here. And I think we're much better at it now than we've ever been. And I think that is the case regardless of if rates are at 1%, 5%, or 7%. And if you need to know what I'm talking about, kind of take a look at a buyout model and sensitize every 100 basis points of interest rate move, what does that mean to your overall return? You may pay down a little bit less debt, but that happens one time.

If you can take a business and double its profitability, you get a multiple on every incremental dollar of that profitability that you create, it's much more powerful than any impact of interest rate moves. And so in a way, if you're going to kind of buy lower and keep creating value, we actually think the return opportunity is at least as compelling as it's been. And so I appreciate you asking the question because unless you've actually been around our industry before the financial crisis, you don't know what I'm talking about. That's what actually the math shows you, and that's been our experience.

Operator: Our next question comes from Devin Ryan with Citizens Bank.

Devin Ryan: So I want to take the realization conversation from a slightly different angle. You drew the contrast of the record capital being returned by KKR to your investors this year in a year where the industry is not doing a great job of that, which is part of this kind of K-shaped narrative. So it would just be great to make this a little bit more tangible. How much are LPs actually realizing the differentiation? Is it bringing new LPs to KKR? Is it speeding up fundraising, improving cross-sell? What areas of the business are you seeing kind of the most positive sentiment?

Just trying to get to maybe more of the specific implications of that outperformance and what it means beyond what we're seeing in the actual financials today.

Scott Nuttall: Devin, it's Scott. So I just came off the road to kind of Europe, Middle East, Asia. We are definitely hearing about this from our investors. They are noticing that firms, and we're not alone, but firms like ours that have a broader, longer experience set are giving more cash back and the portfolios are performing a lot better than some others. And keep in mind, in a kind of a more normal environment, the difference between a top quartile performer in private equity and bottom quartile can be 1,600 or 1,800 basis points. So you want to be with top quartile managers.

We think that kind of differential is actually going to go up as we head into the next few years. So no doubt, the color when you're in these meetings and say, wow, you guys are doing something different. And that's why you hear the optimism in our voice. We had 2010 through 2020 that we felt we were doing the right things, portfolio construction, linear pacing, being really thoughtful about diversification, and the risks we were taking that had been informed by prior cycles we've been through. It did not matter because there was a rising tide and everybody looked smart. That was a period of time it was really straightforward to confuse a bull market with brains, right?

The reason that we're having more fun right now is that you can actually see a huge difference in kind of how we built portfolios relative to how some others have built portfolios in our space. And that's showing up in capital raising. So you can see kind of what's happened in most recent private equity and infra funds in particular. You can see that showing through. And so it's clearly showing how we're differentiated. And so it's much less frustrating time for us right now. I appreciate the question.

Operator: Our next question comes from Crispin Love with Piper Sandler.

Crispin Love: But curious if you can share your initial thoughts on the midterm elections from last week. Market seems to be trying to figure it out, but wondering your view, potential impacts to KKR and the alternatives broadly could be related to data centers or just other areas worth calling out.

Robert Lewin: Crispin, so one of the really nice things about our business model is the long duration of our capital. And so as we think about our investment periods, in most cases, they outlast political cycles, and we remind our teams of that all of the time. And so certainly, there could be some volatility coming out of the midterms and sitting here with substantial dry powder, I think that can be a real advantage for our platform, our people, our access to capital. And so we'll watch what transpires, but the benefit of our business model is we get to focus on the long term and take advantage on behalf of our clients, any kind of short-term volatility.

Operator: Our next question comes from Brian Bedell with Deutsche Bank.

Brian Bedell: I just want to come back to Cap Markets. Just in terms of the longer-term trajectory of that business, obviously, you had fantastic growth over that historically, the last 3 years, including this year is hovering more around that $1 billion level. If you can talk about what you see as the potential inflection to grow that from here on an annual basis. And you mentioned, of course, having a better contribution from GA over time. And I think you also mentioned geographically, you're looking at opportunities in Asia and what other things, I guess, on the client coverage side and product might also help inflect that.

I don't know if you're able to comment on 4Q and what you're seeing in cap markets for this upcoming 4Q as well.

Robert Lewin: Sure. Let me start with business building, which we think is a pretty exciting opportunity. And I'd really bucket it into 4 areas, Brian, for us. Number one, as KKR does more around the world and deploys more capital, we think that should be a real benefit to our capital markets platform given the resources that we have built out on the ground across the world. Number two, we have talked of the opportunity around insurance-related capital markets fees. Scott talked about the several hundred million dollar annual type of opportunity. We are making progress, but we are certainly not there, but believe with our platform and what we've created, that is certainly an attainable target for us.

Third piece of it, where I think we've got a very differentiated approach is on third-party capital markets. And the way we approach our third-party clients across the world is really with our private credit capital alongside our capital markets expertise. And so we can go to clients and be able to hold their capital structures through our private credit business, distribute their capital structures through our capital markets business. And often, it's a combination of the 2. That is a very unique approach to third-party client coverage where we can pull everything together. And we know that middle market buyouts, as an example, have been slower.

That won't stay slow forever given the amount of dry powder on the sideline, and we're really well positioned there. And then the fourth area, you hit on it in your question, is going to be Asia Pac. And as the Asia Pac markets continue to mature and become more institutionalized, I think that is an opportunity for our leading platform in the region. In terms of Q4, listen, we've got, I would say, a healthy pipeline heading into the quarter. Hopefully, we'll finish out a strong year here, but we'll see how that pipeline materializes and go through that in some detail with you on our Q4 call.

Operator: Our next question comes from Patrick Davitt with Autonomous Research.

Patrick Davitt: Since you're leaning into KKR's age and experience on the call today, I want to ask another historical perspective question related to the AI opportunity. A lot of the naysayers like to point to the fiber build-out of the late '90s as a corollary to what's happening today with the AI infrastructure build-out. So as you look at the nature of the investments you and others are doing today, I think it'd be helpful to get your historical perspective on that specific comparison and why you think this is a different and/or better investment opportunity than what you saw back then?

Scott Nuttall: Patrick, it's Scott. Thanks for the question. I think it is different. I mean I get that some aspects of it could rhyme. But if you think about back at the time of the fiber build-out, we were largely just an equity-focused firm, largely just private equity. So a pretty small percentage of the opportunity was kind of relevant to what we did at the time. Obviously, now with the capabilities we have across, in particular, infrastructure and credit and the ability that we can invest and do invest meaningfully in investment-grade opportunities, I think that is a critical distinction.

The opportunity set now, if you think about the risks we're taking, as I mentioned, we're really focused on being on the other side of highly profitable investment-grade hyperscalers and governments around the world. So as we think about the risk that we are taking as all this develops, it's quite a bit different than maybe what other people might be taking. And certainly, there are some aspects of it that as you think about people that are building data centers on spec, we don't do that.

If you think about folks that are taking risks with companies that are less investment grade in terms of their status and less cash flow that they develop from other parts of their business, we've been more cautious on that front in aggregate than the market at large. So I really do think it's about how you approach it. And given the tools we have now, I feel quite good about the risks that we're taking and hopefully the downside protection that we will have as part of how we're doing this. But it is -- has some similarities.

And I think if you're taking those types of risks, we are not, that's where I think you better make sure you're getting the reward because back to what I said, nobody really knows how this is going to play out, and that's just not what we do.

Operator: Our next question comes from Dan Welden with Wells Fargo.

Daniel F. Welden: I had a question on real estate. You talked about North American real estate equity as a deployment driver this quarter. And I wonder if you could elaborate on where you think you can underwrite the most attractive returns right now. You've talked in the past about some of the best opportunities in sort of one-off high-quality assets with motivated sellers. Are you beginning to see a broadening in the market opportunity and a greater deployment opportunity in real estate?

Craig Larson: Dan, it's Craig. Why don't I start? Look, we started our real estate business back in 2013. If you look at where we are today, we've got about $85 billion of AUM split pretty equally between credit and equity, again, with professionals now on a global basis. I think your point is well taken in terms of the opportunity today. Real estate has always been a cyclical asset class. And in our view, in pockets, you're seeing some very positive fundamentals. So I think you're seeing a decline in supply across in-favor assets where you're seeing positive demand. In our view, there are opportunities to buy assets below replacement cost.

And that's with inflation expected to continue to impact new supply at the same time. And I think all else equal, in this asset class, look, you'd rather put capital to work with a 10-year Treasury at 4.85% versus a 2% Treasury environment. So I think while capital formation has still been difficult, the investing environment for this vintage actually still feels pretty good to us. And I think for those clients that have an appetite for some cyclicality and some volatility, we're constructive on this environment.

Operator: Our next question comes from Arnaud Giblat with BNP.

Arnaud Giblat: I was wondering if you could get an update on the 401(k) opportunity and how the results of the midterm elections might have changed the time line here.

Craig Larson: Arnaud, it's Craig. Why don't I start? Thanks for the question, and thank you for being patient. Look, I think we've talked a lot on these calls historically about 401(k) and about retirement broadly. You won't be surprised to hear that we think there's a lot of industrial logic to introducing alts as individuals invest behind their future retirement and as they're thinking about asset allocations decades out. And we're -- we welcome the DOL's efforts to provide some greater clarity on how 401(k) plans can access private investments in an effort of enhancing diversification as well as risk-adjusted returns at the same time. So we think this shows progress. We think it's going to take some time.

But again, we remain very constructive on what this can mean for us over the long term. So I don't think you need to adjust your models for Q4 of '26. But as we think about the long term, we think this has an opportunity to be another meaningful tailwind for us in our industry.

Operator: We have reached the end of the question-and-answer session. I would now like to turn the call back over to Craig Larson for closing comments.

Craig Larson: Rob, first, thank you for your help in a longer call. Thank you, everybody, for your interest in KKR. Please feel free to reach out directly if you have any questions. Otherwise, we look forward to speaking with everyone in 90 days or so. Thank you so much.

Operator: This concludes today's conference. You may disconnect your lines at this time, and we thank you for your participation.

#3130. You can change Windows settings directly from a search now – how to try it

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

The latest Windows 11 Insiders Preview enhances the Search feature so that you can access specific settings right from a search window.

Microsoft has been on a kick lately trying to improve and enhance Windows 11, including sprucing up Search, which is now simpler, cleaner, and friendlier. And there’s another cool trick that Search has up its sleeve: Available in the Beta channel of the latest Windows 11 Insiders Preview, Search will give you access to specific Windows settings and commands. Known as inline actions, this latest skill is designed to help you directly complete certain tasks. That means you no longer need to know exactly where or how to find the setting you need.

Also: Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now

Curious about built-in features such as Dark mode, Bluetooth, screen brightness, Remote Desktop, the Windows clipboard, or Windows Update? Just type the name or phrase in the Search field. The results then display an Open button that you can select to go directly to the related setting.

“A new Windows Search experience built on WinUI 3 is beginning to roll out,” Microsoft said on a web page announcing the latest Insiders build. “It’s faster, more efficient, and features a streamlined design that makes results easier to scan. Inline actions let you quickly complete tasks directly. Turn on dark mode or Bluetooth, adjust your screen brightness, mute your device, or arrange windows from Windows Search.”

I tried this with several different Windows settings, and the results window pointed me to the right screens for tweaking them. Though I know where most Windows settings are located by now, there are still times when I forget how to reach certain ones. This new skill promises to be a time saver whenever I face that challenge.

Also: 11 Windows apps I replace on every new PC

Here’s another handy enhancement. How often do you type a word or term in Windows Search only to misspell it? With the latest update, Search will now better understand what you actually mean and match you with the correct results. Type “drak” instead of “dark,” for example, and you’ll still see the results for Dark mode.

Microsoft promises these latest improvements to Windows Search will continue to be fine-tuned over the next few weeks. And there’s more in the new Preview build.

Ever run into trouble using Windows Hello facial recognition in a dark area? Now, your screen will temporarily brighten up to help you sign in under those conditions. To enable this option, head to Settings, select Account, select Sign-in options, and then click Facial recognition. Turn on the switch for “Automatically adjust screen brightness during face recognition.”

The latest Insiders build also tweaks features such as Live captions, Gaming, File Explorer, and Microsoft 365 cloud storage.

Also: How I used ChatGPT to talk me through fixing a corrupted gaming PC

To grab this update, you’ll have to join the Windows Insiders Program if you’re not already registered. You can then sign up for the Beta or Experimental channel, either of which will give you access to the new Search skills and other features. Make sure you’re running the Beta Preview Build 26320.9876 or higher. To check, go to Settings, select System, and then click About. The Windows Info section will indicate the build number.

As for regular Windows users not enrolled in the Insiders Program, the new changes should reach you relatively soon. I’d expect them to roll out with the December Patch Tuesday update arriving on December 8, so that Microsoft can squeeze them in before the end of the year.

#3128. Why Nvidia Stock Was Down Today

Nvidia's board is investigating CEO Jensen Huang after reports that he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

Nvidia Corporation (NVDA -4.27%) stock fell 4.3% on Monday, Nov. 9, after the company's board opened an investigation into its own CEO, Jensen Huang.

The S&P 500 (^GSPC +2.35%) and the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +2.74%) finished up 2.4% and 2.8%, respectively.

On Sunday, Nvidia's board of directors said it was opening a probe into recent reports that Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. In a letter to employees, the Nvidia chief admitted to intimate relations with Alice Huang, an executive of the cloud computing company Megaspeed. Alice Huang is an alleged Chinese asset, according to reporting from the New York Times (NYT +5.57%).

The board said it had no reason to believe national security or Nvidia's secrets were compromised and said that it "has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team."

The story broke at an already sensitive time for chipmakers and the AI trade. Three House Republican committee chairs have already asked Jensen Huang for a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18, and it's possible that more thorough investigations follow.

None of this is going to affect the numbers Nvidia reports this quarter, but depending on the results of the board's inquiry -- or any potential government investigations -- there could be real consequences long-term. Jensen Huang is not just any CEO.

#3127. Anthropic Introduces New Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 AI Models

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Overkill for the average user, but the models are smarter than ever for professionals.

Anthropic took the wraps off yet another set of AI models on Monday, Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, which are ready to use and make substantial improvements over their predecessors. While an average user may not see the benefits of the latest models, Anthropic says they’re best for the “most ambitious, open-ended work.”

The new Claude models show greatly improved metrics in areas like coding (don’t they all?), reasoning, vision, cybersecurity and biology. The latter of which have strong safeguards against misuse in the Fable model, which give Anthropic enough confidence to release it to the public.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 generate output up to 30% faster than their predecessors and are available at lower prices — a trend we’ve continued to see lately with most new AI model releases.

Anthropic dropped a series of benchmarks showing off how much better the new models are compared with the previous ones. And generally, they’re impressive. Fable 5.2 outperforms Fable 5.1 in one agentic coding benchmark at 49.1% versus 32.4% at “Xhigh effort,” bringing a meaningful distance in performance. As far as cybersecurity benchmarks are concerned, Mythos 5.2 scores a jump from 61.7% to 76.3% — a rather impressive jump — if you’re using the model to its fullest potential.

Anthropic says Claude Mythos 5.2 is its most capable model for cybersecurity engineering. The new model is capable of catching more vulnerabilities and is better at reproducing and fixing them. That said, Mythos 5.2’s cybersecurity features are locked to a specific group right now: Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program.

The company boasted about enhanced capabilities in the latest model improvements in mathematics, science and engineering. It also says that testers of Fable 5.2 found the new model more capable of more ambiguous tasks that require abstract reasoning when it came to research and analysis.

Anthropic makes a big deal about the alignment of Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Alignment tracks whether and how the intention of the (human) user is executed by the model. And as agentic AI becomes more prevalent, there are more stories of AI deciding to go out of its way to complete a task, even with devastating consequences. Fable 5.2 includes guardrails that block risky cybersecurity activities — like penetration testing and exploit generation — and advanced biology capabilities.

#3126. We Write About Saving Money; Here’s How We Trick Our Brains Into Doing It

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Even personal finance writers and editors need psychological hacks to save money. Here are the tips we use, and why they work.

While staring at the Container Store cart on my phone at 11 p.m., I did something for the first time that I’d read about a hundred times. Instead of spending $200 on more organizational boxes that I categorically did not need, I transferred that amount to my savings account.

Normally, my willpower is no match for the very real psychological phenomenon called present bias: Our brains light up more when we’re rewarding our current selves than our future selves.

Research has also shown that you imagine your future self almost like a stranger — it’s tougher to care about that stranger than about who you are right now. But that night, I saw near-future-me using that $200 on next summer’s vacation. I wanted the vacation more than the boxes. So I abandoned my cart.

I had managed to use a psychological savings trick: Find a goal that helps you envision your future self. With this epiphany in mind, I asked some of my fellow Nerds to share the savings habits they’ve put to work in their own lives. Perhaps reading these can give late-night you some saving inspiration.

Kimberly Palmer, senior writer and spokesperson: I let nonessential items sit in my online shopping cart for at least 24 hours before buying them. It definitely makes me realize I don't need a lot of them! I also informed my children of this rule, and it has helped cut down on their requests — or at least they know they have to be patient.

Karen Gaudette Brewer, head of content: Fellow let-it-sit-in-the-cart person here. I wait for notifications that something's at least 30% off before I make any moves. Ideally, 40% to 50% off.

Julie Myhre-Nunes, managing editor: When I browse online, I add an item to my shopping cart and wait 24 to 48 hours. After that, I either decide it’s a waste of money/an impulse purchase and delete it from my cart (or forget about the cart altogether), or I decide I want it and make the purchase — it’s the former 99% of the time.

Why it works: “Waiting 1 to 2 days allows me to take the emotion out of purchasing. I no longer succumb to marketing or sales, and instead make spending decisions based on what my family and I actually need or can use.” — Julie again, eloquently making the point for me.

Caitlin Constantine, managing editor: My one real shopping weakness is books, and I’ve found I can get a very close approximation of that feeling without spending an outrageous amount of money by going to the library, wandering around the stacks to see what books might look interesting, and checking out a bunch of them. Even if I don’t end up reading them, I’m still helping the library with circulation numbers, so I see it as a win-win.

Spencer Tierney, senior writer: Plus one to Caitlin Constantine’s “my one real shopping weakness is books.” If I want an older or smaller book, I'll try to find it at one of four libraries I belong to on Libby, the library e-book reader app. (The Libby waitlist for new books can take months, so I have to account for that.)

Why it works: There’s no secret here: It’s nice to get free stuff. You might be surprised what the library has to offer, like movies, magazine subscriptions, games, classes and theater tickets.

Pamela de la Fuente, managing editor: We always tell people to automate savings, and I do in my high-yield savings account, but Dasha Kennedy, the woman behind “The Broke Black Girl”, told Elizabeth Ayoola on the Smart Money podcast that you should invest, even a little bit every week or so, for future you. So I just set up a small recurring deposit to my robo-advisor.

Why it works: You only have to make this decision once for your future self, not over and over again. And if you do it early enough, you could avoid being part of the 41% of Americans who wish they had started investing earlier, according to a 2026 NerdWallet survey.

Athena Cocoves, managing editor: To cut down on food delivery, I started cooking when I feel like it instead of when I’m supposed to. I exercise free will and make soup at 10 p.m. It sounds more obvious than it feels, and it's made a big difference in my budget. And it'd make an even bigger difference if I wasn't also rewarding myself with fancy spices and vinegars, but a girl's gotta splurge somehow.

Ryan Brady, lead writer: My wife takes advantage of a T-Mobile freebie that gives us a discount for DoorDash deliveries. She uses it to buy groceries from Aldi instead of takeout. Aldi is far from us. Publix is right across the street, but more expensive. So this saves us money on the actual items and also helps us not impulse buy (as we often do when we're in-store shopping).

Why it works: You don’t need to call on willpower if you can avoid the situation that tempts you to spend money.

» Read more: Strategies to save on groceries that actually work

Kenley Young, managing editor: I use credit cards for most purchases to get those sweet, sweet rewards, but there's a lot in this article that I've also taken to heart.

I've started using library resources more, and it's saving me money on things like monthly subscriptions.

I've negotiated down several monthly bills, too: refinanced my car loan, got cheaper homeowners insurance, opted for a little less auto coverage in exchange for a lower premium, and haggled online with everyone from Xfinity and SiriusXM to my local newspaper until they all gave me a discount.

Plus, I've opted for some home improvement projects with the expectation that my utility bills would be lower. A plumber finally fixed our toilet, which has led to lower water bills, and I even installed solar panels.

Lastly, my analog skill (playing live music) has become a steady side hustle. I play eight to 10 gigs a month, where (on top of my baseline rate) I also get tips, free food and beer.

Why it works: Because you’re Kenley and you put in a lot of effort.

But you don’t need to be Kenley to find a savings habit that works for your personality, your financial situation and even your musical talents. You just need to experiment. Pick the strategy that speaks to you most, and test it out. Which one are you going to try first?

#3125. iOS 27.3 Could Bring More Audio Intelligence and the Redesigned Health App Soon

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems

The Health app overhaul and new Apple Intelligence features lead the latest public beta.

Apple launched the first public beta of iOS 27.3 on Monday, about two months after the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro lineup and iOS 27. The headliner here is the return of the new Health app: After briefly testing the redesigned Health app in an early iOS 27.2 beta, Apple has put the app back in the recent beta cycle.

Apple historically releases an iOS update in December, so I expect iOS 27.3 to land on iPhones later this year.

Since this is a beta, I recommend downloading it only on something other than your primary device. This isn’t the final version of iOS 27.3, so the update might be buggy and battery life may be short, so it’s best to keep those troubles on a secondary device.

Also, since this isn’t the final version, there could be more features to land on your iPhone when Apple releases 27.3.

Here are some features developers and beta testers can try now in the first iOS 27.3 beta.

The redesigned Health app returns in the iOS 27.3 beta after Apple tested the feature in the iOS 27.2 beta process. Developers and beta testers can explore the refreshed app and see things like a new Longevity tab and your Health Age.

Apple wrote online that we can expect the redesigned Health app to land on devices later this year.

If developers and beta testers have an Apple Watch that is running the watchOS 27.3 beta as well as an iPhone running the iOS 27.3 beta, those folks can test out Apple’s Live Rewind and Siri Recap in Audio Intelligence.

Live Rewind allows you to pull up a text transcript of a conversation in the past 15 seconds on your Apple Watch, and Siri Recap can automatically give you a summary of meetings, conversations and other events. Live Rewind snippets are replaced by new audio and then deleted, and Siri Recaps delete themselves after seven days if you don’t manually delete them sooner. However, you can also save both of these in the Siri app and export them to the Notes or Journal apps on your iPhone.

While both Live Rewind and Siri Recap are automatically deleted over time, I’m uncomfortable with the ability to save snippets or recaps, which raises concerns about people recording my conversations without my knowledge. Even if Audio Intelligence just summarizes what I said, I still find both features creepy.

And while I recognize the utility for certain groups of people, I also think it’s better to just, y’know… talk to someone instead of asking your watch what they just said.

Each workout recommends exercises, reps, sets and weights in order to help you meet your goals. And if you’re unfamiliar with an exercise, you can also watch video tutorials to see how to perform that exercise.

Siri AI gets a huge update in the iOS 27.3 beta. The feature can now do more actions in supported apps, like Apple Music and Messages. For example, if you go into Apple Music, you can ask Siri to create a playlist for you, and in Messages, you can ask Siri to schedule, edit or unsend messages. If you open an app and ask Siri what it can do in the app, the digital assistant should give you some examples of its capabilities.

The beta also brings Siri AI to traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish and Norwegian.

StandBy mode also gets an upgrade in the iOS 27.3 beta. In the beta, you can add full weather and calendar slides to the mode and choose from more colors.

Apple introduced StandBy mode alongside iOS 17, and it was one of my favorite iPhone features. I’m happy Apple is finally showing it some love and adding more features and capabilities so it feels more like a home or desk hub.

If you’re a fan of dark mode, the iOS 27.3 beta has a treat for you. The beta gives you a new setting in Safari called Adaptive Dark Mode. When enabled, it forces dark mode onto webpages in Safari that may not have a dark mode option otherwise.

1. Tap Settings.2. Tap Apps.3. Tap Safari.4. Tap Adaptive Dark Mode.5. Tap On.

Those are a few of the new features developers can try now with the first beta of iOS 27.3. Apple has not said when exactly it will release iOS 27.3 to the general public, but we expect it to land on devices before the end of the year.

For more iOS news, here’s what to know about iOS 27.2, why you may have missed iOS 27.1 and our iOS 27 cheat sheet.

#3124. AI-Driven Tech Layoffs Could Trigger a 1.6 Million Job Recession

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

With more than 200,000 job cuts in the tech industry in 2026, the bigger question is if layoffs will spread to retail and finance.

When Meta began laying off 8,000 people in May, it felt like an omen. Meta, the parent company of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, had seen several high-profile failures, from the death of the metaverse to its multibillion-dollar court setbacks. The Magnificent Seven — the tech giants that drive US stock market gains — seemed to hit a plateau over the last year, as more investors expressed concern about a potential AI bubble.

A wave of recent tech layoffs and buyouts reveals a growing volatility in the tech industry, as major companies restructure to cut costs and redirect spending toward AI. In just the last few weeks, Google extended its voluntary buyout program to select employees in five countries, and the graphic design platform Canva reduced its staff by 22%, laying off or relocating 1,271 employees.

Companies that have laid off or offered buyouts to 1,000 or more employees this year include Microsoft (60,000), Oracle (21,000), Amazon (17,000 in addition to 14,000 in 2025), Uber (3,300) and Netflix (1,000). According to the TrueUp tech layoffs tracker, layoffs are accelerating faster than last year, with over 200,000 workers reduced so far in 2026. The cuts aren’t limited to struggling companies, but are affecting profitable organizations with strong revenues.

The dominant factor behind layoffs has been AI. Companies have spent billions of dollars on the technology, plus a terrifying $3.2 trillion (with a “T”) that, Goldman Sachs says, doesn’t show up on balance sheets. With current returns failing to justify the massive scale of capital expenditure, companies are slashing labor costs and relying on AI to offset the resulting productivity losses.

While the US isn’t officially in a recession (yet), there are growing fears that mass layoffs could spread to other sectors, such as retailers and financial companies, creating a large wave of workforce reductions in the country. Analysts warn that if job losses extend beyond the tech industry, it could result in another 1.6 million people being laid off, bringing the formal unemployment rate closer to recession-level.

With several economic pressures at play — inflation, higher interest rates and rising energy and computing costs — buyouts and layoffs allow company executives to reduce operating expenses while investing heavily in AI infrastructure, automation and specialized technical talent. That hasn’t worked out in all cases. A handful of companies, including Salesforce and Ford, ended up rehiring or hiring new people after AI-driven layoffs.

Even companies currently reducing their workforce, such as Canva, appear to be offering friendly terms, potentially to avoid burning bridges. As part of its severance package, Canva gave outgoing employees $10,000 grants, MacBooks, six months of salary and a year of healthcare. For many workers without a union contract, that will be the best-case scenario if the economy goes south.

Canva’s terms for departing employees are both exceedingly generous and a window into modern tech:* Six months salary* A year healthcare* A year of LinkedIn premium* A $10k grant to start a business* Keep your MacBook https://t.co/Hqdegdb8Ek pic.twitter.com/pKuj8lJDvB

Job instability, stagnant wages and rising prices have been the norm for several years, arguably since the last major US recession in 2020, at the start of the pandemic. Given that recessions historically occur about every six years (regardless of which party is in the White House), a larger downturn could be on the horizon, especially if an AI market correction triggers further stock declines and widespread layoffs. If high-cost data centers lose clients and major IPOs falter, enterprises will likely slash spending and jobs as the promise of AI-driven efficiency fades.

So far, layoffs don’t appear to be spreading to other industries, and overall job cuts are the lowest since 2022. But the job market has become increasingly precarious, especially for younger workers, according to Lisa Countryman-Quiroz, CEO of JVS Bay Area, a workforce nonprofit.

For example, entry-level hires are down by a third in the most AI-exposed occupations since 2021, which could affect sectors like retail and finance —typical entry-level gateways for many young people. Household wages aren’t keeping up with expenses, and many job seekers have found themselves unemployed for more than six months. “While we may or may not see broadening layoffs, I’m concerned about the erosion of stable career pathways,” Countryman-Quiroz said. The one bright spot seems to be in healthcare, with 42,000 jobs added last month.

The 2026 midterm elections could also indirectly affect tech layoffs, mainly due to changes in the political and regulatory environment around AI and data centers. In the lead-up to the midterms, the backlash against data centers and tech billionaires became a pressing issue for candidates. Campaigns around data center moratoriums helped some Democratic candidates, including Gina Hinojosa, the surprise gubernatorial winner in Texas, where Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has his home and business headquarters.

Pausing new data center construction will be a shot in the arm for communities protesting the drain of AI infrastructure on local resources. But any slowdown in the buildout could also reduce demand for construction, chip suppliers or technical roles tied to AI expansion.

The midterm elections also affected financial markets, with technology and AI-linked stocks falling as investors worried that Democrats might impose new guardrails on AI. A weaker market can often make companies more cautious about hiring, capital spending and staffing, which could exacerbate cost-cutting pressures and lead to more layoffs and buyouts.

Countryman-Quiroz suggested that Congress could address AI’s disruption by investing in more job training, especially in growing areas like healthcare. “Current federal funding is only sufficient to train about 200,000 workers per year, a fraction of what’s needed,” she said. “Workforce development has historically enjoyed bipartisan support, so there is an opportunity for both parties to work together on solutions.”

#3123. Exxon and Chevron Are Near Record Highs. Here's What History Says Happens Next.

These integrated energy giants are built to survive the entire energy cycle.

ExxonMobil (XOM -0.69%) and Chevron (CVX -0.86%) are two of the world's largest energy companies. Their share prices are high today because energy prices are high today. If history is any guide, neither of those situations will last forever. But the really important thing to understand about these two companies is that they are built to survive the entire energy cycle while still rewarding investors with dividends. Here's what you need to know.

Exxon and Chevron are what are known as integrated energy companies. That means that they have operations across the entire energy sector, from the upstream (drilling) through the midstream (pipelines) and to the downstream (chemicals and refining). That diversification is meant to help soften the impact of commodity price swings.

That said, these two energy giants remain heavily dependent on commodity prices for their revenues and earnings. When oil prices are high, they do well; when they're low, they don't do as well and can even lose money. Energy is a commodity with a long history of volatility, rising and falling in response to supply and demand, natural and man-made disasters, and geopolitical conflicts, among other things. Right now, oil prices are high due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

History is very clear: at some point the conflict will likely end, and oil prices will decline. When that happens, Exxon and Chevron's stock prices will fall. In fact, if you are patient, the best time to buy one of these companies isn't when energy prices are high, but when they are low. Of course, that requires stepping in to buy when others are selling, which can be difficult.

The thing is, Exxon and Chevron are well aware of the energy cycle and prepared to deal with it. For example, they have debt-to-equity ratios of 0.13x and 0.17x, respectively. They have the lowest leverage in their peer group. This enables the two companies to take on debt during energy downturns, allowing them to continue funding their businesses and supporting their dividends.

Dividends are a key feature here, with Exxon having increased its dividend annually for 43 consecutive years. Chevron isn't far behind at 38 years. That's the proof that their diversified business models, built atop rock-solid balance sheets, work. And it is also why these two stocks are always solid picks in the energy sector for dividend-focused investors.

Still, there are better and worse times to buy Exxon and Chevron. If you absolutely have to buy an energy stock right now, you wouldn't be making a mistake if you chose either of them. However, Exxon's yield is currently around 2.5%, while Chevron's is 3.3%. Those aren't outlandishly low figures historically, but during the deep oil downturn during the coronavirus pandemic, Exxon's yield rose above 10% and Chevron's above 9%.

To be fair, the oil downturn during the pandemic was unusually deep. However, oil downturns are very common. So if you can be patient, now might not be the best time to buy Exxon or Chevron. If you wait for an oil downturn, their stocks will likely retreat from their current highs, pushing their yields to more attractive levels.

Energy is vital to the normal functioning of the modern world. You should probably have some exposure in your portfolio, and Exxon and Chevron are both good options most of the time. However, given the volatile history of energy prices, you may want to wait to buy when oil prices, and likely the share prices of Exxon and Chevron, are lower.

#3122. Ford Just Proved Its EV Battery Health Barely Degrades After 5 Years

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

2021 Mustang Mach-E electric SUVs have kept most of their battery and range after thousands of miles on the road.

Real-world battery life for phones, laptops and other electronic devices can diminish over years of use, but does the same happen to electric cars after thousands of miles and hundreds of recharges? According to data published by Ford this week: Yes, but not as badly as you might fear.

The automaker published a report analyzing the battery state of health of more than 36,000 Mustang Mach-E electric SUVs sold to customers across the US and Canada during the initial 2021 model year. After more than five years on the road — and an estimated 2 billion cumulative miles driven — the fleet averaged 92% battery health.

I call that impressive, but not totally surprising. That battery durability data is largely in line with what I’ve seen reported across the industry by other automakers and independent analysts.

One of the biggest concerns of early EV adopters a decade ago (also shared by fence-sitters today) is long-term reliability. The battery is by far the most expensive component of an electric car, and owners want to know their shiny new EV will last as long as the combustion car it replaces.

Battery longevity is particularly important as more used EVs enter the market. Many experts (myself included) have touted pre-owned and off-lease EV deals as a way to bypass the electric-car price premium, but shoppers may be hesitant to roll the dice on higher-mileage vehicles. Many fear a used EV won’t meet their range needs or, worse, could blindside them with an expensive battery replacement.

Ford’s study is another data point that could help allay those worries.

Ford examined more than 36,000 individual vehicles delivered to customers across all 50 US states and Canada during the EV’s first year of sales. A little more than five years later, the automaker says that around 95% of vehicles surveyed retained between 87% and 97% of their battery health (an average of 92%) across the entire 2021 fleet after an estimated 2 billion cumulative miles driven.

Better battery health means an EV keeps delivering more of its advertised range as the odometer climbs. The 2021 Mustang Mach-E rolled off the assembly line with an EPA-estimated range between 211 and 305 miles, depending on the spec, which means that owners lost around 16 to 24 miles of range over time, according to my back-of-the-napkin math.

That said, there’s no beating the chemistry. Around 2,000 vehicles in the group crossed the 100,000-mile mark, retaining around 91% health. A smaller subset of about 30 drivers reached 200,000 miles in their Mach-Es, with an average battery health of 88%. More miles, it seems, means more wear.

At the extreme anecdotal end of the spectrum, one owner put more than 400,000 miles on his original battery — though Ford didn’t state the specific health of that 2022 Mach-E.

An independent study published by Aviloo earlier this year adds credence to Ford’s reported numbers. An Austrian EV battery diagnostics firm analyzed over 500,000 EVs from 20 global brands to measure battery degradation — at 50,000, 100,000 and 150,000 kilometers — finding that many popular models maintained over 90% battery health at high mileage.

Tesla’s Model Y, which competes directly with the Mach-E, was found to hold around 90.3% battery health at 150,000 kilometers (93,205 miles). Aviloo reported that the Volkswagen ID4 and Hyundai Ioniq 5 showed 90.6% and 92.8% retention, respectively, over the same surveyed mileage. The first-generation Nissan Leaf — a much older EV with a smaller battery — showed more degradation at 86.3%, an unfortunate double whammy given its shorter initial range.

According to Ford’s engineers and battery chemists, the Mach-E’s battery was designed to last at least 10 years, adding that the 2021 models in the study use an older nickel-cobalt-manganese, or NCM, chemistry.

Ford’s new Universal Electric Vehicle platform, which will underpin the upcoming Fathom small electric pickup, will use a newer lithium iron phosphate chemistry. That will come with unique charging needs and different battery management calibration than its Class of 2021. The UEV architecture is also built around robust bidirectional charging, so we’ll have to check back in five or so years to see how using your car to power your home affects long-term battery health.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates dropped today, but inflation data could shake things up next week.

With the midterm elections behind us, mortgage rates are continuing their gradual slide this month. One factor is a sell-off in tech stocks, which can send investors toward the relative safety of bonds and help push mortgage rates lower.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 6.96% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is five basis points lower than yesterday and 11 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Meanwhile, a stronger-than-expected jobs report could slow that slide by reinforcing expectations for another Federal Reserve rate hike in December.

And a reminder: While the economy never sleeps, markets are closed on the weekends. The rates you see Friday are unlikely to change much (if at all) until Monday.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

As for what’s next: Tomorrow’s jobs report, showing October data, could potentially nudge mortgage rates in either direction. To understand the link between jobs data and mortgage rates, keep reading below the video.

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

The recent slide in mortgage rates might reverse course if next week’s inflation data comes in hot.

This week, the Nerds are watching the October Consumer Price Index, which comes out on Tuesday, Nov. 10. CPI is one of two key measures of inflation, which the Federal Reserve aims to keep in check relative to the strength of the labor market. (The Fed looks more closely at the other data set, the Personal Consumption Expenditures Index, which comes out Nov. 25.)

Right now, the labor market is looking pretty darn healthy: The October jobs report, released today from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, showed U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far more than economists expected, and unemployment edged down to 4.1%.

Raising the federal funds rate is the Fed’s main tool for bringing inflation down, but rate hikes are only on the table when the labor market is strong enough to handle it. Right now, it’s looking fairly likely that the Fed will approve a rate hike when the committee meets Dec. 8-9. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but an anticipated rate hike can put upward pressure on mortgage rates, which respond to investors’ expectations for the economy and Fed policy.

Still, a jump in mortgage rates isn’t a sure thing. October’s inflation data will capture the effect of the Fed’s last rate hike, which came in the middle of September. If that worked as expected and inflation shows signs of slowing, mortgage rates will be less affected.
