#3113. GCM Grosvenor (GCMG) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Fee-related earnings climbed as infrastructure and absolute return platforms scaled.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

GCM Grosvenor Inc. (GCMG +6.24%) reported growth across its alternative asset management platform, primarily driven by double-digit increases in fee-paying assets and fee-related earnings. Management highlighted the scalability of its infrastructure and credit verticals, noting that specialized funds and customized separate accounts continue to serve as primary fundraising engines. The company achieved a higher fee-related earnings margin of 47%, reflecting technology-driven efficiencies and stable operating expenses. Strategic expansion into the insurance and individual investor channels has diversified the client base, with 30% of year-to-date fundraising originating from new relationships.

Operator: Good day, and welcome to the GCM Grosvenor Third Quarter 2026 Results Webcast. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this call will be recorded. And I would now like to hand the call over to Stacie Selinger, Head of Investor Relations. You may begin.

Stacie Selinger: Thank you. Welcome to GCM Grosvenor's Third Quarter Call. Today, I am joined by GCM Grosvenor's Chairman and CEO, Michael Sacks; President, Jon Levin; and Chief Financial Officer, Pam Bentley. As a reminder, all statements made on this call that do not relate to matters of historical facts should be considered forward-looking statements. This includes statements regarding our current expectations for the business, our financial performance and projections. These statements are neither promises, nor guarantees and involve risks and uncertainties that may cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to the Risk Factors section in our filings for additional information. We will also refer to non-GAAP measures that are important in assessing our business.

Reconciliations to the nearest GAAP measures are available in our earnings presentation and supplement on our website. With that, I will turn the call over to Michael.

Michael Sacks: Thanks, Stacie. We are pleased to report another strong quarter for GCM Grosvenor. Our assets under management of $98 billion is up 13% year-over-year, and our fee-paying assets under management of $78 billion is up 11% year-over-year. Compared to the third quarter of last year, fee-related revenue grew 10%, fee-related earnings grew 15% and adjusted net income grew 20%. We raised $2.7 billion this quarter and $10 billion over the last 12 months.

Our fundraising was supported by 2 complementary growth engines: the first is our customized separate account business where high client retention, recurring re-ups and expansion into new strategies provide a consistent source of fundraising; the second is our growing specialized fund franchises, where we typically have 5 to 10 funds in market at any given time. We held several fund closings this quarter and looking ahead to 2027, we see meaningful fundraising opportunities across both separate accounts and specialized funds. Importantly, 30% of our year-to-date fundraising has come from new clients. As we illustrated at our Investor Day, our investor relationships are sticky and grow over time.

That dynamic, combined with our contracted not yet fee-paying AUM balance of $10.6 billion bodes well for future growth. Our fundraising pipeline is full with our near-term pipeline 20% larger than it was a year ago. We remain confident that second half fundraising will exceed first half fundraising and believe full year fundraising for 2026 will rival full year fundraising for 2025. With regard to investment performance, we believe we are well positioned to navigate an unsettled market environment, which is notable for high volatility, interest rate fluctuation and technological disruption.

Our fundamental diversification across investment strategies and within those investment strategies by asset class, geography, industry and investment style, benefits our clients and provides a stable growing firm for shareholders. Our absolute return strategies business is a good illustration of this. Our multi-strategy composite was down 2% in the third quarter on a gross basis, influenced in part by the movement in SpaceX. However, ARS has enjoyed excellent year-to-date and recent results with composite gross returns of 13% year-to-date, nearly 19% over the past year and 15% annualized over 3 years through September. Despite a tough October for hedge funds, our highly diversified approach continues to add value for clients and our ARS vertical continues to experience net capital inflows.

ARS fee-paying AUM was $28 billion at quarter end, up 18% year-over-year and an 11% compound annual growth rate since the end of 2023. ARS net flows have been positive for the last 4 consecutive quarters, and we expect positive inflows in the fourth quarter of this year. Our ARS pipeline is the strongest it has been in recent memory. Our accrued unrealized performance fees from ARS portfolios stood at $49 million at the end of October. In private markets, we've delivered for our clients with positive performance for every strategy and sub strategy over the last year. We have talked about how infrastructure and credit are firing on all cylinders, and that continues to play out.

In private equity, which generally has been the slowest of private market strategies across the industry, we see some promise as private equity represented approximately 1/4 of our fundraising over the last year. Private equity co-investment realizations are up approximately 50% by number of transactions and are also up nicely on a dollar basis in 2026. Within private markets broadly, we remain pleased with the quality of our investment activity and the opportunity set. Grosvenor continues to enjoy significant upside from incentive fees, particularly our unrealized carried interest balance. Unrealized carry at net asset value reached a new high of approximately $1.1 billion at quarter end.

Firm's share of unrealized carry at net asset value was $592 million, an increase of approximately $100 million from June 30. While realization timing cannot be predicted with accuracy, that balance represents strong embedded future earnings. The rapid pace of technological change is creating both opportunities and concerns across the market, particularly with regard to AI and the AI data center and power-related capital cycle. We've spoken for several quarters about why we believe our platform is well positioned in this environment, and we continue to hold that belief.

We spoke last quarter about our investment in SpaceX, which is a good example of our origination capabilities that resulted in the largest single investment gain in the history of the firm. We successfully monetized more than $500 million of that investment in the third quarter and firm-wide exposure was just north of $3 billion at the end of the quarter. Our emphasis on diversification in our infrastructure vertical, one of the fastest-growing areas of the firm, has enabled us to make good investments in digital infrastructure and power without taking lopsided risks in any particular sector.

As an example, when we look at our firm-wide AUM, data centers represent around 1% of our total AUM and 5% of infrastructure AUM. A substantial majority of that exposure relates to investments made more than 4 years ago. We remain confident in our Investor Day guidance, including with regard to 2028 adjusted net income and believe we have more upside than downside relative to that guidance. Our margins continue to grow and free cash flow generation can support stock buybacks or dividend increases in the future. We will continue to focus on delivering quality returns and service for our clients and growth in profits for shareholders. And with that, I'll turn the call over to Jon.

Jonathan Levin: Thank you, Michael. This quarter, I'm going to focus on investments we've made to create new sources of growth. We target opportunities where our investment capabilities and client relationships provide an advantage while maintaining financial discipline. There are several investments we've made over the past several years that highlight this approach. First, direct infrastructure. In 2018, we leveraged our established infrastructure platform and deep relationships in the multiemployer pension community to launch a direct investment strategy, leveraging our labor and government expertise to create a competitive advantage for infrastructure investing. Today, that strategy manages approximately $3 billion, contributing to our broader $20 billion infrastructure business, which has grown at a 24% annual rate since 2020.

It's a great example of building on existing strengths to create new growth opportunities, and we believe there's significant runway ahead for that business. Second, we've invested in credit for decades, but our recent growth reflects strategic decisions that we've made over the past several years. We integrated our public and private credit teams to leverage our full sourcing capabilities, expanded into small and emerging managers and strengthened our co-investment and secondaries expertise. In doing so, we positioned ourselves ahead of growing client demand for direct-oriented private credit strategies and greater portfolio diversification. The results speak for themselves. We've raised approximately $4 billion for credit over the last 2 years, nearly half in direct-oriented strategies.

We now manage approximately $2 billion in credit co-investments and recently closed our inaugural credit secondaries fund at $1.2 billion, including related vehicles. We believe these strategies are still in the early stages with meaningful growth potential ahead. We've taken a similar approach to expanding our distribution capabilities. In 2021, we launched a dedicated insurance solutions team and have since raised more than $4 billion through that channel. Insurance has contributed approximately 12% of our fundraising over the last 2 years despite representing just 5% of AUM. Today, we manage approximately $5 billion for 50 insurance clients, offering customized solutions through separate accounts, specialized funds and structured products, including 2 collateralized fund obligations.

Our ability to combine investment expertise with flexible structuring and delivery is a key differentiator. And again, we believe this is an area with significant opportunity for growth. Our individual investor channel provides another example of investing ahead of what we think is a long-term secular growth opportunity. While we've had success with wirehouses for over a decade, in recent years, we've invested in both distribution, such as with the launch of our Grove Lane joint venture, and in product. Since the start of 2020, we've raised nearly $5 billion from individual investors split evenly between ARS and private markets. Approximately $2 billion has come through wirehouses where we've built partnerships with most major platforms.

Our success has also been highly global. 41% of that capital was raised in the U.S., 36% in Europe and 23% in APAC. This channel will take time to scale, but momentum is building. We raised approximately $1.5 billion from individual investors so far this year or 23% of our fundraising and individual investor AUM has grown approximately 40% year-over-year to $5.3 billion. We're also investing deliberately in registered products and distribution, and we believe the opportunity remains very large relative to our current position. Combined with our recurring revenue base and scalable platform, our growth investments provide significant future upside and multiple paths to achieving our long-term objectives. And with that, I'll turn it over to Pam.

Pamela Bentley: Thanks, Jon. We are pleased with our third quarter results, which demonstrate continuing growth in recurring revenues and earnings across the platform. Private markets management fees were $66 million in the quarter, up 7% year-over-year. We continue to benefit from fundraising and the deployment of previously committed capital. Looking ahead, we expect fourth quarter private markets management fees to increase 7% to 9% as compared with the fourth quarter of '25. Absolute return strategies management fees were $47 million, up 19% year-over-year, driven by investment performance and positive flows. For the fourth quarter, we expect ARS management fees to increase in the mid-teens year-over-year. Taking these factors together, total fee-related revenue was $115 million for the quarter, up 10% year-over-year.

Turning to expenses. We continue to invest thoughtfully, while remaining focused on efficiency and operating leverage, and we are definitely seeing the benefits of optimizing technology. Third quarter FRE compensation and benefits remained relatively consistent from the prior quarter at $39 million. We expect fourth quarter FRE compensation and benefits to be approximately $1 million higher than the fourth quarter of 2025. Non-GAAP general and administrative and other expenses were $22 million in the third quarter, and we expect a consistent level of G&A expenses in the fourth quarter. Putting these elements together, fee-related earnings were approximately $54 million for the quarter, up 15% year-over-year, and our FRE margin expanded to 47% from 45% a year ago.

Adjusted net income was $45 million, up 20% and adjusted net income per share was $0.22, up 16% year-over-year. Turning to incentive fees. We realized approximately $25 million of gross incentive fees in the quarter, consisting of $23 million of carried interest and $2 million of performance fees. As of September 30, our gross unrealized carried interest balance was approximately $1.1 billion, with $592 million representing the firm share. As a reminder, private market valuations, including those relevant to the balance, are generally reflected on a 1-quarter lag. The majority of annual performance fees typically crystallize in the fourth quarter.

And as of the end of October, we had $49 million of accrued unrealized performance fees, driven by strong year-to-date performance in ARS. Actual fees will depend on investment performance and applicable fund terms through the relevant crystallization dates. Moving to capital allocation. Our balance sheet remains strong, and we continue to invest for growth, while returning capital to shareholders. Our Board has approved a quarterly dividend of $0.12 per share, and we ended the quarter with approximately $54 million remaining under our share repurchase authorization. We are pleased with the momentum in our business and our ability to deliver strong results, while continuing to invest in the platform. We are now happy to take your questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] We will take our first question from Crispin Love with Piper Sandler.

Crispin Love: Just first on ARS, definitely a standout year so far, but just plenty of volatility in the last few weeks, rates, data center financing fears, the midterms. You did call out a tough October for hedge funds, and we've all seen the headlines. But just curious on your latest thoughts there and if you would expect a significant impact, whether it's from flows or performance kind of near term? Near term it looks pretty good based on your comments, but then it -- further as you look out to '27?

Michael Sacks: Yes. I think -- thanks, Crispin. It's Michael. I think that the picture today is a very good one. We've experienced net inflows the last several quarters, and we were clear on the call, we see -- we'll have net inflows in Q4. In markets like this, hedge funds are a pretty good option. They have a lot of -- a diversified hedge fund portfolio has a lot of features that sort of naturally manage the volatility, naturally provide diversification.

And so there's a lot of good there in markets like this. And I think the sophisticated institutional investor base that we have, sees that, appreciates that, likes that. And the performance over any reasonable time period has been quite good for a while. There's been a lot of alpha there. And so we think we're in a constructive environment. And most importantly, we mentioned our pipeline, which is where we have the most short intermediate-term volatility, our pipeline is up a lot. So we're constructive there, even though we like our 3-year number of a 19% CAGR better than our 1-year number.

Crispin Love: Perfect. I appreciate that. And then your comments on fundraising on the call seem very positive kind of looking out. But drilling into that a little bit deeper, just specifically on the individual investor channel, can you just drill into that on fundraising and individual investor, the outlook over the near to intermediate term? It's definitely a growth area for you guys. So just curious on the outlook there?

Michael Sacks: Yes. Our outlook there remains -- so first, your interpretation of our comments on fundraising generally and our outlook is correct. And for us to say that we think the full year '26 can rival full year '25 is not an insignificant thing in terms of what that implies for Q4. It doesn't mean we get all the way there. But that's a pretty strong statement with regard to our expectations for Q4. The individual investor is -- offers a tremendous amount of opportunity and growth and -- for Grosvenor, for the whole industry, we've talked about that a lot.

We continue to raise there at a rate well in excess of what the individual investor represents in our total AUM. The rest of the firm is growing, so it's hard to flip those numbers, so to speak, but we continue to raise there at a very significant rate. I think it was 23% of our fundraising year-to-date, it's up 40% year-over-year. Our -- The AUM of the individual investors is up 40% year-over-year. And so we just think that space is going to continue to grow. And as we've talked about in the past, it grows through a number of different efforts, meaning product on shelf, but also meaning private label partnership, also meaning firm-level partnership.

So we have a lot of ways to win there, and we just look forward to continuing to build that out.

Operator: We will take our next question from Bill Katz with TD Cowen.

Ryan Langston: This is Ryan on for Bill. I was just wondering if we could expand on the commentary on the ARS pipeline? So is -- what's driving the growth, current clients increasing their allocations? Or is it also new clients signing on board? Michael Sacks: Yes. So it's all of the above. We're winning new mandates from new clients. We're winning hedge fund mandates from existing clients. But usually, there's just a market movement and hedge funds have delivered for a while. And again, the attraction is to some significant degree, just the inherent diversification, the inherent sort of shock absorbers inside the portfolios like these. And that combined with their recent performance makes it interesting.

Ryan Langston: Great. And also, if we could just stick on fundraising. On specialized funds, which funds drove the inflows in the quarter? And what's going to be -- what funds should we expect to be in the market next quarter and for next year, across which asset classes?

Michael Sacks: So we mentioned in the script that we have 5 or 10 funds in market at -- pretty much at all times. And so it's hard to sort of do -- each fund raised this much money in this period of time and is open until this period of time. I think that the growth of that business makes that a little more challenging to report out on and track and model. We do have, as we mentioned, a number of funds. From the beginning of the year, we've been seeing low catch-up fees this year. The funds in market are sort of freshly in market and/or don't have catch-up fees. So I don't expect that this year.

But next year we will have funds in market, that have been in market a little longer, that have catch-up fees or that are newly in market. So I think that next year, we -- a lot of funds in market where the momentum has started and we've had first closes and we're now moving on towards second closes, final closes, things like that. So we're anticipating, as we said, a good year for specialized fundraising next year.

Jonathan Levin: Just to give you a sense of it to put some further detail around it. For our private market specialized funds, if you look at it on a year-to-date basis, just to give you a little more sense than just 1 quarter, there was probably about 7 funds that contributed to the specialized fundraising. Some of the bigger ones I would call out would be our MAC fund. We are still in market with both, some direct infrastructure product as well as diverse infrastructure product. We're in market with secondaries product. And obviously, you have your evergreen funds like your Interval fund for infrastructure.

And then at all times, you have various evergreen products available in the ARS business as well. So it's pretty broadly diversified, to Michael's point. I would expect, as Michael said, like that will kind of be the story going forward as well, where there will be many different drivers of that number. And what we will always endeavor to do is to make sure that you all understand which of those funds are relevant from a catch-up fee perspective and the timing around that so that we can make sure people can understand that from a modeling perspective.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] We will take our next question from Ken Worthington with JPMorgan.

Kenneth Worthington: When we look at CNYFPAUM, $8.7 billion will become fee-paying as invested. Over what period is that $8.7 billion likely to be invested? And is that investment likely to be even over the term or more front-end or back-end loaded?

Michael Sacks: I think, Ken, a conservative way -- it's Michael, by the way. Thanks for the question. I think a conservative way for you to think about it is 3 years, maybe that equal weighted. The reality is, I think it probably is a little bit more front-end weighted. But I just think if you're modeling it, that, that's kind of a conservative way to think about it. It doesn't mean it couldn't stretch a little longer than that. But I think that's where I would -- how I would suggest you model it on a base case.

Kenneth Worthington: Great. And then you mentioned catch-up fees earlier and kind of highlighted that we still shouldn't expect much for catch-up fees in 4Q. As we're thinking about these funds being more tenured in 2027, is there a past year that 2027 might look like from a catch-up fee perspective that we can get a rough idea of what to expect for next year?

Michael Sacks: I think it's hard to pick out like a given -- a particular year, and we are not prepared today to give sort of guidance on that. But we will keep our eye on that and probably talk about that a little bit more next quarter.

Operator: We will take our next question from Jeff Schmitt with William Blair.

Jeffrey Schmitt: The -- On the SpaceX realizations, how much occurred in private markets funds that were already in a positive carry position? And can you help us think about how those realizations should translate into carried interest in Q4 and then the outlook for additional realizations from here?

Michael Sacks: Yes. I think the best way to answer that is -- and Jon, Pam can jump in and help me. But I think the best way to answer that is that the carry revenue that we've seen thus far is not significantly attributable to -- in private markets, it's not significantly attributable to SpaceX. When you start talking about in-carry position, you start to -- and by the way, first, it's hard to ever say anything is directly attributable to something unless you are both in carry position, which a lot of our funds are, but you're also through your waterfall on DPI where you're sharing in the carry, right?

So there's being in carry position and obviously, with a close to $600 million firm share of carry it in NAV, which is the amount of money that would come to the firm if everything were liquidated as of the last quarter. We're clearly in carry position in a lot of places, and that grew by $100 million in the quarter, and some of that is the SpaceX mark, and it's great. But you have to look at the fund level -- so you're in carry position, but where are you in the waterfall? And that's an equally important question as to being in carry position.

And so I think we still have our very best days ahead of us in terms of revenue -- realized revenue from carry. And I think that $600 million, $590 million firm share of carry is your biggest and best indicator there. We have sold, as we mentioned, SpaceX in Q3. We're continuing to sell SpaceX in Q4, and that is -- it has contributed to carry -- has or will contribute to performance fees based on marks. And it's obviously just an overall positive for the firm.

Jeffrey Schmitt: Okay. Great. And then the insurance, it continues to be a strong fundraising channel for you. And just given the scrutiny around private credit right now, have you seen any change in insurance company demand or a shift in their allocations toward infrastructure secondaries or other strategies?

Jonathan Levin: No, I think -- this is Jon. Thanks for the question. I think in general, we view the insurance opportunity in a similar manner to the individual investor opportunity in which you'll have, I'm sure, bumps along the road, whether it's private credit or whatever the concerns of the day might be, but you have a secular trend of a current asset allocation towards alternatives that is lower than what the target asset allocation towards alternatives is. And I think that, that will be a very strong driver of opportunity for us for a while.

And what I would say about the specific question on private credit, and we've talked about this on some of our previous calls, our goal with everything that we do, and I think it's particularly important in credit investing generally, is to provide diversified open architecture, broad solutions that's diversified on every kind of metric in terms of the different food groups within private credit, sponsor lending, asset finance, geography, size, all of those metrics that are very, very important. Also diversification with respect to implementation, fund investing, co-investing, secondary investing.

And so we closed -- when we closed our inaugural private credit secondaries fund, one of the big drivers of capital formation for that fund was insurance companies looking to create a diversified solution with some J-curve mitigation, with some return options, optionality to the upside relative to kind of a traditional implementation style. So will everything always be linear? No. Will there be different challenges that come along the way? Sure. But for us, we see that as still a great growth opportunity. And importantly, I think we see the way in which we can provide solutions to insurance companies gives us an advantage when you have dislocations or concerns, whatever the word might be in the market environment.

Operator: We will take our next question from Chris Kotowski with Oppenheimer.

Christoph Kotowski: I just noticed, like your customized separate accounts were still up growing like nicely double digits, like 11% or more. And a number of your peers, that has slowed down, in some cases down to the kind of low single digits as they say more institutions are going for the kind of evergreen fund structure. And I know you have a couple in the market, but I'm wondering, do you see that demand on the institutional side for the evergreen fund structures and maybe is there the demand there? And is it less of a heavy lift than doing the retail route for the evergreen fund structures?

Jonathan Levin: I'm happy to... Go ahead, Michael.

Michael Sacks: I'm going to take it, Jon, and then ask you to kind of finish up. What I will say is the wealth channel, the individual investor channels dominated by evergreen or open-end structures. The institutional channel is not. There has always been, and it is a kind of constant conversation, some debate between closed-end structure or evergreen structure. I think that -- and then the market has historically been dominated by closed-end. Solutions and custom separate accounts are a bit of a hybrid, and the clients are, I think, coming around very clearly to liking those custom separate accounts and liking a solutions approach.

It seems a lot of providers -- that everybody kind of wants to be a solutions company these days -- a solutions provider these days. And so our pipeline is full with no shift in the mix of what we provide, which is both Evergreen and closed-end and custom separate account solutions. And it is a -- the pipeline is full. There is demand, and we see plenty of growth, as we kind of pointed to in our comments. So I don't think there's a, like a real preference there or anything that I would call a market shift or materially easier to raise money institutionally in one place or the other or any change in that.

I think that has been a conversation for a while, and it almost comes down to preference of a particular investor or preference of a particular consultant.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I will now turn the conference back to Ms. Selinger for any additional or closing remarks.

Stacie Selinger: Thank you very much for everyone who joined us this morning. We appreciate the questions and the engagement. If you do have follow-ups, very happy to take them offline. And otherwise, we look forward to seeing you next quarter.

#3110. Affiliated Managers (AMG) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Record alternatives inflows and buybacks fueled a strong quarter for the manager.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Affiliated Managers Group, Inc. (AMG +5.56%) reported record quarterly results as the company continued its strategic evolution toward alternative investment strategies. Management reported that assets under management reached an all-time high, supported by record inflows into alternatives and strong investment performance. The company stated that alternatives now account for approximately two-thirds of EBITDA on a run-rate basis, up from approximately one-third seven years ago. Management indicated that its business model generates significant unencumbered cash flow, which the company intends to deploy toward new affiliate investments, supporting existing affiliates, and share repurchases. CFO Dava Ritchea noted that organic growth in the alternatives segment was driven by four specific secular trends: secondaries, infrastructure, absolute return, and tax-aware strategies.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to the AMG Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. I'd now like to turn the call over to your host, Patricia Figueroa, Head of Investor Relations for AMG. Thank you. You may begin.

Patricia Figueroa: Good morning, and thank you for joining us today to discuss AMG's results for the third quarter of 2026. Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that during this call, we may make a number of forward-looking statements, which could differ from our actual results materially due to a number of factors, including those described in today's earnings press release and our most recent Form 10-K and subsequent filings with the SEC. AMG assumes no obligation to update these statements. Also, please note that nothing on this call constitutes an offer of any products, investment vehicles or services of any AMG affiliate.

A replay of today's call will be available on the Investor Relations section of our website, along with a copy of our earnings release and reconciliations of any non-GAAP financial measures, including any earnings guidance provided. In addition, we have posted an updated investor presentation to our website and encourage investors to consult our site regularly for updated information. With us today to discuss the company's results for the quarter are Jay Horgen, President and Chief Executive Officer; and Dava Ritchea, Chief Financial Officer. With that, I'll turn the call over to Jay.

Jay Horgen: Thanks, Patricia, and good morning, everyone. Today, AMG reported another quarter of record results. Given the quality of our earnings and the scale of our business, AMG's profile has never been more compelling. AUM, aggregate fees, fee-related earnings, adjusted EBITDA, economic earnings per share and organic flows into alternatives were all at record levels in the third quarter. On a year-to-date basis, AMG generated nearly $1 billion in adjusted EBITDA and $26 in economic earnings per share, representing growth of 41% and 56% year-over-year, respectively.

To put these impressive results in perspective, in just 3 quarters, our business generated economic earnings per share roughly equivalent to what we delivered in all of 2025, and nearly 95% of that was driven by fee-related earnings. AMG also delivered its sixth consecutive quarter of net inflows. With $21 billion in net inflows in the quarter and $85 billion over the last 18 months, our business continues to generate strong organic growth. And these results understate the exceptional momentum in higher fee, higher-margin alternative strategies, which attracted more than $31 billion in net inflows in the quarter and $150 billion over the past 6 quarters.

Assets under management increased to a record $974 billion, driven by our affiliates' growth through both net inflows and investment performance, setting the stage for ongoing earnings growth momentum in the fourth quarter and into next year. And given AMG's significant growth, our increasingly attractive alternatives profile and the compelling valuation of our shares, we stepped up our repurchases meaningfully, deploying $400 million in the quarter and bringing our year-to-date total share repurchases to $775 million. The momentum across our business is a direct result of the successful execution of our strategy to evolve our earnings profile towards alternatives.

After nearly 20 years at AMG, I am very proud of our team's many accomplishments, but the one that stands out the most is the transformational impact of the strategic shift towards alternatives that we embarked on in 2019. In just 7 years, we will have evolved from generating less than 35% of our earnings from alternative strategies to nearly 70%. It is a remarkable transformation, underscoring the power of disciplined and deliberate capital allocation and the advantages of our unique business model, particularly our strong cash flow generation and our ability to redeploy that cash to areas of secular growth.

Today, AMG's earnings profile is that of a diversified alternatives business across private markets and liquid alternatives, characterized by high growth, high fee, high margin and long-duration assets. As we have discussed over recent quarters, 4 secular trends continue to drive our organic growth profile. First, the accelerating client demand worldwide for secondary strategies across private markets. Second, the ongoing client demand for infrastructure strategies broadly. Third, the growing appetite for absolute return strategies within client portfolios; and fourth, the continued expansion of tax-aware investing.

Together, these 4 growth areas, secondary solutions, infrastructure, absolute return strategies and tax-aware strategies contributed to our record alternative inflows in the quarter and have been the driving force behind the $150 billion in net inflows into our affiliates' alternative strategies over the past 6 quarters. Our affiliates' performance across private markets and liquid alternatives has been outstanding. And with clients increasingly seeking differentiated sources of return and diversification against the backdrop of a more complex market environment, we have high conviction that these strategies can be a powerful growth driver for years to come.

More broadly, over the last 12 months, our assets under management have increased by approximately $170 billion or 21%, including $69 billion as a result of new affiliate investments. Following an active first half, including the completion of our investments in BBH Credit Partners, HighBrook Investors and an incremental minority investment in Garda Capital Partners, our investment pipeline remains strong. We are excited to execute on our opportunity set and form additional new partnerships that further diversify our business and drive additional earnings growth. AMG is a strategic partner that can magnify the competitive advantages of partner-owned firms while preserving the very thing that makes them so special, their independence.

No other institutional partner can match our 3-decade track record in meeting the needs of and magnifying the opportunities for independent firms, which is why AMG's unique partnership approach continues to strongly resonate with prospective affiliates. And given our competitive differentiation, our robust capital position and our pipeline of new prospects, we have a sizable opportunity to drive additional earnings growth and further evolve our business profile by forming new partnerships as well as investing in and alongside our existing affiliates. AMG's business is highly diversified across nearly 40 affiliates operating in private markets, liquid alternatives and differentiated long-only strategies.

This unique business profile generates significant unencumbered cash flow, enabling us to navigate periods of uncertainty and changing market conditions while also making accretive investments in new and existing affiliates. In addition, given our forward growth prospects and the strength of our capital position, we have been a buyer of AMG shares in size, repurchasing approximately 2.3 million shares or 9% of the shares outstanding through the third quarter and 30% since the beginning of 2024. And we expect to continue to take advantage of this truly unique opportunity to invest in industry-leading growth through a diversified alternatives business at an extremely attractive price. That is, we will continue to invest in AMG itself.

Our alternatives profile and our ability to invest substantial capital in the areas of highest growth and return across new and existing affiliates and in our own shares provides us with the opportunity to continue to generate a long-term compound annual growth rate in economic earnings per share between 15% and 20% as we have done over the past 5 years. And given the ongoing successful execution of our strategy, that growth rate has accelerated. In 2025, we generated growth in economic earnings per share of more than 20%, and we expect that growth rate to more than double to approximately 50% in 2026.

As we look ahead, our capital allocation decision-making will continue to be by far the most impactful element of our strategy. We expect our cumulative free cash flow over the next 5 to 7 years to approximate our entire current market capitalization enabling us to continue to strategically evolve AMG's business towards areas of growth in our industry. And with our unique partnership-centric cash-generative, return-focused model, we will continue to deploy that capital with discipline, further diversifying and enhancing our earnings power and our ability to create long-term value for our shareholders. And with that, I'll turn it over to Dava.

Dava Ritchea: Thank you, Jay, and good morning, everyone. AMG's outstanding third quarter results reflect the ongoing evolution of our business towards differentiated alternative strategies with durable client demand trends. This strategic evolution continues to expand our earnings base and enhance our earnings quality. Four complementary factors drove our results: strong organic growth, investment performance, growing contributions from recent investments and the impact of share repurchases. The momentum across these factors, together with our balance sheet strength and financial flexibility, further enhances our ability to continue to execute our growth and capital allocation strategy.

In the third quarter, AMG's assets under management ended at a record level of $974 billion, up 3% compared to the prior quarter, driven by strong liquid alternative investment performance and alternative net inflows. On an LTM basis, AUM increased 21% due to investment performance, strong organic growth in alternative strategies, including record fundraising in private markets and the addition of new affiliates. Turning to flows. AMG's affiliates generated net client cash flows of $21 billion in the quarter, including a record of more than $31 billion in alternatives.

Over the last 12 months, firm-wide net client cash flows were $68 billion, representing 9% organic growth, including $113 billion in alternatives, driven by the 4 key growth areas Jay highlighted: secondaries, infrastructure, absolute return strategies and tax-aware investing. This activity reflects sustained client demand for liquid alternatives and private market solutions as well as our affiliates reach across the institutional and wealth channels. Given that many of the strategies attracting assets carry higher fee rates and margins, the impact of these flows on adjusted EBITDA is approximately 2x what the organic growth rate alone would imply. Private markets were a standout this quarter.

Our affiliates raised $10 billion in the quarter and a record $30 billion over the last 12 months, representing 21% organic growth. Fundraising was broad-based across secondaries, infrastructure and specialized private market strategies with contributions from several affiliates. The diversity across our 11 private markets affiliates with $161 billion in total AUM underpins a more durable fundraising profile and a more consistent organic growth rate over time. Capital raised in these strategies is typically committed to long-duration locked-up vehicles that generate management fees and the potential for carried interest. AMG participates directly in the margin expansion of these businesses, which provides further uplift to our earnings profile as they grow.

Liquid alternatives generated $22 billion of net inflows in the quarter, driven by demand for absolute return and tax-aware strategies. Year-to-date performance has further enhanced the appeal of these strategies, building on our long-term investment track records and highlighting the diversification and resilience they bring to client portfolios. Our affiliates now manage $338 billion in liquid alternatives, and together with private markets, our alternative affiliates manage approximately $500 billion and contribute approximately 2/3 of our EBITDA on a run rate basis. These inflows were partially offset by $12 billion of net outflows from differentiated long-only equities, consistent with the trends we've discussed in recent quarters and with the broader industry.

While these strategies account for a declining share of our overall AUM and earnings, we continue to see pockets of strength within the category, supported by strong long-term investment track records at certain affiliates. Multi-asset and fixed income generated $1 billion of net inflows in the quarter, reflecting continued demand for credit-oriented strategies across retail and institutional channels. In aggregate, our third quarter flows further increased the earnings and organic growth contribution from alternatives. Growth across a broad range of affiliates, strategies and client channels underscores the value of AMG's diversified model. We are well positioned to generate sustained positive organic growth over the long term. Turning to third quarter financial results.

Adjusted EBITDA was $354 million, an increase of 41% year-over-year. Underlying fee-related earnings increased 35%, driven by organic growth, investment performance and margin expansion at certain affiliates. In addition, we recognized $14 million of net performance fees and $15 million of incremental fees, primarily from private market catch-up fees. Economic earnings per share grew 56% year-over-year to a quarterly record of $9.50, reflecting higher adjusted EBITDA and the benefit of our ongoing share repurchase activity, which has reduced our average economic share count by approximately 11% compared to the prior year period. Our third quarter results build on strong performance in the first half of the year.

For the first 9 months of 2026, adjusted EBITDA grew 41% year-over-year to $987 million, reflecting organic growth, investment performance, margin expansion at certain affiliates and contributions from recent new investments. Economic earnings per share grew 56% year-over-year to $26, further benefiting from share repurchases. Now moving to fourth quarter guidance. We expect adjusted EBITDA to be in the range of $405 million to $475 million based on current AUM levels, reflecting our market blend, which was down 2% quarter-to-date as of November 6. This includes recurring fee-related earnings of $335 million to $345 million, up from $325 million in Q3. Our outlook assumes no material private market catch-up fees.

We anticipate net performance fees in the range of $70 million to $130 million, bringing the full year net performance fee earnings to approximately $145 million to $205 million, which at the midpoint is in line with our 5-year average. We expect fourth quarter economic earnings per share to be between $11.37 and $13.43, assuming an adjusted weighted average share count of 25.1 million for the quarter. Finally, turning to the balance sheet and capital allocation. We repurchased approximately $400 million of AMG common stock in the quarter, bringing year-to-date repurchases to approximately $775 million. We are increasing our full year 2026 repurchase guidance to more than $900 million, subject to market conditions and capital allocation activity through year-end.

At this pace, we expect to reduce our average economic share count by 10% this year and by approximately 30% since the start of 2024. Our balance sheet remains in a strong position with leverage below our historical average levels despite substantial capital returns and growth investments earlier this year. Growth in fee-related earnings has increased our recurring annual after-tax cash flow to more than $1 billion, expanding the earnings base supporting our leverage capacity. With our significant free cash flow, long-dated debt maturity profile and access to the capital markets, we have substantial flexibility to fund attractive growth investments while continuing to return capital to shareholders.

In summary, our results in the quarter and so far in 2026 demonstrate the superior earnings quality and growing earnings power of AMG's business. Looking ahead, AMG's strong organic growth, our affiliates' excellent investment performance, the growing contribution from recent new investments and our disciplined approach to capital return will together support a stronger forward earnings trajectory. With substantial financial flexibility, we remain well positioned to invest for growth and compound shareholder value over time. Now we are happy to take your questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from the line of Alex Blostein with Goldman Sachs.

Alexander Blostein: Jay, I wanted to go back to the point you made around just the amount of free cash flow the business generates over 5-ish years or so essentially equal to your market cap, which is a pretty powerful statement. As you think about deploying that capital and just the technicals around the buyback, given how much you guys have done over the years, is there just a natural limit in terms of how much more share repurchases you guys could just practically do given the float on the public size? Or therefore, if that's the case, should we be thinking more deals on the forward? Or do you think you have flexibility to kind of keep the two fairly balanced?

Jay Horgen: Yes. Thanks, Alex. So yes, let's talk about that. I think it has been the thing that's driven AMG over the last 5 to 7 years, which is our free cash flow. And just to maybe say it again, we believe that our free cash flow over the next 5 to 7 years will approximate our entire market capitalization. That incorporates our view of the current cash flow that we're receiving and also an implied growth rate on that cash flow as we see these long-term secular trends continuing to power our business and just making sure that I mentioned those, that's the secondaries, infrastructure, absolute return and tax-aware that continue to drive the flows.

That cash flow that we're receiving, we can deploy it in many different ways. We can deploy it into new affiliates through our origination efforts, we have an active pipeline of making new investments. And then we can invest in existing affiliates, both in and alongside those affiliates, whether that's increasing our stake in an affiliate or investing in seed products for our affiliates or investing in resources platforms to help our affiliates grow, magnify their benefits. So we actually have quite a number of ways to use our capital to help our affiliates grow as well, as you point out.

And then as it relates to investing in what we believe to be one of the fastest-growing asset management businesses with one of the best profiles and one of the most compelling valuations, which is AMG itself. Yes, we continue to, and we've actually stepped up our repurchases in AMG shares. I think that the natural limit to us repurchasing is a long way off. Our dollar-weighted volume has actually gone up over the years. You can see that if you do longer-term trend analysis on AMG. And I think in the medium, maybe even to the long term, we think we'll be a buyer of our shares.

We do not offer a dividend or at least a very small dividend, I should say. And we like that capital flexibility to repurchase our shares. It's a way that we compound earnings -- it's a way that we are able to offer excess returns to our shareholders. It gives us the opportunity to measure our success not only through making new investments, but also to invest directly in our own business because we believe in that business. When you think about the way AMG grows, it really grows in several different ways.

We obviously have the existing business that can grow both through flows, which we've shown over the last 6 quarters to be meaningful, investment performance and that investment performance compounds over time. We can invest in new affiliates, which we've done and proven over many, many years, and we can invest in ourselves through repurchases. So when you add all that up, we believe that we'll continue to grow at 15% to 20%, just like we have done over the last 5 years. And so we think we have ample opportunity both in making new investments as well as repurchasing our shares.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Bill Katz with TD Cowen.

William Katz: I'm going to ask for two, if that's okay. Just to follow up on Alex's question. I guess the broader question is, what's the utility to remain a public company since you don't really use equity in your transactions given your statement about cash flow growth versus where the multiple is on the stock. And then the other question I have for you is just in terms of following the elections last week, just 2 areas I think folks are probably interested in would be sort of the outlook for the infrastructure business as well as tax-aware and how I think about the resilience of that just given the shift in leadership in Washington.

Jay Horgen: Yes. Thanks, Bill. Both good questions. I'll take them in the order in which you gave them. So first, just on why does AMG need to be public. I think the short answer is we believe it is valuable to be public. So let me just make a couple of points, I think, that are unique to our model. First, I think given the long-term nature of our partnership model, which you all know well, our core promise is to support independence. So permanent capital and permanence more broadly support our competitive advantage in attracting new affiliates. And it also enables us to invest in and alongside those existing affiliates because we have a long-term view.

I guess my second point would be, and I guess, related to the prior point, if we did go private, that would likely be disruptive to our affiliates and their clients. And so it would increase the risk across our franchise. Other benefits of being public, I think, are obvious. Our ability to access the public debt markets as well as the AMG brand in the market. It continues to be important. It's a competitive advantage to us, lets us have an attractive cost of capital, tremendous flexibility. We like repurchasing our shares, for example.

So I mean, I guess that maybe leads to my final point, which is given the volatility in our shares, it allows us to take advantage of dislocations like we did this last quarter, repurchasing $400 million worth of our shares. So we've seen tremendous value creation in that for our shareholders. So maybe now turning to your question on sort of the changing political landscape. I guess you won't be surprised that I'll say I think it's too early to tell. It's pretty fresh. I think it's too early to tell on any of the 4 trends that have been driving our organic growth into alternatives for the last several years.

Those 4 areas are the secondary solutions in private markets, the growing interest in infrastructure strategies, the need for absolute return as a diversifier in client portfolios and tax-aware. It is -- it has been, and I think it is continuing to be our view that these 4 trends -- each of these 4 trends, they all have long-term tailwinds, and we will expect them to continue to contribute to our earnings growth. But maybe related to the first question that Alex asked, our business model it's really unique. It makes us more agile. We are highly diversified across 40 affiliates operating in private markets, liquid alternatives and differentiated long-only strategies. Today, nearly 70% of our EBITDA comes from alternatives.

This diversified group of firms, they generate significant unencumbered cash flow. It provides us significant flexibility to continue to reshape our business profile toward the most attractive growth areas as they emerge. So we can further diversify our business and allow us to navigate the changing market environment. This statement that we expect to receive our entire market cap back in cash flow over the next 5 to 7 years, well, it allows us to reshape our business if needed. But I think at the moment, we think the trends that are affecting our business will continue to power our flows.

So we're excited about these trends, and we're also excited about looking for the new emerging client demand trends and using our flexible cash flow to make those investments. So we believe we're in the best position as a capital allocation business, one where we believe we have great discipline to be able to evolve our business to the areas of highest growth and return. Thanks, Bill.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Dan Fannon with Jefferies.

Daniel Fannon: So I was hoping just to dig in a bit more around the flows and the diversity of them in the quarter. You've obviously talked about the themes that are powering these that you think are sustainable. But can you talk about either at an affiliate level or strategy level, both on the liquid and illiquid side in terms of the diversity across those trends or affiliates to provide some additional context?

Dava Ritchea: Sure, Dan. I'm happy to take that one. First, I would say organic growth has just been exceptional recently. We've generated record alternative net inflows of more than $31 billion in Q3 and $113 billion over the last 12 months. Flows have been broad-based across the 4 themes that Jay discussed; infrastructure, secondary solutions, absolute return and after-tax investing. And that's what's driven a firm-wide organic growth of nearly 10% over the past year. Within private markets, Q3 was a record quarter and capped 12 months of fundraising, generating 20% organic growth in long-duration assets that support recurring management fees with future carry potential.

These results reflect the breadth of our platform and our 11 affiliates are raising capital across multiple strategies, vehicles and channels with strong demand in infrastructure and real assets, secondaries and specialized areas like decarbonization and health care. In liquid alts, we generated nearly 40% organic growth over the past 12 months. That was led by tax-aware strategies, while the rest of the business also grew 14% on strong institutional demand across multiple affiliates. Our affiliates are benefiting from broader industry trends of increased allocations to liquid alternatives, particularly to the largest managers. And we believe the market conditions and investor sentiment will continue to attract flows to this asset class.

Over the past 7 years, we've been positioning the business for growth with the objective of creating higher quality, more diversified earnings. And these results show that shift towards alternatives is working, and we believe it gives us a strong foundation for sustained positive growth over the long term. Thanks for the question.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Craig Siegenthaler with Bank of America.

Craig Siegenthaler: Jay, congrats on another good flow quarter here.

Craig Siegenthaler: So for a question, I wanted to dive a little deeper on the long/short tax-aware suite. As you know, there were a few developments in the quarter. One of the largest RIA custodians started capping new accounts and the second largest one still has a pause in place. But this really didn't seem to impact your strong liquid alt flows given new platform additions. Also, we just had a midterm election. So the blue sweep could indicate higher taxes longer term. This can make these products more valuable. But last point, there has been some news out of the IRS and U.S. Treasury around these products.

So I know there's a lot of moving pieces, but this business has become incredibly important to your net flow trajectory. So I'm wondering if you could provide some perspective around these headwinds and tailwinds.

Jay Horgen: Sure. Thanks, Craig. I'm going to say one thing before I jump right into the answer to your question. I think there was an implication that you made in that last statement, which I think I will just take issue with. We had a record private markets flow quarter here. I don't want that to get lost on anyone. It was a tremendous quarter for us for private markets and really over the last 6 quarters have really over the last 2 years have been really strong for private markets. And the other thing that I want to just point out is that the quality of our earnings have gone up.

95% -- just under 95% of our earnings year-to-date have been fee related. And year-to-date, we've had economic earnings per share equivalent to all of last year. So just wanted to make these 2 points because there were some implications in what you just said that I disagree with. But let me just take all of those questions that you just asked and point out that there is a lot of viewpoints on this topic, including insights that AQR itself has posted on its website at aqr.com. And I'll just mention that first. And then let me tell you kind of where I think we are on the tax-aware evolution.

And I think you pointed out there's some headwinds and tailwinds, but maybe, in our view, more headwinds -- sorry, more tailwinds, excuse me, than headwinds because the history on this has gone way back. Tax-aware has been around for 30 years. So there's a lot of activity recently, but it's really just a continuation that's been going on for a really long time. That long/short liquid alts, it's just the next generation of these products. And so maybe to talk about where we think we are now on this journey, we're about 3 years into it for AMG.

It's generated significant inflows, as you point out, but it has still been just a contributor to the 4 main trends that we're experiencing, reminding you, those are secondary solutions, infrastructure and absolute return. Each of those other 3 strategies have generated significant inflows into AMG. So where we are in 2026? At the end of 2026 with tax-aware, there are multiple managers, multiple products, multiple channels and a broad swath of the advisory community accessing these tools to not only achieve excellent pretax returns, but also to achieve better after-tax returns. But the ecosystem is evolving. It's continuing to evolve.

And the availability of these strategies are expanding, including more firms with institutional prime brokerage capabilities, more products being offered. And so I think this ecosystem is really in the broad adoption phase, and we expect it to continue to expand because the mindset shift on the part of the clients and advisers, it's not a tactical one. It's a strategic asset allocation shift, and it will impact portfolios and all asset classes, in our opinion, for years to come. We see the opportunity to continue to generate net organic growth here at AMG for several reasons. And the first is AQR is an incredibly innovative firm, and it has very strong pretax returns.

As we all know, performance is an important indicator of future flows. In addition, we expect the turnover in these products to be low. Investors typically integrate these strategies into a long-term broader financial plan. And we expect net contributions from existing clients to continue as they experience the benefits of these strategies. So we do think that tax-aware, along with the other 3 major secular trends will continue to be a positive contributor to our flows. And for all these reasons, we think it's a durable growth trend. Thanks, Craig for your question.

Operator: Our final question this morning will come from the line of Brian Bedell with Deutsche Bank.

Brian Bedell: Maybe shifting to, I would say, organic base fee growth that's exceeding the organic AUM growth, and that's evidenced by the improvement in the overall EBITDA realization rate even after you strip out performance fees and catch-up fees. So Jay, can you talk about the sustainability of that even in, let's say, a scenario, let's say, where tax-aware inflows slow down dramatically, not go to outflows, but just slow down substantially. I know AQR is a substantial contributor to given your ownership contributor to the higher fees.

But even in that scenario, are you confident the breadth of the rest of your franchise, particularly in private markets and other absolute return strategies could potentially keep that organic base fee growth rate exceeding the AUM growth rate and have improvement?

Jay Horgen: Yes. Thanks, Brian, for your question. And good question. It is a nuanced question, but I'll let Dava, and I'll try not to steal her thunder here on a couple of these points. Maybe just to couch it in the history of AMG, as you all probably recall, for the first 1 to 2 decades of AMG, we were largely a revenue share business. And that is not the case today. So in general, we own margin at our affiliates, more than half of our affiliates, we own margin. And when you overlay that with private markets and liquid alternatives, it's almost exclusively margin.

So maybe that's right around the moment where I'll turn it over to Dava just to couch it in that history. But just to talk about the sustainability of it, it's the largest part of our business, and it is overlapping with the nearly 70% that is alternatives. So it is endemic into our business today that we have margin expansion opportunity. So maybe now I'll turn it to Dava to talk a little bit more about how we're experiencing and what we're experiencing.

Dava Ritchea: Thanks, Jay. And I think that let me just echo a couple of the points that Jay made because they're really starting the foundation of what we have seen as the shift in our business towards alternatives and how that impacts the bottom line EBITDA. So that first shift really coming from moving the alternatives business from about 35% of EBITDA to 70% over time. And that has led to what we believe to be much more durable long-term organic growth trends. The second as Jay mentioned was in many of our alt businesses and particularly some of our largest, we own that underlying margin. And so as our affiliates grow their businesses, we are experiencing that margin expansion.

The third point is, as we're growing in alternatives, it is shifting the business towards higher management fee products, which leads to a higher management fee contribution to EBITDA. These tend to also be in longer locked strategies. And in some cases, they also have future performance fee and longer-dated carry potential. So all of those factors combined are what's driving that overall margin growth rate to be about 2x what we're seeing in our organic flow rate.

Operator: Ladies and gentlemen, that concludes our question-and-answer session and we will conclude our call today. We thank you for your interest and participation. You may now disconnect your lines.

#3108. Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling

A version of the S&P 500 without AI briefly pulled ahead of the traditional index this year and is now neck-and-neck as investors rotate into other areas of the market.

A proprietary Goldman Sachs index tracking the S&P 500 without stocks classified as "AI enablers" was up 12.4% through Oct. 22, edging ahead of the standard S&P 500's 12% gain. The Goldman index is now neck-and-neck with the S&P 500 as tech rallied in Monday trading.

Tech and AI-related companies make up about 45% of the S&P 500. That heavy weighting has helped power the index for years, but it's turned into a liability lately; the S&P 500 tech sector is down about 7% this month while other sectors have held up.

Investors have soured on debt and equity issued by companies like CoreWeave and Oracle. Shares of Meta Platforms sank almost 7% Thursday after it outlined more plans to spend heavily on capex and issue additional shares.

Companies supplying power and equipment for the buildout have been hit hard — names like GE Vernova, Bloom Energy, Vistra and Quanta Services all suffered steep declines during the recent selloff.

Goldman, which launched the measure earlier this year with S&P, uses the S&P 500 as its starting universe and excludes companies perceived to be enablers of AI before applying S&P 500 Index weighting methodology to the remaining universe of companies.

The ex-AI index lagged the S&P 500 for most of the year as investors continued to favor chipmakers, cloud-computing companies and other firms benefiting from heavy AI spending. However, that advantage has been narrowing and it disappeared last week.

Meanwhile, investors are rotating into defensive areas. ETFs like State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF, State Street Health Select SPDR ETF and State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF are up 7% to 10% this month. Energy is ahead 10% too, though that's more related to the war in Iran.

Some analysts recommend sticking with non-AI companies for diversification and protection against more pain in tech. The "AI pendulum has swung back in favor of non-AI exposure over the last two weeks," Oppenheimer technical analyst Ari Wald said in a note on Oct. 24.

Two industries that Oppenheimer favors now are commercial services and insurance. The firm upgraded those industries to overweight last week, recommending Republic Services, Cintas, Verisk Analytics, Broadridge Financial Solutions, MetLife and Arthur J. Gallagher.

Berkshire Hathaway is also capitalizing on the rotation out of tech. Its Class B shares are up 8% this month, though it's still lagging behind the S&P 500 this year.

Berkshire owns a wide swath of operating companies, including insurance giant Geico and Burlington Northern Santa Fe railroad. It also has a $364 billion stock portfolio including companies like Apple, Coca-Cola, Alphabet and Bank of America. That diversification may help Berkshire continue to outperform if the tech sector drags down the S&P 500.

Trivector Research sees potential in "non-tech compounders." Healthcare giant Eli Lilly is one idea. The stock is up 22% on the strength of Lilly's weight-loss drugs. The company has more in the pipeline, including a next-generation obesity drug that Lilly plans to file for FDA approval early in 2027.

Viking Holdings, a cruise operator, is also proving durable. The company said on its August earnings call that 40% of its river capacity and 60% of its ocean capacity was already booked for 2027. "Based on recent events, we've seen our guests have proved to be resilient and are continuing to book 2027 and future seasons," the company told investors.

Viking stock is up 15% this year but it may still have upside. The average Wall Street target is $109, above recent prices around $82. Barclays recently upgraded the cruise operator to overweight with a $102 target, citing the company's "compelling risk/reward."

TL;DR: Mortgage rates went up today, but they're still in a much better place than this time last month.

Mortgage rates are higher today, but only by a little. And they're still hovering below 7%, which is much better than what we saw around this time last month.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked up to 6.98% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is two basis points higher than Friday and five basis points higher than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Mortgage rates have more room to rise, as a stronger-than-expected jobs report reinforced expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike in December.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

As for what’s next: Tomorrow’s jobs report, showing October data, could potentially nudge mortgage rates in either direction. To understand the link between jobs data and mortgage rates, keep reading below the video.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds are watching the October Consumer Price Index, which comes out on Tuesday. CPI is one of two key measures of inflation, which the Federal Reserve aims to keep in check relative to the strength of the labor market. (The Fed looks more closely at a different inflation measure, the Personal Consumption Expenditures Index, which comes out Nov. 25.)

Right now, the labor market is looking pretty darn strong: The October jobs report, released Friday from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, showed U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far more than economists expected, and unemployment edged down to 4.1%.

Raising the federal funds rate is the Fed’s main tool for bringing inflation down, but rate hikes are only on the table when the labor market is strong enough to handle it. Considering Friday’s jobs data, it’s looking fairly likely that the Fed will approve a rate hike when the committee meets Dec. 8-9. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but an anticipated rate hike can put upward pressure on mortgage rates, which respond to investors’ expectations for the economy and Fed policy.

Still, a jump in mortgage rates isn’t a sure thing, and market sentiment could shift over the next month. October’s inflation data will capture the effect of the Fed’s last rate hike, which came in the middle of September. If that worked as intended and inflation shows signs of slowing, mortgage rates might remain around 7%.

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.48% or higher.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

#3105. Ionis (IONS) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Launch ramp slows and cash flow breakeven shifts a year to 2029.

Ionis Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (IONS -21.36%) is managing multiple commercial launches while navigating pipeline setbacks and updated sales forecasts. Management reported total revenue of $243 million for the third quarter, a 55% increase year over year when excluding a prior-year onetime payment. The company reduced its full-year TRYNGOLZA net product sales target to approximately $50 million due to a more gradual launch ramp but reaffirmed its total revenue range based on strength in the DAWNZERA franchise and partnership milestones. Recent clinical milestones included approvals for ZANVASTRO and HIBSAGO along with positive Phase 3 readouts for sefaxersen and ulefnersen. Management extended the projected timeline for sustained positive cash flow by one year to 2029, citing the impact of the TRYNGOLZA ramp and setbacks in two late-stage neurology and cardiovascular programs.

Brett Monia: Thanks, Wade. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us on today's call.
