In addition to TRYNGOLZA for FCS and DAWNZERA for HAE, our Ionis-owned commercial portfolio now includes TRYNGOLZA for severe hypertriglyceridemia or sHTG, our first launch in a large patient population and ZANVASTRO, our first independent launch in neurology. Although 2 recent Phase III readouts did not deliver the outcomes we hoped for, we have achieved a number of other important firsts for patients across our business that position us for further growth.

This includes the approval of HIBSAGO for chronic hepatitis B virus in the U.S. and Japan and positive Phase III results for Sefaxersen in IgA nephropathy and ulefnersen in FUS-ALS. Our substantial progress keeps us on track to achieve our full year 2026 total revenue, operating loss and cash guidance, and DAWNZERA's continued positive momentum supports our confidence in achieving its 2026 product sales guidance. For TRYNGOLZA, we are lowering our 2026 full year revenue guidance to approximately $50 million to reflect a more gradual launch ramp than we had anticipated.

As the first and only treatment approved to reduce triglycerides and the risk of acute pancreatitis in people living with sHTG, TRYNGOLZA requires HCPs to adopt a new approach to patient care, which takes time. In these early days, we are encouraged by the fundamentals underlying the launch, including strong physician enthusiasm. We are refining our launch tactics to translate this enthusiasm into action. We've identified key executional priorities and implemented specific initiatives across these priorities, which Kyle will discuss in detail. Importantly, we remain confident in TRYNGOLZA's multibillion-dollar peak sales potential. Beyond TRYNGOLZA, Kyle will provide further perspective on DAWNZERA and share initial insights on ZANVASTRO.

Holly will then go over our recent pipeline progress, and Beth will review our third quarter results and outlook for the rest of 2026. And with that, I'll turn the call over to Kyle.

Kyle Jenne: Thank you, Brett. I'd like to start by recognizing our highly engaged commercial team for their dedication to bringing important medicines to patients. Their deep expertise, strong commitment to each of our launches and clear priorities to expand physician adoption and help patients access treatment gives us confidence in our ability to drive growth across our commercial portfolio. Following TRYNGOLZA's June approval for sHTG, HCPs continue to express strong enthusiasm for TRYNGOLZA's compelling clinical profile, including placebo-adjusted mean reductions in triglycerides of up to 72% and a favorable safety and tolerability profile. These triglyceride reductions resulted in a profound reduction in acute pancreatitis events by up to 91%.

Physicians also appreciate the dosing flexibility and are prescribing both the 50- and 80-milligram doses, allowing them to tailor treatment to individual patient needs. For patients, TRYNGOLZA offers the convenience of a once-monthly auto-injector that can be self-administered in about 10 seconds. We are seeing HCPs prescribe TRYNGOLZA for high-risk sHTG patients who are the focus of our initial commercial efforts. These are patients with triglyceride levels of 880 milligrams per deciliter or higher or 500 or higher with a history of acute pancreatitis or other comorbidities. We are also seeing prescribing beyond our initial focus, consistent with the broad sHTG label. Our post-launch market research reinforces HCP's strong intent to prescribe TRYNGOLZA.

As we establish a new treatment paradigm, we are focused on translating the strong intent to prescribe into action with 3 executional priorities designed to increase prescribing and help patients move efficiently from prescription to treatment. First, we are focused on broadening the prescriber base, specifically among high-priority physicians who care for high-risk sHTG patients. We are accelerating our education efforts across these specialists and practice teams to increase their understanding of the burden of sHTG, the risk of acute pancreatitis and TRYNGOLZA's demonstrated ability to reduce that risk.

In parallel, we are supporting patient education through HCP conversations with their patients and patient support programs so that people living with sHTG better understand their disease, the importance of treatment and the role TRYNGOLZA can play in reducing triglycerides and the risk of acute pancreatitis. Our field teams are meeting more frequently with high-priority HCPs who have not yet prescribed to instill a sense of urgency in patient identification and treatment. The goal is to help physicians incorporate TRYNGOLZA into routine care for appropriate patients. From sHTG approval to the end of September, approximately 1,500 prescribers across all anticipated specialties had prescribed TRYNGOLZA.

In the weeks since our field team put these initiatives into action, our initial prescriber base has started to broaden further. Second, we are focused on increasing the depth of prescribing among HCPs who are early adopters of TRYNGOLZA. Since the sHTG launch through the end of September, approximately 24% of prescribers had written more than one prescription. Prescribers want to see how a patient responds to treatment before prescribing more broadly, consistent with how HCPs often adopt new specialty medicines. We saw a similar pattern when we launched in FCS, where physicians became more confident prescribing TRYNGOLZA as they gained experience and observed its impact.

While the sHTG population is much broader, our FCS experience gives us confidence that TRYNGOLZA's novel mechanism of action and groundbreaking patient outcomes can support broader prescribing over time. Our field team is executing on this priority by following up with prescribers to discuss their initial treatment experience and support them in identifying additional patients who may benefit from TRYNGOLZA. Notably, we have seen recent increases in repeat prescribing, suggesting these efforts are starting to have an impact. Third, we are working to make the path from prescription to treatment more efficient. As expected at this early stage of the launch, a majority of TRYNGOLZA prescriptions required a medical exception.

Some physicians are hesitant to prescribe newly approved therapies broadly before formal coverage is in place, a pattern seen in other specialty launches, especially in the cardiovascular space. To address this, our dedicated access team is educating physician offices on the reimbursement process and payer requirements. Additionally, we have a Quick Start program that enables patients to begin TRYNGOLZA treatment while coverage is being secured. The program has been well received with meaningful utilization to date, and we expect it to continue to expand. Ionis Every Step, our patient support program, also helps eligible patients navigate the insurance process and access treatment. We are working with payers to establish coverage policies and are making good progress.

By the end of September, plans representing 33% of commercial lives had added the sHTG indication for TRYNGOLZA to their formularies. Importantly, all current policies provide coverage aligned with the broad TRYNGOLZA label for adults with triglyceride levels of 500 or higher, extending beyond the high-risk patients who represent our initial commercial focus. As payers review the reimbursement policies for TRYNGOLZA, we are on track for additional policies to take effect this year with more expected throughout 2027. As we address these early launch dynamics, we remain confident in TRYNGOLZA's potential to achieve more than $3 billion in peak annual sales. That confidence begins with the substantial unmet need.

More than 3 million people in the U.S. have sHTG, including approximately 1 million high-risk sHTG patients. TRYNGOLZA's efficacy, dosing flexibility and self-administered auto-injector provide a compelling profile for these patients. As we establish a new treatment paradigm and build the market, our priorities are clear: broaden and deepen prescribing and improve payer access to simplify the path to treatment. While we recognize it will take some time for these initiatives to deliver accelerating prescription volume, we are confident our actions position TRYNGOLZA for future growth. Outside the U.S., Sobi is continuing to advance the launch in FCS while preparing for the upcoming anticipated broader launch in sHTG following the recent positive CHMP opinion. Turning to DAWNZERA.

The launch continues to gain momentum with product sales increasing substantially each quarter since launch. DAWNZERA has continued to capture a meaningful share of the U.S. HAE prophylaxis market where adoption is largely driven by patients switching therapies. We are seeing a growing base of repeat prescribers alongside adoption by patients with different treatment histories. In addition to growth from patients switching from other prophylactic therapies, we have also seen patients initiate DAWNZERA treatment who were previously only using on-demand treatment or who were treatment-naive. Physician and patient feedback has been positive, highlighting DAWNZERA's strong efficacy and favorable safety, differentiated RNA-targeted mechanism and compelling switch data.

Its patient-friendly profile, including dosing every 4 or 8 weeks with a self-administered auto-injector, is also resonating with physicians and patients. DAWNZERA has been a key driver of commercial revenue growth through the third quarter. Its growing base of repeat prescribers and adoption across patients with different treatment histories give us confidence in continued growth ahead. Outside the U.S., DAWNZERA access has continued to expand through our partners. This progress includes the recent approval in Canada and advancement of the European launch with positive reimbursement decisions in multiple countries and additional market access activities underway. Turning to ZANVASTRO.

The recent approval provides children and adults with Alexander disease, the first FDA-approved disease-modifying treatment for this progressive and often fatal neurological disorder. As planned, we were able to get ZANVASTRO into the channel shortly after approval, and I'm pleased to share that the first patients have received commercial treatment. Our launch is centered on 4 priorities. First, we are working to transition patients receiving ZANVASTRO through the clinical study or expanded access program to commercial therapy while ensuring continuity of care. This will take time as patients await their next quarterly dose, institutions navigate reimbursement and some patients move to treatment centers closer to home.

Second, we are engaging physicians who care for patients already diagnosed with Alexander disease to provide education on ZANVASTRO and support access for appropriate patients. Although exact prevalence is not well understood, the U.S. prevalence is estimated to be approximately 300 people with about half identified through medical claims. Third, we are raising disease awareness to help identify additional undiagnosed patients. Our focus is on approximately 25 neurology centers, including 12 leukodystrophy centers of excellence with disease education extending to physicians outside this network. Fourth, we are working with payers and treatment centers to establish coverage and access. ZANVASTRO is administered quarterly by intrathecal injection and reimbursed as a medical benefit.

So providing education on the buy-and-bill process is an important part of our launch execution. Our Ionis Every Step program for ZANVASTRO is tailored to the Alexander disease community, providing education and assistance navigating the reimbursement process for patients and families and access and reimbursement support for health care providers and site staff. We expect uptake to increase as patients from our clinical studies and expanded access program transition to commercial treatment, additional patients are identified and access is established. Outside the U.S., Recordati is planning for regulatory filings in the EU and Japan next year with additional submissions to follow. Across our multiple ongoing launches, our priorities are clear.

Our team is focused, energized and committed to delivering on these priorities for patients. With that, I'll turn the call over to Holly.

Holly Kordasiewicz: Thanks, Kyle. This quarter, we made important progress across our wholly owned and partnered pipeline, advancing medicines with the potential to transform care for people with serious diseases. At the European Society of Cardiology Congress in August, we presented new data, reinforcing our leadership in the management of severe hypertriglyceridemia. This included positive long-term data for TRYNGOLZA, the first and only approved treatment to reduce triglycerides and the risk of acute pancreatitis in adults with sHTG. In the CORE and CORE2 open-label extension study, TRYNGOLZA delivered substantial and sustained triglyceride reductions for up to 2 years of treatment. More than 90% of patients achieved levels below 500 mg/dL and nearly 60% achieved normal levels.

Patients also achieved persistent reductions in the risk of acute pancreatitis and the safety and tolerability profile remained favorable. These findings further strengthen TRYNGOLZA's clinical profile, reinforcing its durability and long-term safety profile, both of which are essential in treating a chronic disease like sHTG. Beyond sHTG, our leading neurology pipeline continues to make exceptional progress, highlighted by the recent approval of ZANVASTRO. ZANVASTRO is the first and only disease-modifying treatment for Alexander disease, an ultra-rare progressive and often fatal neurological disorder. We were pleased that the FDA approved ZANVASTRO with a broad label for children and adults. This approval builds on our long history of discovering and developing first-in-class treatments for rare neurological diseases.

Today, our leading neurology pipeline includes 7 wholly owned medicines targeting challenging diseases such as Dravet syndrome, prion disease, and Angelman syndrome. In light of the recent results from the ASPIRE study of apazunersen, I'll review obudanersen for Angelman syndrome and our design of the Phase III REVEAL study. Obudanersen is a product of Ionis chemistry and know-how in delivering breakthrough treatments for CNS diseases, experiences that led to SPINRAZA, QALSODY and ZANVASTRO, groundbreaking approved medicines for devastating neurological diseases. We are evaluating an 80-milligram dose in REVEAL, which was the maximal dose we evaluated in the Phase I/II HALOS open-label extension study.

Based on our data, we believe that the apazunersen dose in ASPIRE was not high enough to be efficacious. Equally important is our choice of endpoints. The primary endpoint in our REVEAL study is expressive communication, measured using the Bayley-4. We selected this endpoint because expressive communication remains stable in natural history data, but showed robust improvement with obudanersen treatment in HALOS. With up to 2 years of treatment data in HALOS, we continue to see durable improvement in expressive communication and other functional domains relative to natural history. We plan to publish an update of our long-term extension study soon and look forward to Phase III results in the second half of next year.

HIBSAGO, partnered with GSK, was recently approved in the U.S. and Japan as the first-in-class treatment offering unprecedented functional curates in chronic hepatitis B, a disease affecting millions of people worldwide. Sefaxersen, partnered with Roche, met the primary endpoint in the interim analysis of the Phase III IMAgINATION study in adults with IgA nephropathy with favorable safety and tolerability consistent with prior data. Roche plans to share the data with health authorities with a potential U.S. approval next year.

We also announced positive Phase III FUSION top line results for ulefnersen, partnered with Otsuka in people with FUS-ALS, a rare and rapid progressive form of ALS that affects a broad age range. These results bring us closer to what could be the first disease-modifying treatment for FUS-ALS. Looking ahead, our pipeline offers multiple opportunities to build on our progress. Next year, in addition to the Phase III results for obudanersen, our growing mid-stage pipeline of wholly owned medicines are advancing to a proof-of-concept data readout that could enable us to further expand our late-stage pipeline. We also anticipate further regulatory progress that will expand the global reach of our marketed medicines.

This includes the planned launch of TRYNGOLZA for sHTG in the EU and the continued launch of HIBSAGO and potential approvals and launches for sefaxersen and ulefnersen next year. Our recent progress reinforces the strength of our R&D engine and our confidence in the next wave of opportunities to reach more patients. And with that, I'll turn the call over to Beth.

And for the prescribers who need educating -- "education", what exactly is the difficulty in understanding the value proposition of TRYNGOLZA? And finally, what were some unexpected hurdles that led you to cut your guidance?

Kyle Jenne: Yes. In terms of the specialties, very consistent with FCS, but a broader number of HCPs that we're reaching at this point. We were reaching about 3,000 mix of cardiologists, endocrinologists and lipid specialists for FCS. As we expanded the sales team last year, we're now reaching, as I mentioned, about 20,000 cardiologists, endocrinologists and lipidologists. The largest percentage of those is cardiology just because of the size of that specialty population. The education is just more about building a market here, right? There is HCP enthusiasm when they learn about TRYNGOLZA. They do see that TRYNGOLZA has a compelling profile. It has a broad indication of greater than 500.

It also has acute pancreatitis as outcomes and reduction in AP in the indication statement. So there is HCP enthusiasm and a belief in a compelling profile. When you get down to the underlying numbers, reductions of triglycerides of up to 72% on top of standard of care that they're using today, up to a 91% reduction in acute pancreatitis and getting approximately 50% -- or excuse me, 60% of patients to goal is very encouraging for these HCPs. So the education is more about which patients do I treat? When am I going to see those patients? And then when am I going to prescribe TRYNGOLZA for the first time in order to gain this clinical experience.

And that just takes a little bit of time is what we're learning here.

Brett Monia: Yes. And on the guidance, it's really nothing more, [indiscernible], than the slower-than-expected launch ramp. We're very pleased with the enthusiasm by HCPs to prescribe. Demand is increasing, and we're very pleased with payer coverage to date. We're getting coverage on agreements that we haven't gotten in place so far to label, which means a very broad label, 500 milligrams per deciliter of triglycerides and above. So the metrics are lining positively. It's just a slower launch ramp than what we initially expected.

Operator: Your next question is from Mike Ulz with Morgan Stanley.

Michael Ulz: Maybe another one on TRYNGOLZA. It looks like out of the gates, you're getting some nice breadth there in terms of the prescribers and starting to see some depth. But as we kind of move forward into next year, what's the key to sort of driving greater depth? Is it just more experience? Is there something else? Is it education? Maybe a little bit more color on your thoughts there.

Kyle Jenne: Yes. I think there are a couple of things there, Mike. Experience is one. And what we're seeing is some of these HCPs are treating the most severe patient first, right, history with AP, for example. So I think that they potentially could start with the highest risk patient and then start moving beyond that to patients that are just greater than 880 or patients that are over 500 with comorbidities, for example. But we believe that really to help these HCPs unlock these patients, they need to see the clinical outcomes of using this new treatment that they've never had access to.

And number two, the process in order to get coverage and access needs to be smooth and straightforward for their offices. And those are the 2 really key things that we're working through these offices with here on the outset and then talk to them about more patients that could potentially benefit and how they could broaden their prescribing.

Operator: The next question is from Jessica Fye with JPMorgan.

Jessica Fye: You've been talking about the TRYNGOLZA launch just progressing a little bit slower than you initially thought. Can you talk about how you think about the time line to get to that $3 billion U.S. peak target? And then my follow-up sort of still related to TRYNGOLZA would just be, can you talk about the specific Quick Start expansion change that you're making is?

Kyle Jenne: So I'll touch on peak, Jess. And we have not, up to this point, provided any insight in towards -- to time to peak. But what I'll mention is the large patient population that is addressable here of greater than 3 million patients, 1 million of which are at high risk of acute pancreatitis. And there's an opportunity for TRYNGOLZA to address a significant unmet need here. And I've been through the profile a couple of times in terms of what the strength of the profile of TRYNGOLZA represents. But we do believe that we will continue to build this market. The HCP enthusiasm will continue to grow.

We will get more experience with new prescribers and those prescribers that have written will prescribe more and access will open up over time. But this is a function of building a new market that has never been in existence before. The Quick Start expansion point, I don't want to get into a lot of the details there just because it's a competitive space. But obviously, we have a number of different programs to make sure that patients can get on treatment and get on treatment quickly and able to stay on treatment long term. And I think that's important for our patient services program, and it's important for the patients that can benefit from those types of programs.

Brett Monia: And on the time line, I'll just add. Thanks, Kyle. Jess, it's really important to remember that we are 3 months into -- these numbers represent 3 months into a launch, delivering a medicine that is providing benefit to patients that physicians have never had experience with before, right? And that requires education, that requires patients -- physicians to bring patients in to get the triglycerides measured and then get them on to medicine. We're looking forward to 2027. We think 2027 will be a very important year for TRYNGOLZA.

Operator: Our next question comes from Eric Joseph with Citi.

Eric Joseph: Just a couple more on TRYNGOLZA. I'd be curious to know on the payer access dynamic so far, if you could speak to the success rate of getting on formulary. Have there been any refusals by any plans to cover TRYNGOLZA for sHTG? And what's your expectation as to when the outstanding formulary reviews could complete?

Kyle Jenne: Yes. Thanks, Eric. So we have not had significant pushback or challenges or issues related to our payer negotiations up to this point. As I mentioned, the end of Q3 through the end of September, we had 33% of commercial plans within a 3-month period already begin putting policies in place for sHTG and adding the 50-milligram dose, so the 50 milligrams and 80 milligrams were available. We believe on a pricing standpoint, we priced at $40,000 WACC, and that took place on April 1 of this year. We priced exactly for this reason, which was to make sure that we had coverage to label, which is for all patients greater than 500.

And we wanted to make sure that we reduce the blocks and limitations where payers didn't put in place restrictions around history of AP or being a high-risk patient over 880, for example. And I think we've been very successful at working with payers and talking about the patient population that's addressable here and putting policies in place that reflect the broad label and also, obviously, the prior authorization criteria being consistent with the clinical trial design, which is typically what we are seeing with these plans. So we're very encouraged by payer access coming on board. We believe we will have more coverage and access open up at the end of this year and going on throughout 2027.

So we're in a good place as it relates to access.

Operator: The next question comes from Akash Tewari with Jefferies.

Akash Tewari: So this is what I'm trying to kind of sparse out. I think in September in an investor transcript, you were saying July and August were good months when you're thinking about scripts for TRYNGOLZA. And then obviously, the implied guidance cut today is a pretty stark contrast. Can you talk about -- when you were talking about July, August being good months, how are you defining that? And then what really kind of broke down? And I think my concern is really if July and August were good months that we're actually seeing a downward trajectory in terms of demand as we got into September and the back half of the year?

And then also, I know you went away from PantherRx to multiple specialty pharmacies. How much of that maybe has played a role with uptake here? Do you feel like patients need more high-touch service?

Brett Monia: Thanks, Akash. So early comments -- comments during the early part of the launch really reflected the data that we had available at the time. We were very pleased with the label we received with the indication statement, including acute pancreatitis reduction. And we also -- were seeing a great deal of enthusiasm by HCPs for the overall drug profile and their desire to prescribe at the time. But remember, we were a few weeks into the launch at that time. So it was really based on what we are hearing from the HCP community and their enthusiasm for TRYNGOLZA, which continues today. Now we just have to bring these patients through and get them on to covered drug.

With regard to the pharmacies, specialty pharmacies and so on, Kyle, would you take that?

Kyle Jenne: Yes. The multiple SPs, Akash, we have the right programs in place. We have the Ionis Every Step program, right, our patient support program to make sure that patients are educated from the disease state standpoint, product standpoint and that we also have programs in place to help financial situations, if necessary, in order for those patients to get on and stay on treatment. So I think we've got the right programs there. As it relates to expanding the SPs, the SPs are doing very well. We've got 4 SPs that address some of the largest payers as well.

And we believe that we've got the right SPs to help us make sure that the prescription process gets navigated and we get drug to patient. But we've also got our field access team out there working directly with offices on the reimbursement process and making sure that we're educating around which plans have policies in place and what the criteria for use are for those respective plans. And so that HCP office education is another key component to this beyond just the SP expansion as well.

Operator: And the next question comes from David Lebowitz with BMO Capital Markets.

David Lebowitz: When you try to bucket how the launch is going in various groups, there's a lot of talk about the high-risk patients above 880, about the patients above 500. What about the patients that specifically have had pancreatitis events? Have we seen any uptick -- notable uptick in that group?

Kyle Jenne: Yes. Thanks, David. We are absolutely laser-focused on the high-risk sHTG patients here out of the gate to establish TRYNGOLZA and to begin building this market. The patients above 500 with history of AP are a cornerstone of that focus. And our sales team and our medical affairs team, obviously educating HCPs around the need to treat those patients and the risk now that these patients have had one AP event of subsequent events going up exponentially in terms of risk potential. So we are seeing those patients get prescriptions. Some of it is an office dynamic of when those appointments are scheduled and when those patients are coming in to see their HCP. So it's a timing situation.

But that is a really strong focus of our communications and our education and the launch in order to build this market and get TRYNGOLZA treated or get patients treated with TRYNGOLZA for the right reasons.

Operator: And the next question comes from Ellie Merle with Barclays.

Eliana Merle: Maybe just to take a step back, could you kind of highlight like, I guess, what exactly contributed to the slower-than-expected launch versus what you had initially anticipated? Is this driven by like reimbursement factors, use of free drug? Or is this slower-than-expected demand? And if you could kind of break that out or characterize that a little bit, I think that would be helpful. And then just again on the Quick Start program, you did mention that there's been meaningful utilization. If you could give us any color or characterize, I guess, what proportion of overall starts are on free drug?

And I guess your expectations for the average duration that patients will have -- will be on free drug before converting to paid.

Brett Monia: Kyle, do you want to reiterate what's driving the slower-than-expected launch?

Kyle Jenne: Yes. Thanks, Ellie. I'll just revert back. We're building a market here. That's the first thing, right? HCPs, the majority, some that have treated FCS have experience using TRYNGOLZA. But the majority of these HCPs that we're calling on are learning about a new modality, a new product and trying to make sure that they understand which patients to treat and the potential value of treating those patients. So it's about market building and creating this market. It requires HCP education, which is exactly what we're doing with our field team with personal promotion.

It also takes nonpersonal promotion like our omnichannel capabilities and the way that we are educating through digital means, which is really important here as well to drive awareness and an understanding of sHTG and TRYNGOLZA. And then there's also the patient dynamics. So we're doing a lot of work to educate patients, not only through omnichannel, but also through our patient advocacy work and the engagements that we're having with different groups in order to make sure people understand what sHTG is, what risks are associated with sHTG and the potential benefits of being treated with TRYNGOLZA would look like. So that's really what's taking time, I think, in terms of the process to build the market.

In terms of Quick Start, I don't want to get into really any more details surrounding that program. I mean it's a program that I think is important for patients to be able to get on treatment quickly and for HCPs to be able to assess how patients are doing and to make sure that patients can stay on treatment long term. So it's an important program for patients and HCPs.

Brett Monia: Thanks, Kyle. Thanks, Ellie. And I think we have time for one more question, please.

Operator: And the next question comes from Myles Minter with William Blair.

Jake Batchelder: This is Jake on for Myles. Should Redemplo be approved in sHTG, do you expect them to take similar headwinds in initial uptake? Or is this just sort of the cursor being the lead blocker here? And then maybe a follow-up for Beth. You changed your breakeven guidance from 2028 to 2029. Just wanted to confirm that the TRYNGOLZA uptake was the key driver there and that there were no other factors for updating that guidance.

Brett Monia: Thanks, Jake. I'll start, Beth, feel free to jump in. But as Beth said in her prepared remarks, our shift to 2029 cash flow breakeven was related to the slower-than-expected ramp -- launch ramp for TRYNGOLZA, but it was also impacted as was stated by the disappointment -- Phase III disappointment for eplontersen in ATTR cardiomyopathy and pelacarsen for Lp(a) CVD. That guidance to achieve cash flow breakeven will be driven among -- in addition to pipeline successes in large part by the TRYNGOLZA launch as we go forward. As far as competitor programs, we have no comments on what they should expect.

We see no reason why they would be in any different position than we are with respect to the dynamics that we're facing for the TRYNGOLZA launch to date. What we're thrilled about, of course, is the compelling product profile that we have for TRYNGOLZA, which has shown unprecedented reductions in triglycerides, reductions in acute pancreatitis, all with good safety, tolerability and convenience. So stay tuned. We're looking forward to 2027 for the launch of TRYNGOLZA. It's a very important year. And like I said, we're very much looking forward to it. With that, I think we're going to end the call. Thanks, everybody, for joining us today.

We look forward to sharing our progress as we further advance our launches and the next wave of medicines from our pipeline. Have a good day, everybody.

#3103. Berkshire Kept Buying Back Stock as Shares Hit Records. Here’s What the Price It Paid Tells You.

Berkshire’s own filing shows the prices at which management found its stock attractive, and how far the shares have climbed since.

One of Warren Buffett's investing lessons has been that the price you pay for a stock matters as much as the company you're buying. Greg Abel, his successor at Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA -0.36%) (BRKB +0.76%), looks to be following the same philosophy.

Berkshire posted its quarterly filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission over the weekend. In it, the company disclosed that it spent $9.6 billion repurchasing its own shares during the third quarter of 2026, more than double the $4.5 billion it spent in the second quarter. That's an eye-opening amount of money, even for a company with Berkshire's incredible financial resources.

But the amount isn't the most interesting part of the story.

Berkshire has strict rules about when it can repurchase shares. And by examining what Abel was willing to pay, investors can get an idea of where management sees value in the stock.

Most large companies regularly repurchase shares, sometimes spending billions of dollars regardless of whether their stocks are trading at attractive valuations.

Berkshire operates differently. Its third-quarter regulatory filing states that repurchases are permitted when the CEO, after consulting with the chairman, believes the purchase price is "below Berkshire's intrinsic value, conservatively determined." Intrinsic value is simply an estimate of what a business is actually worth, based on its assets and ability to generate cash over time.

So, Berkshire isn't buying shares because it has money available or because it wants to support its stock price. Management must believe the company is worth more than the price it's paying.

There are other restrictions. Berkshire won't repurchase shares if doing so would reduce its combined cash, cash equivalents, and Treasury bill holdings below $30 billion. But there's no maximum amount Berkshire can spend, and it isn't obligated to buy anything.

Abel has considerable flexibility to repurchase shares. When Berkshire spends billions buying its own shares, investors have good reason to pay attention.

The company's latest filing provides a monthly breakdown of its repurchases of Berkshire stock, including the average price paid for each class.

In July, Berkshire purchased approximately 3.1 million Class B shares at an average price of $496.24, along with about $1.84 billion in Class A shares. The average purchase price for Class B shares increased to $503.99 in August, when the company bought another 1.5 million shares, in addition to $66 million in Class A shares.

September was particularly interesting. Berkshire purchased approximately 7.7 million Class B shares at an average price of $506.64. It also acquired 1,983 Class A shares at an average price of $758,332.88.

Remember that one Class A share represents the same economic ownership as 1,500 Class B shares. September's average Class B purchase price was therefore equivalent to $759,960 per Class A share. Altogether, Berkshire spent about $9.6 billion on purchases in the quarter.

Those figures don't establish Berkshire's intrinsic value. Management presumably believes the business is worth more than the prices it paid, but it hasn't disclosed by how much. But it tells us that Abel was comfortable committing billions of dollars to Berkshire stock at those valuations.

And the company wasn't exactly running short of money. Berkshire's insurance and other businesses held approximately $352.3 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and Treasury bills, net of related payables, at the end of September.

Berkshire's stock continued climbing after the third quarter, with Class A shares eventually surpassing $863,000. That's nearly 14% above the average price Berkshire paid for its Class A shares in September.

The Associated Press reported that the rally may have prompted Berkshire to halt share repurchases. The company hasn't confirmed that, and its latest filing only covers purchases through September. But the possibility makes sense given Berkshire's repurchase policy.

A stock that looks attractive at $758,000 doesn't necessarily offer the same value now, particularly when management insists on a conservative estimate of intrinsic value.

But investors shouldn't assume Berkshire has established a firm ceiling for its stock price, either. Intrinsic value changes as the underlying business grows, and management's assessment can change along with it. Nor would a pause in repurchases automatically mean Abel believes Berkshire is overvalued. It might simply mean the discount isn't large enough to justify spending shareholders' money. Or the company chose to pause buybacks as Buffett announced his retirement as chairman in September.

So, Berkshire's third-quarter purchases don't provide an official price target or guarantee future returns. They do, however, establish a useful reference point for evaluating the stock.

If shares retreat toward the levels where Berkshire was aggressively buying, investors will have evidence that management recently found those valuations attractive.

And that's considerably more informative than simply knowing the stock has fallen from its highs.

Patrick Sanders has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Berkshire Hathaway. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3100. The Trade Desk Stock is Suddenly on Fire. Here’s Why.

The digital advertising pioneer may have finally turned the corner. Only time will tell.

There's no sugarcoating it: The Trade Desk (TTD +15.47%) has lost much of its luster over the past 18 months. When the company reported its Q4 results in early 2025, investors were taken aback. The Trade Desk had fallen short of its own forecast, marking the first time in 33 consecutive quarters the company missed the mark. It's been largely downhill ever since. The stock had lost 90% of its value, plagued by decelerating revenue growth and falling profits. Despite management's best efforts to right the ship, there was little in the way of good news. Until today, that is.

Anticipation ahead of The Trade Desk's financial report and word that one of the company's co-founders was rejoining the fold sparked a rebound, and the release of The Trade Desk's results further fanned the flames. Investors let out a collective cheer.

The Trade Desk's third-quarter results went a long way toward assuring investors that the company has turned a corner. Revenue declined 0.5% to $736 million. The bottom line held up better than expected, though adjusted EBITDA declined 16% to $266 million, driving adjusted earnings per share (EPS) down nearly 27% to $0.33.

While that might not seem like a reason to celebrate, consider this: Management's outlook was for revenue of $650 million and adjusted EBITDA of $160 million, so the results cleared both hurdles with ease.

Even Wall Street was caught off guard, as analysts' consensus estimates were calling for revenue of $651.4 million and adjusted EPS of $0.25, so The Trade Desk sailed past expectations with room to spare.

The Trade Desk also maintained its history of strong customer retention, which remained above 95% during the quarter, a track record that goes back more than a decade.

CEO Jeff Green noted that "Q3 represented meaningful progress with results well ahead of our expectations entering the quarter." He went on to say that, while there's still more work to do, the company is "moving with greater urgency" to right the ship.

The better-than-expected results come on the heels of another important announcement. Last week, The Trade Desk announced the return of co-founder and former chief technology officer (CTO) Dave Pickles, who stepped down in 2023.

Pickles and Green co-founded The Trade Desk in 2009 after working together at the digital ad exchange AdECN, where Pickles and his team built the entire ad exchange in less than seven months. The company was ultimately acquired by Microsoft in 2007.

As the creator and architect of The Trade Desk's adtech system, Pickles knows the platform better than anyone, according to Green. That deep knowledge and expertise help explain why the stock jumped more than 15% on Monday, giving investors hope that his skills will help facilitate The Trade Desk's recovery.

Beyond the quarter's financial results, investors were pleased with The Trade Desk's vision for the future. For the upcoming fourth quarter, management's outlook called for revenue of at least $755 million and adjusted EBITDA of $280 million. While that will mark sequential gains, it would still represent year-over-year declines of 11% and 30%, respectively.

For context, analysts' consensus estimates called for Q4 revenue of $691 million, so The Trade Desk's guidance was still significantly ahead of Wall Street's predictions.

As a longtime shareholder, I'm cautiously optimistic. While I'm glad to see The Trade Desk making meaningful progress, the real test will be whether the company can maintain its upward trajectory. I personally will want to see another quarter or two of results headed in the right direction before I cue up the victory march.

Even after Monday's rally, The Trade Desk stock is selling for just 15 times earnings. While that's an intriguing valuation, I think the company still has more to prove before I would add any shares.

Danny Vena, CPA has positions in Microsoft and The Trade Desk. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Microsoft and The Trade Desk. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3096. Ionis: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Ionis's $1.9 billion cash pile buys time, but it is still to be seen whether patient switches to DAWNZERA can offset a slower TRYNGOLZA launch.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 9, 2026, Ionis (IONS -21.36%) lowered its full-year TRYNGOLZA revenue guidance to approximately $50 million. Commercial execution across new product launches dictates how quickly the business turns its research investments into long-term profits. Three things management said stand out.

TRYNGOLZA treats severe hypertriglyceridemia, a condition marked by elevated blood fat levels that raise acute pancreatitis risks. Doctors must adopt a new treatment approach for patients, which lengthens the time needed to build prescription volumes.

DAWNZERA treats hereditary angioedema, a rare genetic disorder that causes severe swelling attacks. Repeat prescribing and patient switches from existing preventive options expanded product revenue throughout the period.

Phase III clinical trials are late-stage studies required to confirm drug efficacy before regulatory approval. Unfavorable trial results in two partnered programs forced management to adjust its financial trajectory, even as it preserves $1.9 billion in cash and investments.

Product expansion and mid-stage clinical trials drive the next phase. Patient switches to DAWNZERA, an expanding commercial team, and established partnerships provide structural durability while management monitors prescriber conversion.

Execution across research programs and commercial launches remains central to long-term value creation.

VA mortgage borrowers are quietly navigating a knowledge gap. Here’s how to close it.

If your understanding of a VA home loan starts and ends with “it’s for the military,” you’re not alone. For many eligible veterans and service members, the intricate workings (and benefits) of this U.S. government-backed mortgage are obscured behind lackluster guidance.

While there are classes and resources available, the military is broadly wary of steering members in a specific direction, says Alex Rodino, a real estate agent and U.S. Army veteran who served 10 years as an infantry officer and military advisor. “A lot of the course material is just very generic,” he says.

And that’s not a surprise. Considering the sheer size and scope of the military, providing personalized advice on VA loans to all its members would be no easy task.

That leaves real estate agents and lenders as the last line of defense, which is where a big part of the knowledge gap exists. Rodino purchased his first home in 2020 with a VA loan and says he didn’t like how ignorant he felt during the process.

“The reason I actually got my real estate license to begin with was because of that experience I had,” Rodino says. “Looking back on it, I had a lot of questions that didn't really get answered.”

But how can VA borrowers navigate this knowledge gap without having to become mortgage experts in their spare time? Here are some of the most important things to know when considering a VA loan, according to the financial experts and borrowers who have lived it.

“My mortgage broker said, hey, you might qualify for this, look it up,” says Elizabeth Valente, a real estate investor and former U.S. Army officer who bought her first home using a VA loan in 2021. When it came to the application process, she felt crucial information wasn’t readily available to her or fully explained.

In hindsight, Valente says, working with an agent or lender who had detailed VA loan experience would have been beneficial. Not only would it help untangle the specific paperwork and appraisal requirements, but that expertise offers an important layer of support for military borrowers.

“For some processes in the military, it's very hand-holding,” Valente says. “I'll tell you what to wear, what to bring, when to be there.” But that’s not always true when transitioning back to civilian life, and parsing specifics of a loan process can be challenging. “I don't think a typical Realtor would understand what that person's going through,” Valente says.

Finding professionals with the right expertise involves asking questions — and lots of them.

“If I'm the smartest person in the room, we have an issue,” Valente says. “Don't be afraid to tell someone if something doesn't make sense or if you don't understand the numbers.”

Before agreeing to work with a lender or mortgage broker, ask how their process works, what companies they work with, and how familiar they are with VA loans. Treat the initial conversation like an interview — you’re hiring them, not the other way around.

Knowing where to find your Certificate of Eligibility (COE) and how much you might be eligible to borrow is the responsibility of the person applying, Valente says. “All that information — it is available in the [VA] website but you really have to dig for it.”

And this information isn’t recreational reading — your COE lists your "basic entitlement," which is a crucial figure in VA lending. If you have full basic entitlement, the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) generally guarantees 25% of the loan, which in most cases lets you put 0% down.

Why? With a quarter of the loan guaranteed by the VA, the lender is more protected and thus more willing to forgo a down payment.

So how do you know if you have full basic entitlement? Look for the figure $36,000 on your COE. This dollar amount represents full entitlement. Technically, basic entitlement is for loans up to $144,000, but then your bonus entitlement kicks in and you can go higher. The VA doesn’t set loan limits when you have full entitlement — though your lender will still decide how much you can borrow based on your income, debts, credit and the home’s appraised value.

Let’s say you want to buy a home in Fayetteville, North Carolina, and you need a $200,000 loan. In order to put no money down, your entitlement needs to cover at least 25% of the loan amount — in this example, that’s $50,000. After you purchase the home, your COE will show your basic entitlement as $0 and the entitlement charged to a previous loan as $50,000.

“Serving in the military is a unique investing opportunity that most people don't get,” Rodino says. “I wish someone had told me to buy a house when I got to my first duty station.”

If he’d known it was possible or understood how, Rodino says he would have been able to buy in 2017, move in 2020, rent out his first home and then repeat the process. “I'd have three by now and the first one would probably be paid off.”

This particular plan is partly based on the unique schedule of many military members. “Generally, you're moving anywhere from two to four to six years,” Rodino says. Owning multiple properties also leverages two big (and often misunderstood) perks of the VA loan: It’s possible to have more than one active loan at the same time, and after one year, you may be able to convert your primary residence to a rental.

Let’s go back to Fayetteville, North Carolina. After two years, you decide to rent out the home because you’re moving to Bell County, Texas. The home you want to buy in Bell County is $300,000, and in order to make no down payment, you need the VA to guarantee 25% of the loan ($75,000).

Because you no longer have full basic entitlement — remember, you already have an active VA loan elsewhere — your entitlement is capped at 25% of the conforming loan limit in the county where you plan to buy, minus what’s already being used on your first loan ($50,000 in our Fayetteville example).

Now for the math: The current conforming loan limit in Bell County is $832,750. Multiply this figure by 25% and subtract the $50,000 already in use: You have $158,187.50 of entitlement available to you — plenty to guarantee the $75,000 needed on the new loan.

If all of this sounds overwhelming, you’re not wrong. There are resources out there to help you figure all of this out, Rodino says. “The problem is, they're not always practical or they're not always apparent.”

The VA has a website that can walk you through entitlement calculations, but you should also ask your lender, broker or agent. If you’re working with experienced folks, they’ll be able to explain these details and help you get the most out of the VA’s guarantees.

The key takeaway is this: While each VA loan must initially be for a primary residence, borrowers can leverage their entitlement to build an investment portfolio without needing to cough up large down payments.

But these examples don’t consider all of the factors that go into approvals. Like most mortgages, your income, debts and assets dictate your eligibility. And although the VA doesn’t impose credit score minimums, most lenders do — NerdWallet's analysis shows 620 is a common floor.

It’s also important to note that a VA loan’s 0% down isn’t free. VA loans carry a funding fee based on how much you’re putting down and whether it’s your first or subsequent use (certain disabled veterans are exempt). You can pay this up front at closing or roll it into the loan amount; again, your team of professionals should be able to walk you through your options.

“I think there's the assumption that this is what we do: We get our VA home loan and we go buy a home,” says Julie Soares, financial readiness director for the Wounded Warrior Project. When we’re given access to a benefit that offers discounts and perks, it can be hard not to take advantage of it. But this is why financial awareness is critical.

There are a lot of conversations happening right now around homeownership and whether it’s the right choice, especially as affordability remains challenging. So if you haven’t heard it recently, here’s a reminder: Buying property is not the only way to build wealth or create financial security.

“The financial readiness program at Wounded Warrior Project is really leaning into getting further upstream in those conversations,” Soares says. Having a clear understanding of your benefits before you need to use them allows you to make more informed choices.

While it's helpful to understand your entitlement and what you may be eligible to borrow, you don't have to know every little detail about mortgages, or navigate the process alone. Sometimes, the most important thing to know about VA loans is where to turn for help.

If you are unsure of your eligibility or want more information about home loans, you can call the VA's home loans hotline at 877-827-3702.

“Please reach out to Wounded Warrior Project, reach out to the VA, reach out to any service organization,” Soares says. “Not one organization is gonna be able to fix or solve all of these problems. We have to do this as a group.”
