At quarter end, our net debt to adjusted EBITDA leverage ratio was 1.66x. Given the strength of our third quarter results and the positive trends we continue to experience, we elected again to increase our 2026 full year guidance ranges for revenue, adjusted EBITDA and free cash flow for our Imaging Center segment.

Total net revenue guidance for the Imaging Center segment increased to a range of $2.385 billion to $2.435 billion, an increase of $15 million at both the low and high ends of the range as compared with the guidance we provided after our second quarter results. Adjusted EBITDA guidance for the Imaging Center segment increased to a range of $350 million to $363 million, an increase of $5 million at both the low and high ends of the range. We increased our capital expenditure guidance range by $5 million at both ends to $170 million to $180 million, which is reflective of additional growth investment opportunities we have been pursuing.

Free cash flow guidance increased to a range of $120 million to $130 million, an increase of $5 million at both the low and high end of the range. For the Digital Health segment, we are reaffirming our revenue guidance range of $135 million to $145 million. We increased our guidance range for adjusted EBITDA before noncapitalized R&D to $11 million to $13 million as a result of effective expense management and faster-than-projected integration of acquired operations. We also increased our CapEx guidance for Digital Health by $1 million. I'll now take a few minutes to give you an update on 2027 Medicare reimbursement rates. As a reminder, Medicare represents about 25% of our business mix.

With respect to Medicare reimbursement, as we discussed on our second quarter call, in July, we received from CMS a matrix for proposed rates by CPT code, which is typically part of the physician fee schedule proposal that is released about that time every year. In the proposed rule, Medicare proposed decreasing the conversion factor in the Medicare fee schedule by about 1.68% from $33.40 to $32.84, along with certain other changes to RVUs or relative value units of specific radiology CPT procedure codes and to the Medicare Geographic Practice Cost Indices or GPCI.

Our initial analysis at that time indicated that RadNet would be almost net neutral for Medicare in 2027 with a negative impact of less than $1 million to revenue as proposed increases to RVUs almost fully mitigated the decline to the conversion factor. On November 4, CMS released its final rule, which will govern the 2027 physician fee schedule reimbursement rates. In the final rule, CMS finalized a deeper reduction to the conversion factor that it had proposed, a decrease of approximately 2.3% from $33.40 to $32.63. We analyzed the final rule CPT code by CPT code volume weighted using expected 2027 procedure volumes and estimated that the impact to RadNet's 2027 revenue will be approximately $5 million.

While this impact is slightly worse than the proposed rule from July, much of the decrease in the conversion factor is the result of the expiration of the temporary 2.5% increase Congress enacted for 2026. As it has done in several years prior, Congress may take action before year-end to partially or fully reverse this reduction potentially as part of the broader legislative package in December. There can be no assurance that the Congress will act. Our budget at this -- our budget at this time for 2027 will reflect the final rule is published, and we will update you if Congress takes action later on this year.

On a related note, the 2027 HOPPS or Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System final rule also released on November 14, finalized the site neutrality provision we discussed last quarter under which CMS will reimburse hospitals at the lower Medicare physician fee schedule rate for certain non-contrast imaging studies performed in off-campus hospital outpatient departments. This will contribute to the already significant economic pressure that health systems are feeling within the radiology departments, and we believe this financial pressure will continue to drive more health system partnership discussions. Howard Berger: Thank you, Mark. I'd like to take a moment to go off script and try to share with you the seminal events which have occurred over the last few months here at RadNet. So for instance, breast ultrasound. And again, that's a significant revenue generator as well.

And then last but not least, we actually have onetime perpetual license deals as well. It's the minority, as you know, of our business and maybe not even core to our strategy as we build a SaaS business. But there is a few million of new perpetual licenses that we have secured. So those are the three structural revenue drivers. On top of that, with external customers, we also have what is called installation fees, and that's something that you'll see come through as well. And all of that brings us with a fully underpinned record quarter. And if you can do the math of well above $40 million for Q4.

Operator: The next question is from Clarke Murphy with Truist Securities.

Clarke Murphy: Just wanted to start on, can you talk a little bit more about some of the operational efficiencies and scheduling tools and things like that, that you're working on? And kind of what sort of impact that those could have to throughput and capacity on top of all the things that you guys are doing on the digital side?

Mark Stolper: Sure. The first, and I'll bring Sham into this answer as well. One of the scheduling -- or excuse me, one of the operational implementations that are going on now is what we call digital patient registration, where in the past, every patient who came into our facility had to go up to the front desk, check in, get a clipboard of paper, fill out the paper, go back to the front desk, hand that in and wait for them to be called into the individual waiting rooms of the modalities.

What we're rolling out right now is digital patient registration where a patient doesn't need to go to the front desk, can register on his or her Android or iOS device, either when they arrive at the location or even ahead of time, which does a couple of things. One, it's been allowing us to drive more patient volume efficiently through our centers, number one. Number two is it's alleviated a lot of the labor and the backlog at the front desk, which allows us to have, ultimately, more efficiency there with running fewer shifts and drives patients into the individual waiting rooms quicker. Sham, I'll let you expand on that.

Sham Sokka: Yes. Thanks, Mark. I mean I would really put that into two categories, right? One is the digital scheduling itself, right? So we can actually, more and more start to do app-based or web-based scheduling instead of the call center, which is a significant efficiency on the contact center. So that's one piece. And then I think I want to maybe go a little bit deeper with what Mark just talked about. We've now deployed at about 30 centers in the East and West Coast with this digital registration. And on this tool, people are not only registering, they're doing their payments, they're getting information on whether their insurance covers it or not, how much the insurance covers it.

So the entire journey of a complex imaging scheduling -- imaging registering event, excuse me, is now completely done by a digital tool. In addition, the accuracy of the data and so forth are much better because we can actually record it directly from those individuals. And just to give you some sense of where this is going, in those 31 sites, about one in three right now are fully going through digital without having to touch any front desk staff.

And in our best centers, so this is just to show you the potential because we've now done the training and so forth at our best centers, about 75% of patients are not having to see a front desk or liaison, right? So that's the potential of this technology. We're now rolling that out throughout this quarter, and we hope to be done for the full RadNet centers volume by essentially end of Q1, early Q2, right? So that we anticipate will have a significant impact on the operational side of the business as we move forward.

Clarke Murphy: Great. And then just another question that we had was just on the inbound interest that you guys are getting on ONRAD. Just wanted to get a little color on, is that something that's potentially helping accelerate JVs ahead of the acquisition or any other benefits that you guys are seeing in either of your segments right now from the announced acquisition of ONRAD?

Howard Berger: Yes. We've gotten more interest from our current joint venture partners who are all wrestling with the same problem, and that is the shortage of radiologists and increasing demand. But new customers of ONRAD that they've been pursuing once they saw the announcement have told the ONRAD leadership that they'd like to talk to RadNet about a more fully integrated solution for their radiology, both inpatient and outpatient. And our discipline is that we're anxious to talk to any and all comers, but they're going to have to adopt our program to give us the benefit of maximizing the outcome of the tools that we have now been developing, believe it or not, for over six years.

And many of them, if not most of them, embrace that simply because they don't have the internal expertise to implement something like this or even understand how this what we call fully integrated end-to-end solution can have such a material impact on their entire health care system. So our goal here is to find existing and new partners who embrace everything that we can do to make them deliver better healthcare. And so our resources, at least at this point, both from a human and a capital standpoint, need to be used for those opportunities that will give us and our future partners the maximum benefit.

Operator: The next question is from Andrew Mok with Barclays.

Andrew Mok: 2026 seems to be a relatively clean baseline from which to grow. Are there any items we should consider puts or takes for 2027 and aside from the ONRAD acquisition and Medicare rates?

Mark Stolper: Yes. I mean there's going to be a lot of puts and takes that are going to be built into our 2027 guidance when we announce it towards the end of February of next year. There will be, obviously, the impact of same-center performance as we anticipate much higher patient volumes next year, continued growth in advanced imaging, that's going to continue to drive profitability at our existing centers. We've always said the best and most profitable way we can grow is by driving more revenue, more patient volume through our existing fixed cost base. So that's going to be a big positive impact for next year. We will see positive impacts on the centers that we purchased in 2026.

So continued improvement in Southwest Florida, which already the integration is going very, very well from centers we bought earlier this year. As well as Indiana, where there's a lot of upside opportunity still to be had there as well as some other tuck-in acquisitions we've done throughout the year. Again, there's going to be substantial growth, as Kees talked about and Sham talked about in the Digital Health division, where we're rolling into 2027 with $140-plus million worth of ARR that converts to GAAP revenue as we implement those customers. And the $100-plus million of new contract value, some of that will be implemented within 2027.

There will be further tuck-in acquisitions, which we are eager to complete and announce in the coming quarters, which will contribute to next year. There will be new joint ventures with health systems that are in our pipeline, both expansions of existing partnerships as well as new partnerships that we look forward to announcing. So what I would tell you, Andrew, is when we stack this up, we think that we're very encouraged about how next year should look for us in terms of continued growth of everything that we're doing throughout the company.

Andrew Mok: Great. And I just wanted to follow up on the terms of the ONRAD transaction. Can you confirm the specific EBITDA target and how the earnings sliding scale will work?

Mark Stolper: Sure. So we will pay when the deal is closed, $350 million of cash and 5 million shares of RadNet common stock. And then there is an earn-out provision that looks at ONRAD's 2027 EBITDA results. And for every dollar of EBITDA above $56 million, we will pay them 15x that dollar. And that can be paid at RadNet's election in either cash or stock.

Operator: The next question is from Matthew Gillmor with KeyBanc.

Matthew Gillmor: I wanted to circle back on the initiatives to create capacity. You mentioned that a couple of times. Is there a way to give us some sense as you think about the growth with advanced imaging the 8.9%, how much is being contributed by the capacity initiatives that you've talked about? And I guess the way we think about it is scans per machine per day, but if there's any way for us to sort of think about the contribution from that driver, that would be great.

Mark Stolper: Yes, sure. Thanks, Matt. Yes, a lot of our ability to grow advanced imaging is around expanding capacity. And there's many different ways of expanding capacity. One way is simply to keep your centers open longer. So in certain markets and certain centers, we're able to expand hours and scan later into the evening and into weekends. For instance, in Midtown Manhattan, we're regularly scanning at 10:00, 11:00 at night. We've got some centers here in Los Angeles area that are open into the early morning hours to scan patients. Other ways are, as Dr. Berger was talking about, are some of the investments in the newer hardware, the newer technology.

We've talked a lot about in the past, the MRI equipment that has much more sophisticated post-processing software that allows for shorter scanning times and uses software to essentially increase the resolution for the radiologist. Dr. Berger mentioned what we're seeing now in terms of some of the newer PET/CT technology. We're also looking -- the patient registration and the digital registration and the digital scheduling has been able to drive more patient volume into our sites. We've opened sites more aggressively and spent more of our CapEx dollars on de novo centers. We had originally intended to open seven sites this year. I believe by the end of the year, we'll actually have opened 10 sites.

So several of the projects that we had started that we felt that we're going to open in 2026 will actually open in -- excuse me, in 2027 will actually open in 2026. So continuing to build these de novo centers has also expanded our capacity as well. So some of the things that we're doing today 5 years ago, were not even on our radar screen and weren't even a thought. And I suspect that things that we'll see in the future around technology, technology development -- that we can't anticipate today will allow us to continue to build capacity in the future.

The other thing we love to do is we love to acquire other operators who are not as efficient and haven't deployed the same tools and level of technology where we can then acquire those businesses which have embedded capacity that we can grow through time with implementing all of our programs. And so these tuck-in acquisitions that we do are extremely important to our ability to continue to drive capacity and efficiency.

Matthew Gillmor: And then as a follow-up on the ONRAD acquisition, one of the strategic rationales was to deploy technology and drive greater productivity with those radiologists. I think you talked about a 50% opportunity to improve productivity, which would be really significant. I was curious if you could give us some sense for how long it would take to capture that productivity improvement. Would we see some of that in '27? Or is that more of a longer-term journey?

Howard Berger: It's a great question. We've already begun modeling new opportunities for ONRAD to accelerate their deployment. One of the features that we believe will help that is that through ONRAD's deployment of the DeepHealth tools, we will be able to deliver to our hospitals all of the artificial intelligence reporting tools and early detection tools through that platform and have that be part of the ONRAD cost because the beneficiary of that is primarily the radiologists. So as we begin to have discussions, which are ongoing almost as we sit here, explaining how we can do that within their own existing radiology group to make them more efficient and more accurate is resonating.

And this is a somewhat difficult concept for them to embrace simply because they're just not familiar with how these tools can functionally improve their performance given how new this industry is. So when we have these opportunities to lay out our bigger vision, I'm extraordinarily encouraged as to how quickly they want to embrace this and take our lead. So perhaps what I'm trying to suggest here is that for any one of these systems, this is a heavy, heavy lift. We're talking about hundreds of thousands, if not millions of images.

We're talking about broad-based access to imaging throughout their entire enterprise and the need to make certain that other facets, which we believe we can work with them together, such as cybersecurity and movement to the cloud is something that they get comfortable with protects their institution. And I think our team in DeepHealth as well as our own cybersecurity capabilities add a dimension to that conversation that will give them that greater degree of comfort. So there's a new term I've coined here and rather than it be this foxhole-by-foxhole recruiting, it's what I'm going to be talking about in the future of a land and shift.

In other words, taking the existing radiology department, incorporating it into ONRAD and expanding its capabilities. And the people that we've begun talking about this are very excited about the potential implications of it and will allow us to, I believe, accelerate piece by piece, getting them to the overall enterprise imaging system-wide capability that they need to have.

Operator: The next question is from Yuan Zhi with B. Riley Securities.

Yuan Zhi: For the EBITDA margin in 4Q, it seems to be lower than 3Q. In the past, 4Q tends to have the highest EBITDA margin in the year. Can you maybe talk about factors contributing to that?

Mark Stolper: Yes. And we've said this in the past, Yuan, and thank you for the question. When we modify our guidance or amend our guidance like we did after the first, second and third quarters, we don't reforecast the rest of the year. We simply add to the guidance, the beat that we have in that quarter essentially. So we've always cautioned investors, analysts to try to imply a margin for the rest of the year. So what I would tell you is that the trends that have driven the performance this year, the positive trends on the volume side on the advanced imaging side so far have continued into the fourth quarter.

I mean, we're in early November here, and we are anticipating growth in the fourth quarter. And as you correctly point out, the fourth quarter has been our strongest quarter now for several years in a row, and that's partly due to the seasonality of the business where, first of all, fourth quarter incorporates Breast Cancer Awareness month, which usually drives strong mammography and breast-related imaging in the fourth quarter. And then, of course, as many of us have gone towards a higher deductible programs, meaning the patients we have all utilized health care much greater in the second half of the year than in the first half of the year before deductibles reset in January.

And so we often see kind of a rush to get exams done in the fourth quarter leading into next year. So we're anticipating a continuation of many of the strong trends that we've seen in the first 3 quarters.

Yuan Zhi: Got it. Got it. Maybe I ask this question in a different way versus the prior questions. If we fast forward to 3Q 2027, when you have more than 50% of imaging volume going through AI applications, what would that mean to your revenue with increased capacity and gross margin as a result of using AI?

Howard Berger: Well, running the every exam through AI is primarily a benefit for our radiologists, not so much margin, except to the extent that we eliminate the strong demand that there is for radiologists that are driving up our cost. So our goal is to make all of our radiologists more productive, perhaps even by 50% or more as we gain more and more traction of having all of our eventually. And I think as Sham mentioned, we expect it to be close to 60% of everything that we do by mid-quarter -- by second quarter of next year.

And then taking the AI clinical read and putting it through our new reporting solution, which will give a radiologist a full report with findings and characterization to essentially review the report that AI has created and either accept it or -- and sign off on it or edit it. I can tell you from both personal experiences as well as out in the field here, it takes a radiologist longer to dictate the findings in a report than actually interpret the exam. So most radiologists will tell you the bottleneck has been in how much time they have to spend on repetitive tasks that we are essentially automating for them.

And I'm most proud to say that all of these will be done with FDA approval so that anybody that uses these knows that it has not only been created under the auspices of FDA approval, but our commitment to make certain that these tools stay on track and don't as they like to talk in the industry, hallucinate. So our commitment is not just to have something off the shelf, but to be a constant monitor of accuracy and performance that will be built into the -- that is built into the DNA of the DeepHealth division.

The early returns that we've had now that about 300 or so of our radiologists as we roll out these new reporting tools is that it's a game changer. And we still have a ways to go to fine-tune it and make it even better. But I know we're all extraordinarily gratified that taking away this tool would be a big blow to our radiologists and they fully embrace it. So it's one of the strengths of RadNet is the ability to create and deploy internally, make certain that these tools perform the functionality that they're designed for and then roll them out on a larger scale.

So the DeepHealth team and the services team have been working extraordinarily close together. And I dare say that the ONRAD team or our professional radiology services division will have a similar benefit from this end-to-end solution that we're bringing to the marketplace.

Mark Stolper: Yuan, I'll add one thing. What Dr. Berger was talking to was really the efficiency and the -- of the radiologists and the impact that, that could have on our costs going forward as we continue to grow the business and not have to continue to grow the radiology component or hire as many radiologists going forward, which will drive margin. Where we could see a revenue benefit from arming our radiologists with tools is in the turnaround time. So one of the challenges that you're seeing throughout radiology, whether you're talking about hospital-based radiology or outpatient-based radiology is that because of the shortage of radiologists, you're seeing a lengthening of turnaround time.

So the time at which the referring physician receives the radiology report from whoever is interpreting it. And the ability for the radiologists to be able to turn around those reports sooner has a major service benefit that we see for referring physicians that differentiate our service from our competitors. And I think to the extent that we can continue to have accurate and expeditious reads for our referring physician community, I think we'll continue to drive revenue vis-a-vis our competitors.

Operator: The next question is from Jim Sidoti with Sidoti & Company.

James Sidoti: I know it's been a long call. So just one quick one. Cornelis, I believe you said added 63 customers in the quarter. How many of those 62 customers were existing RadNet customers?

Cornelis Wesdorp: Virtually -- thank you for your question. Virtually none. So this is when we add new customers, we treat them -- we see them as really net new. So in that sense, these were new customer generated both in the U.S., in Europe and rest of world.

James Sidoti: And so is there a potential for these 63 customers to start to use some of the other RadNet offerings?

Cornelis Wesdorp: Excuse me, the other RadNet...

James Sidoti: The other digital health services.

Cornelis Wesdorp: Absolutely. Sorry, I got confused for a second because of -- I thought there were other RadNet services. 100%. And so every new customer win as well as any installed base customer is an opportunity for us to upsell and cross-sell. And when we state, by the way, 63 new customers for Gleamer, already today, some of those customers are then also exposed, and we also deploy some of the non-Gleamer portfolio. In fact, it's a bit hard for me to talk about the Gleamer versus DeepHealth portfolio because those portfolios are now fully integrated. But obviously, we track the Gleamer perimeter because we want to make sure that we live up to the expectations of the original acquisition.

Operator: This concludes our question-and-answer session. I would like to turn the conference back over to Howard Berger for any closing remarks.

Howard Berger: Thank you, operator. Again, I would like to take this opportunity to thank all of our shareholders for their continued support and the employees of RadNet for their dedication and hard work. Management will continue its endeavor to be a market leader that provides great services with an appropriate return on investment for all stakeholders. Thank you for your time today, and I look forward to our next call. Good day.

Operator: The conference has now concluded. Thank you for attending today's presentation. You may now disconnect.

#3079. Booking Holdings: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Independent hotels supply the vast majority of Booking.com's room nights, a supply base rivals would find hard to copy.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 3, 2026, Booking Holdings (BKNG +1.76%) announced financial results that exceeded the high end of its guidance across key metrics. The company continues to demonstrate how expanding its direct traveler relationships and automated tools can widen its cost advantage over competitors. Three key takeaways from management's comments illustrate where the business is heading next.

Management is deploying artificial intelligence, software algorithms that execute complex tasks, to automate routine customer inquiries and streamline code development. Lowering support expenses while expanding booking volumes strengthens operating margins.

Booking Holdings is expanding its Connected Trip initiative, which allows travelers to book multiple travel categories such as accommodations, flights, and attractions together in one seamless transaction. Multi-product bookings lock in repeat customers who return more frequently and book directly on the platform.

The company relies primarily on independent accommodations rather than major hotel chains, giving it a strong supply advantage that rivals cannot easily replicate. Small property owners pay a fee only when a room is filled, aligning property incentives directly with the platform.

Global travel demand remains resilient despite near-term moderation in international travel. Expanding direct mobile app usage, flexible payment processing, and deep partner relationships position the platform for long-term compounding while management monitors international demand trends and flight capacity constraints.

The company continues to deploy capital into strategic initiatives across travel categories beyond accommodations, as well as into automated platforms, to reinforce its market presence in emerging distribution channels.

#3076. As AI becomes more fractured, one name stands out: AMD

As Anthropic rushes to takes its shares public, the AI trade is showing cracks, and they are not confined to fringe players.

We recently wrote about CoreWeave, which fell 15.5% on Oct. 14 as yields on its 2032 notes touched 15%, and its default-swap spreads nearly doubled in October. IREN is down more than 20% this year. Last Thursday, the contagion reached chipmakers, which makes sense since much of CRWV and IREN's spending is going there. AMD dropped 8.1% as Meta's financing plans and a supply warning from Lam Research exacerbated data-center fears about the pace of AI spending.

Because when you screen for factors that demonstrably generate outperformance over time, the list narrows quickly. My screen: price above the 200-day moving average; revenue growing at least as fast as the S&P 500 (5%+ per annum); EPS growing at least as fast (7%+); rating upgrades; a PEG below 3; and ROE and ROIC of at least 12%. Of the names reporting in the next two weeks, AMD is effectively the only one that makes the list. Yes, you can (and arguably should, as our staples article described) position your portfolio with slightly less tech exposure than the broad indices provide, but we can't ignore the market's biggest and most transformative sector entirely.

Especially because the growth in this case doesn't just meet my criteria; it blows past them. Consensus for Q3 calls for EPS of $1.94 on revenue of $13.06 billion, versus $1.20 and $9.25 billion a year ago. That's YoY growth of nearly 62% and 41%, respectively. The recent drawdown came from a sector selloff, not anything AMD reported, but it shows that if some names in the space get hit, even the larger players are likely to feel it. On Oct. 6, Lisa Su said AMD would substantially increase supply in 2027 because AI orders keep outrunning capacity.

So how do you balance factors we know work for a fast-growing company against a backdrop of cracks in the AI trade? Options.

Owning the stock outright means absorbing a roughly 9% to 11% implied earnings-related move (day of). Earnings are about a week out, and over the past four quarters the smallest move over a similar window was more than 9%, and the largest move, after the company reported its Q1 26 results, was 38%! Of course, that kind of volatility means options aren't cheap, and that rich premium is also a reason not to simply buy calls.

A call spread risk reversal does both jobs: it reduces risk if the cracks widen, and the short options offset the elevated volatility we would otherwise pay for. The bottom chart shows that, by sacrificing about $1,700 of upside for $5,000 in outperformance during a severe downside move, and given how jittery this trade has been lately, this is a way to stay in it with considerably less risk. $5,000 less, specifically. Of course, selling that out will tie up some cash, but less so than simply buying the stock. And selling both the out and the call reduces long call purchase by 66%

#3074. Elon Musk Just Gave the Top End of His SpaceX Revenue Forecast About a 2% Chance. His Best Guess Sits at the Bottom End.

Even the low end is five times this December's pace. How much of that is already in the stock?

On SpaceX's (SPCX +5.81%) Oct. 20 earnings call, CEO Elon Musk said its annual recurring revenue by year-end 2027 would be "somewhere between $500 billion and $1 trillion."

At the Baron Investment Conference on Nov. 6, he said which end he meant. Musk said it "seems quite likely" that annual recurring revenue (a yearly pace based on December) will top $500 billion in December 2027. He called that his "best guess" and "not a promise."

As for $1 trillion, he said it's "not out of the question" and put the odds at about 2%.

Even the low end is five times the $100 billion yearly pace SpaceX expects to hit this December. But at around $140 as I write, the stock trades a few percent over its $135 initial public offering (IPO) price and about 38% under its 52-week high of $225.64.

It's tempting to think investors are ignoring Musk's forecast. I don't think they are.

Elon Musk. Image source: The White House.

SpaceX's revenue climbed 87% sequentially to $14.6 billion in the third quarter, after a 66% gain in the second. Musk said at the conference that fourth-quarter revenue will likely grow about 70% from there, which comes to roughly $25 billion.

But CFO Bret Johnsen guided for $33 billion to $37 billion in the first quarter of 2027, about 41% over that number at the midpoint. (Musk floated about 70% again, which would top that range.)

Hitting a $500 billion pace by next December from that midpoint would take about 45% to 50% revenue growth in every quarter left in 2027. Put another way, growth would need to stop slowing almost right away, on a far bigger base.

The forecast relies mainly on computing capacity, which SpaceX rents to other businesses and uses for its own artificial intelligence (AI) products. SpaceX had 1.7 gigawatts on Sept. 30. On the October call, Musk said he's "highly confident" of adding 10 gigawatts next year, bringing the total to around 13.

Even if it all came from computing power, $500 billion split across 13 gigawatts would be about $38 per watt. Musk guessed on the second-quarter call that computing power could pull in $30 to $50 per watt, and Johnsen said in October that pricing is running a bit over the high end of that range.

So I don't think $500 billion is far-fetched.

Of course, the superintelligence segment, where this business sits, generated only about $30 billion annualized last quarter. That comes to roughly $18 for every watt SpaceX had at quarter-end.

Musk also wants to keep about half the capacity for SpaceX's own products. If the rented half made $50 per watt, it would pull in about $325 billion. Starlink and launches run at only around $28 billion a year combined, so most of the other $175 billion would need to come from products like Grok, whose Grok Bot assistant had 800,000 paying weekly users in October.

Pricing might not hold, either. SpaceX's cloud contracts can usually be canceled by either side with 90 days' notice. At $30 a watt, 13 gigawatts would bring in around $390 billion.

At $140 a share, SpaceX is worth around $1.9 trillion.

Now let's say SpaceX gets to $500 billion and earns the 19% operating margin it reported last quarter. That's around $96 billion in annual operating income, or about $76 billion after a 21% tax rate. The stock would then trade at about 25 times earnings. The S&P 500 (^GSPC +2.35%), in comparison, trades at around 18 times its expected earnings over the next 12 months.

Twenty-five times earnings looks fair for a company that size still growing fast. But it's no bargain, even if Musk's best guess is right. And it ignores the cost of getting there. Management expects $35 billion to $40 billion in capital spending in the fourth quarter alone, even as capacity is expected to grow by only about 1 gigawatt.

I've covered Tesla for over 10 years, and Musk's big numbers tend to describe what might happen if most things go well. This time, he told investors it's not a promise.

In the end, I think SpaceX could come close to the $500 billion floor. But at around $140, investors are already paying for a good chunk of it. The metric I'd most want in the next report is revenue per watt.

For now, I wouldn't sell the stock at this price, and I wouldn't be in a rush to buy it.

Daniel Sparks has clients with positions in Tesla. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Space Exploration Technologies and Tesla. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3071. Alphabet Almost Sets a Record No One Wants

Tyler Crowe: Alphabet almost sets a record no one really wants. Motley Fool Hidden Gems Investing starts now. Welcome to Motley Fool Hidden Gems Investing. Matt Frankel: Well, the first thing is Alphabet, or Google. I might still call them Google didn't have a bad quarter. It had an expensive quarter. That's really the narrative here. Tyler Crowe: Jon, you and I, we were actually talking about this before the show a little bit because you got to spend money to make money. Gudonis: These results reflect continued execution on the 4 success pillars we discussed on our last call including building recurring patient sources, expanding payer access, demonstrating operating leverage and investing in product development and clinical research. Our efficiency efforts in the other functional areas are also making a financial impact with our overall volumes up while our headcount is down over the past 2 years. Our fourth success pillar is continued progress with product development and clinical research.

The randomized control trial at the University of Utah continues to make steady progress with 35 of the planned 50 subjects now enrolled up from 25 at the time of our second quarter call Development work also continued on the MyoPro 3 and on the hand only product for the German market. These efforts are a part of our longer term work to expand the evidence base and the applications of our wearable robotics platform. We will provide further updates as milestones are reached. In summary, the quarter showed how executing across our 4 pillars of success reinforce 1 another.

More referral relationships and payer access helped drive record orders and revenue, higher volume, and cost reduction supported stronger gross margin and improved operating performance. We are building on our market leading position by investing in the clinical, commercial and product capabilities needed to serve more patients. To continue scaling our commercial operations, last month we announced that Mary-Katherine McClure has joined Myomo as our new Chief Commercial Officer. She has a successful track record of growing revenues establishing strong referral partnerships and leading a sales and field clinical team from our experience at fast growing Inspire Medical and other medical device companies.

I am pleased to have her bring this experience to Myomo as we execute our plan to further address this large unmet need of chronic arm paralysis in the country. With that overview, I will turn the call over to David A. Henry to review our financial results in greater detail.

David A. Henry: Thank you, Paul, and good afternoon, everyone. Our revenue for the third quarter of 2026 was a record $12.3 million up 22% versus the prior year period. Cash used in operating activities during the second quarter was $1.3 million compared with $1.8 million used during the third quarter of 2025. Cash burn or the change in cash in the quarter was $1.5 million an improvement from $2.2 million in the second quarter.

Despite this expected increase, are maintaining our previously communicated operating leverage objective of limiting the growth of operating expenses in all of 2026 to half the rate of 2026 revenue growth. We continue to expect total cash burn in the second half of the year to be less than $2 million or less than $500 thousand in the fourth quarter. Overall, we are pleased that we are poised to meet or exceed financial and operating objectives for 2026. And we look forward to continued execution in 2027. #3065. Public Policy (PPHC) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Acquisitions and client demand lifted results as full-year outlook held.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Public Policy Holding Company, Inc. (PPHC -0.90%) reported year-to-date revenue growth of 15.2%, driven by a combination of organic expansion in its core government relations business and the integration of four strategic acquisitions. Management indicated that political transitions at federal and state levels serve as catalysts for client demand, as corporate interests navigate new regulatory agendas and institutional changes. The company maintained its full-year 2026 financial outlook while expanding its capital capacity through a new senior credit facility to support further geographic and service-line expansion. Segment performance varied, with government relations exhibiting margin expansion while corporate communications faced temporary headwinds related to the election cycle.

The short answer is that you have maybe heard me say and or others, in our business since we started reporting results. London 5 years ago. The change political change, institutional change of control is good for our business regardless of the partisan outcome of that change. Last week, voters made their voices heard. And now new agendas and some new political factors are already getting to work. This is our team's time to shine as always.

So if you can get any color on what you are seeing there and how that is sort of driving new revenue. And then secondly, on cross selling, I appreciate the TrailRunner Group, when you have added to that with Tancredi and Revemark. This year. Just how are you going to ensure you sort of capture those growth opportunities? Make sure everyone knows the services you now have given that sort of material step change in that business? Thank you.

Thomas Edward Gensemer: I will take the first and give the second to my colleague. On the AI tools, you know, we are finding. 1, we are happy that we did not sort of build group wide capabilities in this at the start of the year or last year because the sand is shifting under all of our feet. Very quickly. And so we have used our federated model to really test different things both bespoke for client needs and then broadly speaking, where we see time-saving opportunities. So I have used before the example of congressional hearings used to take time to reach transcriptions that would then turn into look-to client deliverables.

Now we have sort of agents that are working for that across the sort of federal portfolio, where we have the transcriptions up that is just a very sort of small but meaningful use of time and client execution. We have seen in the comms businesses both on routine things like media monitoring and up to the research side that we are doing synthetic sampling. And synthetic message testing against things that used to just be focus group. We are political practitioners at heart, so we still do human contacts and human samples. But how you can bring insights to clients in cheaper, faster ways using AI tools is profound, and it is changing the research industry.

So where those live, predominantly in our comms businesses, are seeing dramatic test and learn, but also a huge client appetite for bringing new product and new screens. Finally, I will just add, we have done something that is patent pending in 1 of the London operations around a reputation score called GPS, which is allowing people to sort of manage reputational risks across the different LLMs. And we have now sold it across, I think, 6 or 7 of the firms.

So ranging from London to Sacramento and DC. it is something that can incubate within 1 aspect of the group, but then be sort of cross sold through, you know, the work we do bringing the colleagues together as sort of trusted references. So that is called Pagefield GPS, and it is now being rolled out across some of the other companies. Over to you, Roel.

Roeland Jozef Bernard Smits: Sorry. No. that is all good. So your second question, Samuel, was how do we capture the growth between acquisitions in general and between Trail Runner, Tancredi, and Revemark in particular. Yep. Exactly. Yes. And the answer to that is needless to say. We have got our sort of collection of tools that we continue to sort of further build out. About, you know, to encourage this collaboration between our companies, because, obviously, that is where we create a lot of our value. And we do that through very regular business development calls between various business development teams. And we have, you know, twice-a-year-like summit.

We actually had this quarter, we also had our first NextGen Summit, and basically bringing a lot of people together in Texas, 1 of the meetings that Thomas hosted. And, you know, in our business, it is very important that people get to know each other and trust each other because when they want to share their clients with, let's say a sister company, they have to trust and know that company will treat their clients in the right way. So from that perspective, you know, we are still small enough that we can have a lot of actual connections between our people, and that will drive you know, collaboration.

And John Green, our chief client officer, is relentless in terms of pursuing a multi company client prospects So, client prospects that are being pursued by 2 or more companies. And then, you know, as on the finance side, we try to measure that collaboration quantifiably. And then, you know, we have talked in the past about how we measure the percentage of businesses referred, the percentage of business that comes from clients that are being serviced by more than 1 of our companies, and we have trend lines in our monthly management reports.

And as long as that trend line goes up, we know we are doing better than yesterday, but we also know that tomorrow we will still be doing better than today. And now with respect to that new group, the TrailRunner Group in particular, you know, we can leave it to Jim Wilkinson to, you know, be very energetic when it comes to bringing these companies together, you know, for jointly developing client opportunities. And, you know, TrailRunner has a very specific new business culture which I am sure he will try to also infect the other companies with. And, actually, we have already seen that.

And they have been on joint roadshows to meet with a lot of law firms to maybe solicit litigation communications business. I know that there is been roadshows in London, in Italy, So there is a lot going on already on this front, and we will keep doing it. Because this is, you know, frankly, where we add a lot of value.

Samuel Dindol: Brilliant. Thank you. Thanks for the questions, Samuel.

#3062. Hain Celestial (HAIN) Q1 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

A missed lender deadline clouds Hain Celestial's pending $323 million international sale.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

The Hain Celestial Group, Inc. (HAIN -6.56%) reported its fiscal first quarter 2027 results and updated its strategic progress, including receiving final regulatory approvals for the $323 million sale of its international business to Aurelius. Management stated that the company is pursuing a path forward for the divestiture despite missing an October deadline to secure a necessary credit agreement amendment. The company reported a significant increase in North American gross margins to 33.5% following the exit of its snacks business and the implementation of productivity initiatives. Management stated that the go-forward portfolio will concentrate on core brands including The Greek Gods, Celestial Seasonings, and Earth's Best as part of a more streamlined operating model.

Operator: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us, and welcome to The Hain Celestial fiscal fourth quarter earnings call. I will now hand the conference over to Alexis Tessier, Vice President of Investor Relations. Alexis, please go ahead.

Alexis Tessier: Good morning, and thank you for joining us for a review of our fiscal fourth quarter and full year 2026 results. I am joined this morning by Alison Lewis, our President and Chief Executive Officer, and Lee Boyce, our Chief Financial Officer. Slide two shows our forward-looking statements disclaimer. As you are aware, during the course of this call, we will make forward-looking statements within the meaning of federal securities law. These include expectations and assumptions regarding this company's future operation and financial performance and condition. These statements are based on our current expectations and involve risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from our expectations.

Please refer to our most recent annual report on Form 10-K, our annual report on Form 10-K expected to be filed today, our quarterly reports on Form 10-Q, and our other reports filed from time to time with the SEC, as well as the press release issued this morning for a detailed discussion of the risks. We have also prepared a presentation inclusive of additional supplemental financial information, which is posted on our website at hain.com under the Investors heading. As we discuss our results today, unless noted as reported, our remarks will focus on non-GAAP or adjusted financial measures.

Reconciliations of non-GAAP financial measures to GAAP results are available in the earnings release and the slide presentation accompanying this call. This call is being webcast and an archive will be made available on the website. Now I'd like to turn the call over to Alison.

Alison Lewis: Thank you, Alexis. Good morning, everyone, and thank you all for joining the call today. Fiscal Year 2026 was a pivotal year for Hain. Over the past 12 months, we took decisive actions to simplify our portfolio, pay down debt, improve execution, drive greater cost discipline, and sharpen our strategic focus. While there is more work ahead, we are exiting the year with improving momentum, stronger cash generation, and a clear plan to drive growth and profitability in the go-forward business. Earlier today, we announced that we reached a definitive agreement to sell our international business to a private equity firm, Aurelius, for $323 million in cash.

This transaction would represent an important step in the evolution of Hain, and when coupled with the fiscal Q3 divestiture of our North American snacks business, would mark a significant milestone in the simplification and strengthening of our portfolio. We believe we found a strong home for our international business in Aurelius, and I want to thank our international employees for their dedication, passion, and contributions to Hain over many years. They have built remarkable brands, which we are confident will thrive under the new ownership. The sale is expected to be completed in our fiscal second quarter, and proceeds from the transaction would be used to further reduce debt.

As noted in our announcement, the transaction is conditioned upon securing an amendment for our credit agreement to extend the maturity, and we remain in active discussions with our lenders regarding that amendment. Once the transaction is closed, the resulting portfolio would be a North American business comprised of leading brands in attractive categories with a more streamlined operating model and a greater focus on core growth opportunities. Importantly, the strength of this portfolio was demonstrated in our fourth quarter results. North America returned to organic sales growth, expanded gross margin by nearly 1,200 basis points, and increased adjusted EBITDA by 55% year-over-year. These results reflect the benefits of a streamlined portfolio, stronger execution, productivity initiatives, and disciplined cost management.

Looking forward, the simplified portfolio will allow us to concentrate our resources and management attention on the areas where we see the greatest potential to create value. Fiscal 2026 also marked a year of substantial balance sheet improvement. We reduced net debt by $151 million through a combination of actions resulting from our strategic review and strong free cash flow generation of $58 million. This free cash flow improvement was driven by a number of factors, including tighter working capital management, meaningful inventory reduction, productivity initiatives, and disciplined cost control. These factors not only drove cash generation in the year but strengthened our operational foundation.

The international transaction would further reduce debt significantly and position us to continue the ongoing transformation of our portfolio and capital structure. Our focus will now shift to simplifying the organization and aligning our cost structure with the scale of the future North America business to drive growth and profitability. Turning now to our performance. As I mentioned earlier, we exited fiscal 2026 with improved momentum across many areas of the business. Additionally, we made significant progress against our strategic priorities, including portfolio simplification, debt reduction, cash generation, and operational improvement. During the quarter, we delivered sequential improvement in organic net sales growth across the business as our five actions to win continued to gain traction across the organization.

These actions include simplifying our portfolio, accelerating renovation and innovation, implementing strategic revenue growth management, driving productivity and working capital efficiency, and strengthening our digital capabilities. Importantly, we see measurable results from these initiatives. Our innovation renewal rate, or IRR, expanded year-over-year in both North America and international to a high single digit and low teen percentage, respectively, for fiscal 2026. IRR is a measure of the percent of net sales coming from new or relaunched SKUs in the last three years and a strong validation that our innovation is delivering results. E-commerce sales delivered strong double-digit growth in Q4 year-over-year with our largest pure-play and omni-channel customers in North America, reflecting the progress of our digital transformation initiatives.

Productivity efforts in supply chain continue to deliver substantial COGS reduction. While the environment remains dynamic and challenges persist in certain categories, these results reinforce our confidence that the actions we are taking are beginning to strengthen the business and build the foundation for future growth. In North America, organic net sales returned to growth in Q4, increasing 2% year-over-year. For the full fiscal year, North America organic net sales were effectively flat, representing a meaningful improvement from prior years. Our yogurt business remained a standout performer. The Greek Gods delivered strong double-digit growth along with share gains and remains an excellent example of how innovation, brand investment, and disciplined commercial execution can drive sustained results.

We are seeing emerging strength across the rest of our core business, including Celestial Seasonings Tea, which delivered growth in both the quarter and the year, driven in part by the success of our wellness tea innovation. Earth's Best Finger Foods, the largest piece of our Earth's Best business, with strong double-digit growth supported by the continued success of our self-feeding platform. More broadly, the quarter reinforced our confidence in the potential of our go-forward North American portfolio. Within our International segment, while organic net sales for Q4 declined 4% year-over-year, the decline moderated sequentially by roughly 400 basis points relative to the third quarter trends. We saw improved performance sequentially across meal prep, beverages, and baby and kids.

While spreads and drizzles remains a challenge category, we are encouraged by the early response to our Hartley's renovation and innovation launched in the fourth quarter. Combined with the improvements we are seeing across the broader portfolio, the International business is positioned well for its new ownership. We were also pleased with the improvement in profit margins delivered during the quarter. Gross margin and adjusted EBITDA margin both expanded year-over-year, driven by improvement in North America. As expected, following the Snacks divestiture, North America delivered significant improvement in profitability, reinforcing our confidence in the earnings power of the underlying portfolio and the benefits of a more focused business model.

Consistent with trends throughout fiscal 2026, the vast majority of the year's gross margin and adjusted EBITDA pressure remain concentrated within International, where inflation, productivity shortfalls, and unfavorable mix continued to weigh on profitability. More broadly, fiscal 2026 demonstrated that the actions we have taken are producing early tangible results. Exiting 2026, we see indications that the business is stabilizing, profit margins are improving, and we have a stronger operating foundation. As we enter fiscal 2027, our focus is on building on the progress made over the past year while completing the work required to establish a focused, appropriately scaled North American Hain.

Following the completion of the International transaction, our portfolio would be concentrated on leading better-for-you brands in attractive categories, including The Greek Gods yogurt, Celestial Seasonings tea, and Earth's Best finger foods and cereal. Completion of the International transaction would be an important milestone, but it would not be the end of our work. Our priorities for fiscal 2027 are clear and supported by detailed plans already underway. First, we will aggressively align our organization and cost structure with the scale and needs of the future North American business. This summer, we completed a rigorous bottoms-up, zero-based budgeting review across the organization. That work identified specific actions to align cost structure with the size of our go-forward North American business.

These actions are expected to simplify our operating model and deliver more than $16 million of annual run rate cost improvement. In addition, this exercise identified opportunities to optimize our marketing budget, driving greater impact for our key growth brands. Importantly, we expect to increase marketing investment year-over-year on both an absolute basis as well as percentage of net sales. These actions, the majority of which are expected to be implemented in fiscal 2027, support a pro forma gross margin of approximately 30-plus percent and adjusted EBITDA margin of low double-digit percentage. We have clear ownership, timing, and implementation plans and are moving with urgency to deliver these savings.

Second, we will remain disciplined in managing our financial position in light of the upcoming maturity date on the company's credit facilities in December. Proceeds from the International transaction will be used to reduce debt while maintaining rigorous oversight of working capital spending, and transformation investments. Fiscal 2027 will include investments required to execute our cost reduction program and establish the appropriate operating model for the future business. We will balance these near-term requirements with disciplined capital allocation and our continued focus on exploring any and all opportunities to further reduce debt and address the upcoming maturity. Third, we will shift investment behind our strongest brands and growth platforms.

As I just outlined, we have identified opportunities to optimize our marketing spend, and we plan to increase marketing investment year-over-year by approximately 100 basis points of net sales to support brand building and innovation across Celestial Seasonings, The Greek Gods and Earth's Best. This investment will build on the progress we are already seeing across the core portfolio. The work ahead is about establishing the right cost structure, the right portfolio, and the right level of investment to support a stronger North American Hain while continuing to explore all opportunities to maximize the value of the enterprise for the benefit of stakeholders.

The actions taken throughout fiscal 2026, together with the detailed plans underway for fiscal 2027, would position us to become a more focused, profitable, and operationally stronger company. With that, I will turn the call over to Lee to review our financial results and cost structure initiatives in even greater detail.

Lee Boyce: Thank you, Alison, and good morning, everyone. Before discussing our fourth quarter results, I would like to begin with the improvement in free cash flow and the significant reduction in debt, which were among the most important accomplishments of fiscal 2026. As Alison mentioned, we had strong cash flow delivery in the quarter. Free cash flow for the fourth quarter was $7 million, an increase compared to the outflow of $9 million in the year ago period. The improvement was primarily driven by favorable working capital performance, including benefits from accounts payable, inventory reduction, and a lower net loss, partially offset by lower accounts receivable inflow.

Free cash flow for the full year was $58 million as compared to an outflow of $3 million in the prior year. We are pleased with the progress we made on inventory driven by improved operating discipline. Days inventory outstanding improved year-over-year to 80 days in the quarter from 88 days in the prior year period. It was up compared to 73 days in Q3 2026. Note that every day of inventory is worth approximately $3 million. We made sequential progress on our days payable outstanding, with days payable outstanding of 62 days in the quarter, an improvement from 59 days in Q3 2026, but slightly below 65 days in the year ago period.

CapEx of $5 million in the quarter was down from $6 million in the prior year period. Looking ahead, we would expect capital expenditures to decrease year-over-year as our North American business is significantly less capital intensive than our international business. Strong cash flow generation this quarter brought cash on hand to $58 million and net debt to $500 million, a reduction of $151 million, or approximately 25% since the beginning of the fiscal year. We also have $186 million of available liquidity under our revolver and remain in compliance with all credit agreement covenants. With net leverage of 4.5x in the quarter, we have plenty of headroom under our covenant at 5.5x.

We have a disciplined and prudent approach to capital management and continue to prioritize debt reduction. We have reduced net debt by $277 million over the past 12 quarters. We remain in active discussions with our lenders regarding an amendment of our credit agreement to extend the current maturity date. If reached, extension would be a near-term solution and an important step that provides additional flexibility as we continue to work on reducing our leverage. We are working closely with all parties and will provide an update when we are able. We have made significant progress in the elimination of stranded costs resulting from the sale of the North American snacks business.

In fiscal 2026, we initiated actions to remove the entirety of the $25 million in stranded costs, which was ahead of our initial timeline. Additionally, our Transition Services Agreement, or TSA, is generating proceeds from providing ongoing support to the divested snacks business. Together with the actions taken to date, this has essentially eliminated any near-term stranded cost impacts. As Alison mentioned, this summer, we completed a robust bottom-up, zero-based budgeting review across the organization that identified specific actions to align cost structure with the size of our go-forward North America business. We have concrete action plans in place to enact $16 million of annual run rate cost improvement.

We expect the vast majority of that savings capture to be completed by the end of fiscal 2027, with the full completion within 18 months. We estimate the one-time cost to implement these savings will be approximately $20 million, with 70% of that incurred in fiscal 2027, and the remainder incurred in fiscal 2028. These actions will simplify our operating model and support the future growth of our North American business, implying pro forma gross margin of approximately 30%+ and low double-digit percentage adjusted EBITDA margin. Turning now to performance. For the fourth quarter, we saw an organic net sales decline of 2% year-over-year as lower sales in the international segment offset organic net sales growth in North America.

The decline in organic net sales reflected a two percentage point decrease in volume mix and flat price. Adjusted gross margin was 22.7% in the fourth quarter. This represents a 230 basis point increase year-over-year. The year-over-year increase was driven primarily by volume mix and productivity savings, partially offset by cost inflation. Additionally, there was a $1.9 million positive impact from tariff refunds in the quarter. SG&A decreased 7% year-over-year to $63 million in the fourth quarter, primarily driven by a reduction in employee-related expenses. SG&A represented 23.8% of net sales for the quarter as compared to 18.6% in the year ago period.

The increase in SG&A as a percentage of net sales was primarily driven by costs associated with the strategic review and the lower sales base. We delivered adjusted EBITDA of $19 million in the fourth quarter compared to $20 million a year ago. The decrease was driven primarily by cost inflation and a decrease in volume mix, partially offset by lower SG&A and productivity savings. Adjusted EBITDA margin was 7.1%, a 160 basis points increase from the prior year period. Interest expense fell 7% year-over-year to $12 million in the quarter, primarily driven by lower outstanding borrowings. We have hedged our rate exposure on more than 70% of our loan facility with fixed rates at 7.1%.

We continue to prioritize reducing net debt over time. Adjusted net loss, which excludes the effect of restructuring charges amongst other items, was $4 million in the quarter, or $0.05 per diluted share, as compared to adjusted net loss of $2 million or $0.02 per diluted share in the prior year period. Turning now to our individual reporting segments. In North America, organic net sales growth of 2% year-over-year was primarily driven by growth in meal prep due to strength in yogurt, partially offset by lower sales in baby and kids. Fourth quarter adjusted gross margin in North America was 31.1%, an increase of nearly 1,200 basis points versus the prior year period.

The increase was driven primarily by an increase in volume mix following the divestiture of the snacks business, as well as productivity savings, partially offset by cost inflation. Again, there was a $1.9 million positive impact from tariff refunds. Adjusted EBITDA in North America was $16 million, reflecting an increase of 55% from the year ago period and representing 14.4% of net sales. The increase resulted primarily from the reduction in SG&A as well as productivity savings, partially offset by lower volume mix and cost inflation.

In our international business, organic net sales declined 4% year-over-year in the quarter, an improvement from the 8% decline year-over-year in the third quarter, driven by sequential improvement in baby and kids, beverages, and meal prep. The year-over-year decline was primarily driven by lower sales in meal prep and baby and kids, partially offset by growth in beverages. International adjusted gross margin was 16.6%, a 555 basis points decrease versus the prior year period. The decrease was driven primarily by cost inflation, partially offset by productivity savings. Adjusted EBITDA was $12 million, reflecting a decrease of 41% compared to the prior year period and representing 8.1% of net sales.

The decrease was driven primarily by cost inflation and lower volume mix, partially offset by productivity savings. Now turning to category performance. In baby and kids, organic net sales were down 11% year-over-year, driven primarily by formula and purees in North America and purees in the U.K., partially offset by growth in finger foods in North America. We have simplified our portfolio of Earth's Best purees and are seeing a 30% increase in base velocity as a result of these strategic winning portfolio actions. Formula remains a small piece of our Earth's Best brand, where we are implementing strategic actions with a focused set of customers.

We continue to prioritize Earth's Best investment behind our key growth platforms, finger foods and cereal. In international, we are seeing improvement in Ella's Kitchen as we lap last year's industry-wide declines. In the beverages category, organic net sales were down 2% year-over-year, as 3% organic net sales growth in both tea in North America and private label non-dairy beverage in international was more than offset by the lack of promotional activity in North America. Wellness teas remained strong, growing dollar sales up high single digits and gaining share. In meal prep, organic net sales growth was 3% year-over-year. The increase was driven primarily by yogurt in North America.

The Greek Gods continue to outpace the category, growing dollar sales by high teens percent and gaining share. As a reminder, following the sales of the North American snacks business, the snacks category is comprised solely of jellies in the international segment. Organic net sales growth in snacks was down 7% year-over-year, driven by SKU rationalization as we prepare for the brand relaunch. Turning now to our outlook. As mentioned earlier, subject to the satisfaction of the closing conditions outlined in our SEC filings, we would expect the international divestiture to close in our fiscal second quarter. Net proceeds from the transaction are expected to range between $305 million and $310 million.

With these proceeds, we will pay down the entirety of our outstanding term loan and more than 35% of the outstanding balance of our revolver. Our pro forma total debt outstanding as of June 30th, 2026, would be approximately $250 million, a reduction of approximately 55%. Again, these numbers are based on the current Forex rates and are subject to change relative to Forex rates at the time of the transaction close. We remain in active discussions with our lenders to reach an agreement on the amendment of the company's credit agreement to extend the current maturity. The international divestiture is contingent upon the company securing this amendment, and there can be no assurance that an amendment will be obtained.

If the amendment is not obtained within 30 days of signing, Aurelius would have the right to terminate the agreement. We will provide updates on both the international divestiture and the credit agreement amendment as we are able. As we begin fiscal 2027, our top priority is managing our capital structure and debt while continuing to align our North American business for growth. Throughout the year, we expect that there will be various one-time costs associated with the execution of our plans. I will provide regular updates on our quarterly calls to showcase our progress. We are actively pursuing multiple components of our strategic review process that make providing traditional guidance challenging.

I look forward to sharing more on future calls. Now I turn the call back to Alison for some closing remarks.

Alison Lewis: Thanks, Lee. In closing, fiscal 2026 was a defining year for Hain. We made meaningful progress in simplifying the portfolio, paying down debt, improving cash generation, and sharpening our strategic focus on areas where we believe we can create the most value. While our transformation is not complete, we are entering fiscal 2027 as a more focused company with a stronger operational foundation and a clear plan for the work ahead. We are encouraged by the early operational progress and the improved execution across the business demonstrated in the quarter and plan on continuing to work to strengthen Hain's financial position and create value for all stakeholders.

Our priorities are straightforward: manage our capital structure and balance sheet, align our cost structure with our future North America business, continue improving operational performance, and unlock the full potential of a focused North America Hain. Given the ongoing discussions with lenders and the pending international sale, we will not be hosting a Q&A session this quarter. The update we provided on today's call and in our SEC filings is the extent of the detail that we are able to share publicly. We will provide relevant updates on the transaction and the strategic review as we are able. Finally, I want to thank our employees, customers, consumers, and other stakeholders for their continued support throughout this transformative year.

Thank you again, and I appreciate all of you joining today.

Operator: This concludes today's call. Thank you for attending. You may now disconnect.

#3060. Ripple strikes deal with Robinhood to expand its RLUSD digital dollar

Ripple has struck a deal with Robinhood to expand the reach of its digital dollar, RLUSD, strengthening trading and financing links between their institutional businesses and improving Robinhood's internal money management.

The partnership involves using RLUSD to settle institutional trades, automate Robinhood's treasury operations and expand access to digital asset trading and financing through Ripple Prime and Bitstamp, the global crypto exchange acquired by Robinhood last year.

It also helps meet Robinhood's ambition of becoming a global financial superapp, centralizing its customers' financial lives while expanding the underlying infrastructure that can serve both retail and institutional clients.

"Utility is what moves stablecoins forward. Working with Ripple, Bitstamp and Robinhood will have access to RLUSD for institutional settlement, Ripple Treasury for our operations and Ripple Prime for financing," Robinhood Crypto General Manager Johann Kerbrat said in a statement shared with CNBC. "That is what a connected, global financial system looks like."

Stablecoins have long been a workhorse of the crypto world, giving traders a way to move money among exchanges, buy and sell crypto assets, and park funds between trades without having to convert back into traditional currency. But as the crypto industry evolves beyond trading and markets move toward 24/7 liquidity, stablecoins are becoming essential financial infrastructure because of their ability to enable near-instant settlement and move dollar-denominated value at any time, regardless of traditional banking hours.

As firms look to do more with stablecoins beyond simply listing them on exchanges, stablecoin issuers are betting they'll favor a one-stop-shop approach that bundles the technology and services needed to move money, settle trades and manage cash.

"Stablecoins have evolved from a crypto trading tool into a critical piece of financial infrastructure," Ripple President Monica Long told CNBC. "The clearest evidence of this is where they're now being embedded — from corporate payments to capital markets. Our partnership with Robinhood reflects that evolution."

"This is about much more than trading," she added. "It's about fundamentally changing how money moves and is managed — giving institutions the ability to operate 24/7/365, unlocking liquidity and putting capital to work more efficiently."

Circle Internet Group, a Ripple competitor, is positioning itself for a similar future, where winning platforms, in addition to issuing stablecoins, also provide the infrastructure to put them to work. Earlier this year, for example, it launched the Circle Payments Network, connecting financial institutions and payment providers using its flagship USDC stablecoin and other digital assets for cross-border payments.

The network is Circle's answer to the 8-year-old Ripple Payments business, a service that helps businesses move money across borders, using any of several assets moving through that system, including USDC, Ripple-created XRP and, as of its debut in December 2024, RLUSD.

RLUSD's market cap has grown to more than $2.5 billion. Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC still dominate the total stablecoin market, which now exceeds $300 billion.

RLUSD will also be listed on Robinhood's trading platform, and is currently available to traders on Bitstamp as well as Robinhood Chain, the company's home-grown blockchain for tokenized stocks and other assets.

Robinhood, which reports third-quarter results for the three months ended in September after the market closes, rose about 2.5% in early trading Tuesday, snapping a three-day decline.
