#3059. What Tech Leaders Get Wrong About AI Restructuring And Morale

AI is pushing tech companies to rethink how they organize teams, assign work and plan for the future. However, while an AI-driven restructuring plan may promise greater productivity and a stronger competitive position, those benefits don’t necessarily make the changes easy for employees to navigate.

For leaders, the challenge isn’t just deciding what needs to change; it’s managing how those changes affect the people expected to carry them out. Below, members of Forbes Technology Council discuss leadership mistakes that can damage employee morale during AI-driven restructuring, even when the business rationale is sound.

One mistake is asking employees to embrace AI while making them audition for their own survival. If showing you how to automate their work puts their jobs at risk, you’ve made hiding knowledge a rational response. Be explicit about what is changing; “AI made us do it” is an abdication of command. You cannot demand adaptability from your people while outsourcing your own accountability. - Frederik Gregaard, Cardano Foundation

The mistake is leading with the math, not the mission. Announce that “this role gets automated,” and people check out, even when the logic is airtight. At Agiloft, we never mandated AI. Instead, we showed the work: weekly demos, real wins and leaders doing it alongside everyone else. People don’t resist AI; they resist being told to adopt it without seeing why it’s worth it. - Eric Laughlin, Agiloft

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

The biggest mistake a leader can make is to not bring employees along on the AI journey. Leaders who intentionally bring their entire workforce on this journey can pilot new technologies more broadly, implement rules and processes faster, and foster an organizational culture of innovation. At MetLife, we deploy a federated, CEO-led AI strategy where the ability to adapt is centered on our employees’ appetite to learn, unlearn and relearn skills at scale. - Bill Pappas, MetLife

Make a clear distinction between what AI will be utilized for and where human intervention and decision making will still be paramount. Do not use a “replace the process using AI and increase efficiency” narrative across the board. It can create job insecurity and bring down morale. Instead, get the workforce trained on the safe use of AI, and help them think about where they can bring efficiency into their own roles. - Komal Goyal, 6e Technologies

Don’t perpetuate AI hype. Contrived fear-mongering is suffocating, and leaders who either knowingly or unwittingly succumb to it kill their credibility with their teams, their stakeholders and their customers. The hype- and fear-based mania takes various forms, including elimination of jobs, industries and companies. Leaders who cannot separate fact from hype are starting to stand out in most undesirable ways. - Ricardo Madan, TEKsystems Global Services

The biggest mistake is asking people to automate their work without clearly explaining what their roles will be in the future. It risks each “efficiency boost” via AI being seen by employees as a signal that they are needed less and less, which is naturally a big hit to morale. Leaders need to give their people a clear plan and opportunities to contribute to the decisions and changes being made. - Roman Eloshvili, XData Group

The critical mistake is treating employee hesitation as stubborn obstruction rather than recognizing the natural friction between established tradecraft and emergent tools. When leaders dismiss anxiety as mere drag, they alienate the domain experts whose judgment and institutional trust are essential to navigating the transition. - Sean Maday, Game Plan Tech

One mistake is restructuring work around AI without restructuring career paths. The routine tasks AI can automate are often the same tasks through which employees build experience and prepare for more complex roles. Remove that work without creating new ways to develop, and people may stop seeing a future for themselves in the organization. Leaders need to show not only how work will change but also how employees can continue to grow as it does. - Klaudia Zaika, Apriorit LLC

The biggest mistake is announcing the “what” without a plan for the “who.” When AI is framed only as cost cutting, people see it as an enemy. Leaders must share a different mindset: AI is an ally that helps us improve in our roles and deliver more—and better—work. Pair every change with reskilling, and help teams bring AI into their day-to-day work. People commit when they see themselves in the future. - Maritza Diaz, ITJ USA, Inc.

The mistake is letting actions contradict the message. If AI is about productivity and not headcount reduction, prove it: Invest in training, give people time to adapt, and redeploy talent into value-added work. When employees see leadership follow through on what they’ve promised, they lean in. When they don’t, trust breaks, and every AI initiative after that encounters resistance instead of adoption. - Samuel Martinez, SDG Group

The most damaging mistake is announcing the AI strategy without redesigning the work. Leaders explain why AI matters, then leave teams to figure out on their own which tasks change, who decides what and how performance will be measured. People rarely lose morale because of change. They lose it because of ambiguity. When the old process stays in place and AI is layered on top, employees end up doing both jobs, and the technology starts to feel like a threat instead of relief. - Alessio Alionco, Pipefy

One of the most serious mistakes tech leaders can make is rushing to implement AI tools without the necessary safeguards and governance measures in place. If employees see their leaders creating unnecessary vulnerabilities by introducing poorly managed AI solutions without a plan in place to secure them, it sends a damaging message that harms morale and erodes faith in leadership. If those vulnerabilities lead to negative outcomes, that faith can be hard to win back. - Peter Garraghan, Mindgard

Don’t project certainty you don’t have. Leaders often don’t yet know how every role will change, so they either go quiet or promise too much; both erode trust once reality diverges. Say plainly what has been decided, what hasn’t, and when people will hear more. Then involve teams in redesigning their own work; the people doing it often see first where AI truly helps. - Kuldeep Chowhan, Walmart

A huge mistake is positioning AI as a competitor to human roles. Most human roles will be redesigned because of AI, not completely replaced. The relationship between people and AI is that of a tango: It requires rhythm, balance and trust. Positioning AI as a collaborator and focusing on getting the human side ready to work with AI is the best recipe for getting people engaged with the initiative to make AI work, even when the business case is not clear. - John Kostoulas, Dayforce

One leadership mistake is treating AI restructuring as a business decision that only needs to be explained, rather than as a human transition that needs to be led. Employees can understand the need for change, but vague communication and prolonged uncertainty make people feel disposable. Clarity, transparency and empathy are critical to maintaining trust and morale. - Nandish Dave, BitGo Inc.

One mistake is cutting the entry-level rung because AI now handles junior work. Every senior engineer built judgment on that kind of work. Remove the rung, and mid-level staff see a ladder with nobody climbing behind them, while seniors wonder who will ever succeed them. Redesign junior roles around reviewing and correcting AI output, and count that review work toward promotion so that the pipeline keeps producing the experts who will someday check what the AI gets wrong. - Kuan Archer, Archer Innovative Solutions Group, LLC

It’s a mistake to believe that AI exists in a vacuum. In fact, the applications of AI with the best business outcomes are those that have been implemented under the strategic guidance and management of talented human beings. Morale is murdered if employees believe that they’re being undervalued and are expendable, when in fact the opposite is true. - Scott Burgess, Continu

One of the biggest leadership mistakes is treating AI transformation as a technology journey rather than as a people journey. No matter how compelling the business case may be, leaders must engage employees early, communicate openly and empower them to participate in the change. For example, when automating a function, leaders could have employees participate in the change process, identifying where AI can augment their capabilities so they are not casualties of it. - Babajide Ojuola, International Energy Services Limited

#3058. Forget Palantir? This IPO Candidate May Be the New "Autonomy Giant" in Defense.

Shield AI nearly quadrupled in value over the past year -- and it hasn't even IPO'd yet.

If you follow defense stocks -- and artificial intelligence (AI) -- you probably know about Palantir Technologies (PLTR +5.50%). Privately owned for years before its September 2020 IPO, Palantir attracted significant investor interest even before it went public. Since Palantir went public, the stock is up 16-fold over barely six years, enough to make many investors into millionaires all on its own.

So what are the chances lightning like that could strike twice?

The chances may be better than you think, and amazing as it may sound, there's even a chance it may strike the very same kind of company: a popular defense stock focused on AI called Shield AI.

Much as Palantir was, Shield AI is a company that few people have heard of -- but it's been getting quite a lot of coverage lately and attracting the attention of defense investors. Just last week, defense news site Tectonic reported that Shield AI is raising $2.5 billion in cash at a $28.8 billion valuation to help pay for the acquisition of radar specialist Echodyne.

To put those numbers in context, Tectonic points out that as recently as March, Shield AI was valued at only $12.7 billion. So the valuation has doubled in the last eight months. What's more, as recently as 2025, Shield AI was worth only $5.3 billion. So in fact, the valuation has doubled twice in just the past year.

What is this defense contracting wunderkind? Well, according to its own website, Shield is a defense tech company with the ambitious goal of using AI-powered autonomy to guide "every military asset: aircraft, drones, ships, satellites, and submarines" by 2030.

Shield calls its own autonomy solution by the totally-not-terrifying name Hivemind -- it's the brain behind the company's V-Bat unmanned aerial vehicle (drone), its X-Bat vertical takeoff and landing fighter jet, and its Aechelon simulation platform for training both drone pilots and drone flight systems. (Aechelon also, incidentally, permits Shield's drones to operate without guidance from global positioning systems.)

As recently as a couple of months ago, I was writing about how Shield's software had become so capable that defense heavyweight L3Harris (LHX +4.44%) was enlisting its help in improving the performance of L3's VAMPIRE counter-drone rocket systems. Just one month later, Shield signed up another defense leader -- Italy's Leonardo -- to use Hivemind to power its Hivemind Proteus helicopter drone.

Elsewhere in the military, the U.S. Air Force has put Shield AI on its short list of candidates to provide autonomy software for its new fleet of Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) drone warplanes.

Clearly, Shield AI is a company on the move. Tectonic calls it the new "autonomy giant." It is also, apparently, contemplating an IPO. As Tectonic reports, Shield management is coy about its timetable, but confirms that it is definitely interested in "having the option to go public should we choose to."

Company co-founder Brandon Tseng says Shield AI is on course for $540 million in revenue this year, "up more than 80%" from 2025, according to Fortune magazine. Revenue is growing nearly as fast as the company's valuation. What's more, Tseng confirms that "we don't expect growth to slow down."

So what does this imply for Shield AI's valuation? Well, $540 million in revenue on a stock with a $28.8 billion valuation means Shield stock is valued at approximately 53 times sales. That's actually a bit less than what Palantir stock costs (61 times sales), despite Shield being earlier in its growth trajectory and having more room to grow.

Granted, Palantir's a much bigger player in this market. Its $7.3 billion in trailing revenue still dwarfs Shield's $540 million. But with the momentum Shield is showing, that may not remain the case for long. In a growing military market that's clearly very interested in autonomy, Shield AI could prove a popular choice -- for the Pentagon and for IPO investors.

Rich Smith has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends L3Harris Technologies and Palantir Technologies. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3057. Axon Enterprise: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Axon's $15.8 billion in future contracted bookings gives the company a multi-year runway, but its inventory buildup is already weighing on free cash flow.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 5, 2026, Axon (AXON -3.14%) announced an expanded partnership and a $1.2 billion investment in autonomous drone maker Skydio. For long-term shareholders, the moves reveal how the public safety technology maker plans to capture airspace intelligence while managing shifting federal hardware timelines. Three things management said stand out.

Management put $1.2 billion behind autonomous aerial technology to secure exclusive public safety distribution rights in the U.S. and Canada. Building out hardware supply chains requires substantial capital, so taking a 37% equity stake lets Skydio fund its development while Axon integrates flying hardware directly into its software ecosystem.

Complex federal counter-drone deployments involve extended procurement processes and site preparation. Because these large hardware shipments create quarterly revenue volatility, management reset its forecasting practice to include federal deals in official guidance only after shipments are fully confirmed.

Management added over $100 million in inventory during the third quarter to shield operations from potential component shortages. Carrying extra inventory reduces near-term free cash flow conversion, but the company's core hardware avoids obsolescence risk and protects customer trust.

High-margin software revenue is expanding across real-time operational platforms, while management focuses on monetizing its multiyear contracted backlog. The company maintains durable moat protection through deep customer relationships, proprietary body sensors, and connected software workflows. Strategic priorities center on operational leverage and disciplined inventory control.

As public safety agencies deploy artificial intelligence and connected hardware, maintaining agency trust is essential to long-term market leadership.

#3055. TransMedics: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Its ENHANCE heart and DENOVO lung programs target thousands of procedures that currently use no machine preservation at all.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 5, 2026, TransMedics (TMDX +6.29%) announced full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $764 million to $774 million. The company is advancing several clinical initiatives to expand the use of its medical devices across donor organs. Three things management said stand out for long-term investors.

Third-quarter revenue reached $203 million, up 41% year over year, despite the typical summer lull in donor activity. Increasing customer adoption of organ preservation technology helped offset a 6% drop in overall U.S. donor organ availability during the quarter.

Management is expanding enrollment in its ENHANCE heart and DENOVO lung clinical programs, which use warm perfusion and cold storage options to broaden patient eligibility. These initiatives aim to capture thousands of annual procedures that currently use no machine preservation technology.

TransMedics is developing a portable kidney system to address organs currently discarded due to prolonged ischemia or damage from lack of blood flow during transport. First human clinical testing remains scheduled for the second half of 2027.

Case volumes are reaching all-time highs as hospital adoption expands. TransMedics relies on its owned aviation fleet and donor screening services while management tracks European expansion and clinical trial progress.

Manufacturing efficiencies and next-generation organ preservation systems are expected to drive operating leverage as new clinical indications scale.

#3047. AI debt fears ease ahead of Oracle, Alphabet and Amazon updates. Here's what to watch.

Fears over artificial intelligence debt have eased after a bout of volatility. But more tests for AI debt are coming.

Oracle holds its Investor Day on Wednesday. And hyperscalers Alphabet and Amazon.com are scheduled to report quarterly results after the market close on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively.

Credit markets are on edge over a flood of AI debt, though fears have eased up a little lately. Meta Platforms' plans for a $95 billion stock offering, announced on Monday, helped bring down its credit-default swap spreads. Those spreads had risen last week when the company reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter. Other CDS spreads had moved higher too, though they have since backed off.

Investors had expected Meta to bring a large bond deal to market shortly after its earnings announcement, said Richard Cheng, head of Nuveen's investment-grade corporate sector team. The fact that it wasn't announced came as a relief.

"Just the absence of the bond deal itself is a direct catalyst for AI-related spread tightening," he said.

A credit spread is the difference in the yield between the corporate bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. When spreads tighten, it means investors are becoming more confident about the bond issuer.

The market action over the last few days shows that investors are recognizing that "credit fears may have been overblown," said CNBC contributor Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets.

"I expect that these better feelings, maybe not good but better, may continue as companies announce their quarters over the next few weeks."

Still, spreads on CDS remain wider over the past year due to a surge of debt issuance and free cash flows turning negative across the AI space. Meta's CDS spread, for instance, is still up 177% year to date, while Amazon's spread has gained 129%.

"It's not necessarily fundamentals," said CreditSights analyst Jordan Chalfin. "It's more, I'd say, 80% driven by technicals and sentiment."

Alphabet and Amazon pose the next big hurdle for tech bonds as they update their capex plans and free cash flow forecasts. Microsoft's earnings are also due Wednesday, but the company has yet to issue any bonds to pay for its AI spending.

Both Amazon and Alphabet reported negative free cash flow in the second quarter and analysts expect that trend to continue.

Analysts expect Alphabet to report free cash flow of -$2.3 billion while spending $55.2 billion on capital expenditures in the third quarter, according to FactSet consensus estimates. Amazon is expected to report -$9.9 billion in free cash flow against capex of $58.7 billion.

S&P Global Ratings estimated in an August report that the hyperscalers will have negative free operating cash flow in 2026 and 2027.

More critical will be their outlooks, Cheng says. "The singular focus on the investors' minds is really what the capex guidance trajectory looks like across the hyperscaler space."

Meeks believes elevated capex is a sign of strong AI demand. The hyperscalers have "decided that with all the evidence they have — and they have more than you and me — that this is worthwhile spending, and not just worthwhile; it's required," he said.

CreditSights' Chalfin doesn't expect the hyperscalers to announce major new bond issuance around their earnings reports. Oracle's updates may be more critical for credit markets. The company has issued $117 billion in long-term debt and is clinging to an investment-grade credit rating of BBB-, the lowest level of investment grade above junk, according to S&P.

"It's the most important IG tech credit, just given how it's a bit more stressed relative to the A-rated names," he said. "It's trading more like a high-yield credit, even though it's IG, and so there's just a lot of investor concern on that one."

One wrinkle to the AI debt story: balance sheets don't reveal the whole picture. The companies are using complicated off-balance sheet arrangements for data centers and chip financing, and they aren't fully transparent, S&P Global said in a September report.

"There are commitments they are entering into, for example, into data center leases or purchase commitments on chips that aren't necessarily treated as debt," Mark Habib, digital infrastructure sector lead at S&P Global Ratings, said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Monday.

S&P is trying to provide the market with more visibility on those commitments "to give a fuller picture of what kinds of obligations they're actually entering into," he added.

Oracle aside, hyperscaler credit ratings are all comfortably above A levels — reflecting the fact that they have broadly diversified revenue streams, ample coverage for interest payments, and capacity to add leverage if they choose.

Nuveen's Cheng isn't concerned, pointing out that while there has been some credit repricing, there is no credit crisis.

"They continue to have exceptional credit profiles, strong cash generation liquidity," he said of the largest hyperscalers.

"The market is really not concerned about credit quality at this point," Cheng added. "It's really just the trajectory of the capex needs and the supply of debt to fund that. Both of those are pointing in one direction — and that's up."

Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that Oracle's investment-grade credit rating is BBB-, according to S&P. A previous version mischaracterized the company's credit rating.

#3045. HF Foods (HFFG) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Fuel squeezed profits even as seafood growth and the Searay deal lifted sales.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

HF Foods Group Inc. (HFFG +1.36%) reported its seventh consecutive quarter of top-line growth, driven by seafood volume gains and pricing improvements in the produce and commodity segments. Management indicated that quarterly profitability was impacted by industry-wide fuel inflation and nonrecurring professional fees associated with the Searay Foods acquisition and credit facility refinancing. The company has transitioned its transformation program from the implementation phase to the optimization of warehouse and route efficiencies. The acquisition of Searay Foods establishes a platform for Canadian expansion and adds higher-margin proprietary brands to the seafood category, which currently constitutes 35% of total net revenue. Management reported that the company remains the leading scale food service provider in the Asian specialty market with over $1.2 billion in annual net revenue.

Operator: Greetings. Welcome to the HF Foods Group. Third Quarter 26 Earnings Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. A question and answer session will follow the formal presentation. Please note this conference is being recorded. I will now turn the conference over to Anna Kate Heller, ICR. Anna Kate, you may begin.

Christine Chang: Hello, everyone. Welcome to HF Foods Group's third quarter 26 earnings conference call. Joining me on today's call are Felix Lin, the company's president and chief Executive Officer and Paul Magari, the company's Chief Financial Officer. Before we begin, let me remind everyone that today's discussion contains forward looking statements based on management's current beliefs and expectations about future events which are subject to a number of known and unknown risks and uncertainties. Including statements regarding our recently completed acquisition of Sea Ray Foods, Inc. The integration of that business and the anticipated benefits of the transaction.

If you refer to HF Foods Group's earnings release as well as the company's most recent SEC filings, you will see a discussion of factors that could cause the company's actual results to differ materially from those expressed or implied by these forward looking statements. The company undertakes no obligation to update or revise these forward looking statements in the future. In these remarks, the company will make several references to non GAAP financial measures, including adjusted EBITDA, and non GAAP diluted earnings per share.

We believe that these measures provide investors with a useful perspective on the underlying growth trends of the business, and have included in the earnings release a full reconciliation of non GAAP financial measures to the most comparable GAAP measures. Now I will turn the call over to Xi Lin.

Xi Lin: Thank you, Christine, and good afternoon, everyone. I will start with a business update, and Paul will speak to our third quarter financial results. Then we will open up the line for Q&A. Our third quarter delivered solid top line growth. Net revenue increased 4.1% year over year to $319.6 million making our seventh consecutive quarter of year over year net revenue growth. Driven primarily by volume growth in seafood along with pricing improvement in produce, and commodity. Gross profit increased 5.9% to $53.4 million. And gross margin expanded to 16.7% from 16.4%. Adjusted EBITDA was $11 million compared to $11.7 million in the prior year. Our bottom line was held back this quarter primarily by fuel.

Industry wide fuel price inflation caused a significant year over year increase in our auto and truck expense. We partially offset that with operating efficiencies from our transformation work and we have implemented fuel surcharges across our customer base to share a portion of this burden with our customers. The foundation of our transformation program is now largely built. With investments made in our sales operations, digital infrastructure and facilities, Now our focus has shifted from implementation to optimization. Including route and warehouse efficiency, purchasing discipline. Cross-selling across the Southeast and Midwest remains an important opportunity. But it is 1 we are building out over the next 3 to 5 years paced by the capacity and capital we put behind.

We remain confident these investments are building a stronger foundation for sustainable profitable growth even as we continue to navigate some near term pressure from elevated fuel costs. Regarding facilities, our Charlotte location is largely ready. But we are still awaiting final permitting from local authorities. That process has taken longer than we anticipated, and is largely outside of our control. We anticipate resolution of this process by the end of this calendar year. The biggest milestone of the quarter was closing our acquisition of Sea Ray Foods on August 31. A leading Canadian importer and distributor of ethnic and specialty frozen seafood.

Based in Richmond, British Columbia. it is our first acquisition outside the United States and extends our proven M&A playbook into a new geography. Sea Ray brings 6 proprietary brands, including Sea Ray, Ocean's Best, Hanoi's Best, SmartFish, Diamond Shrimp, and Go Label into our seafood category. Which already makes up about 35% of our net revenue. It has been just over 2 months since we closed, and we are approaching this integration deliberately. Our first priority was continuity. And on that point, the transition has been smooth. Sea Ray's management team led by Derek Ng continues to run the business day-to-day. Customers and suppliers have stayed with us. And Sea Ray's results are not part of our reporting.

We will share more specific milestones as we hit them. In its first month under ownership, Sea Ray contributed $4.2 million on net revenue and $600 thousand of adjusted EBITDA. That is an adjusted EBITDA margin in the mid teens consistent with the profile we described in the announcement and well above our consolidated margin. The fourth quarter will be our first full quarter with Sea Ray. With Sea Ray closed, M&A remains a core pillar of our growth strategy. You have heard us describe HF Foods as the only scale food service provider in the Asian specialty market in The United States.

And as an acquirer of choice in our space, Sea Ray is that strategy in action a higher margin business that chose to join the platform for the scale and operating expertise we bring. Our criteria have not changed. We look to expand our footprint in high potential markets. Capture operational synergies broaden our customer base, and enhance our product and service capabilities. Just as important, our first priority now is integrating Sea Ray well. We will pursue additional opportunities only at the right price with the right fit, and where we have the capacity to integrate them. Within that discipline, we continue to evaluate opportunities in 2027 and beyond. Sea Ray also changes the landscape of our opportunity.

It gives us our first platform outside The United States. In a Canadian market where Sea Ray has spent 25 years building its brand and relationship. It adds proprietary brands and a higher margin business to our seafood category. And it brings retail and wholesale customers alongside our core restaurant base. At over $1.2 billion in annual net revenue. We are now the largest and leading player in the Asian specialty space. And Sea Ray gives us new avenues to build on that position. No 1, whether larger or smaller competitors, is better positioned than HF Foods to capture this opportunity in the coming years.

With that, I will turn the call over to Paul to walk you through our financial performance for the quarter in more detail.

Paul E. McGarry: Thanks, Xi. I will now review our results for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, versus the same period in 2025. Let me start with the bottom line. Because that is where the quarter fell short. We grew net revenue for the seventh consecutive quarter expanded gross margin and generated strong cash flow from operations. Our profitability was not where we wanted it to be. 2 things drove that. Fuel and a concentration of nonrecurring costs tied to the refinancing of our credit facility and the Sea Ray acquisition. I will walk through both along with what we are doing about them. Net revenue for the quarter increased 4.1% or $12.6 million to $319.6 million.

From $307 million in the prior year quarter. The increase was primarily due to volume growth in seafood and pricing improvement in produce and commodity, partially offset by price deflation in meat and poultry, specifically chicken. Net revenue also included $4.2 million from Sea Ray, reflecting 1 month of contribution following the close of the acquisition on August 31. Gross profit increased $3 million or 5.9% to $53.4 million for the quarter compared to $50.4 million in the prior year quarter. Gross profit margin increased 16.7% for the quarter compared to 16.4% in the prior year quarter.

The increase was primarily driven by volume growth in seafood and the higher margin contribution from Sea Ray, both of which we expect to carry forward, as well as tariff refunds received during the quarter. Distribution selling and administrative expenses or DS&A increased $5.9 million or 11.9% to $55.2 million for the quarter and were 17.3% of net revenue compared to 16.1% in the prior year quarter. I would split that increase into 2 pieces. More than half of it was professional fees tied to nonrecurring events, the amendment and upsizing of our revolving credit facility, the refinancing of our property portfolio, the Sea Ray acquisition, and other legal matters.

Those costs are excluded from adjusted EBITDA, and the transaction related portion is largely behind us. The rest was primarily due to auto and truck expense reflecting elevated fuel costs, and higher truck lease expense. Partially offset by lower repair and maintenance costs from the investments we made into a newer fleet. Felix touched on our fuel surcharge program. Like much of the industry, we have responded to higher fuel costs, with the surcharge across our customer base. it is a partial recovery by design, and we will continue to manage it actively as diesel prices move so that it helps offset fuel cost over time while keeping our pricing competitive.

Adjusted EBITDA decreased 6.3% to $11 million for the quarter compared to $11.7 million in the prior year quarter. And included $600 thousand from 1 month of contribution from Sea Ray. Adjusted EBITDA margin was 3.4% compared to 3.8% in the prior year quarter. For the first 9 months, adjusted EBITDA was $34.7 million down less than 2% from last year despite the fuel headwind. Fuel headwinds in the quarter and year to date were approximately 1.4 million and $3.2 million, respectively. Total interest expense was $3.4 million for the quarter compared to $2.9 million in the prior year quarter.

The increase reflects the higher term loan balance following our July refinancing partially offset by the mortgage debt we repaid as part of that transaction. Net loss attributable to HF Foods was a loss of $4.2 million for the quarter compared to a loss of $1.1 million in the prior year quarter. The increase of $3.1 million was primarily driven by a $2.9 million decrease in income from operations and a $900 thousand unfavorable change in income taxes partially offset by a $900 thousand favorable year-over-year change in the fair value of our interest rate swaps. Adjusted net income attributable to HF Foods was $2.1 million for the quarter compared to $4.3 million in the prior year quarter.

Loss per share was $0.08 for the quarter compared to a loss of $0.02 per share in the prior year quarter. Adjusted net income per share was $0.04 per quarter compared to $0.08 in the prior year quarter. Now on CapEx. We spent approximately $22.3 million for the 9 months ended September 30, 2026. The largest item remains the purchase of our previously leased Chicago distribution center. Which we discussed last quarter, along with investments in solar and capacity expansion. With the Chicago purchase behind us, spending slowed meaningfully in the third quarter. On the solar investment, we expect to benefit from a onetime investment tax credit that will reduce our overall solar investment by approximately 40%.

Separately, our fleet renewal is already paying off in lower repair and maintenance costs, and we expect this to continue. Turning to the balance sheet. As we discussed on last quarter's earnings call, we refinanced and upsized our credit facility in July. #3039. LifeVantage (LFVN) Q1 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

Sales slid 22% as management overhauls strategy and shifts its fiscal calendar.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

LifeVantage Corporation (LFVN +1.34%) reported a double-digit revenue decline for the first quarter of fiscal 2027 as management initiated a comprehensive strategic transformation. The company is shifting toward a brand-driven, consumer-focused model intended to stabilize a base of active accounts that decreased by 19% year over year. Financial priorities include resetting the cost structure and reinvesting in digital capabilities to modernize the selling proposition. To align strategy with performance cycles, the company will transition its fiscal year to match the calendar year beginning Jan. 1, 2027. Management did not provide formal financial guidance for the upcoming period but emphasized a focus on operational efficiency and the stabilization of average order sizes.

Operator: Good day, ladies and gentlemen. Thank you for standing by. Welcome to today's conference call to discuss LifeVantage's first Quarter Fiscal Year 27 Results. Terrence O. Moorehead: Thank you, Reed, and good afternoon, everyone. Today, I am going to walk you through some of the initial progress we have made and provide a brief outline of our plans moving forward. Carl is going to walk you through our first quarter performance and financials in a few minutes. But I want to use my time today to focus primarily on where we go from here. I have been with LifeVantage for just over 90 days. And during that time, I have taken the opportunity to listen, learn, and work with our consultants, consumers, employees, and board. I joined the company believing LifeVantage, had far greater potential than its current scale reflects.

And after a comprehensive review of the business, I believe that even more strongly, today. But we have a lot of work to do. In the first quarter, our sales saw revenue decline 22% to $37.1 million and adjusted EBITDA was $1.9 million The decline was driven by a decrease in both orders and average order size, which reinforces our belief that we need to pursue meaningful change. The type of change that we are committed to delivering. Fortunately, we are moving forward from a position of financial stability. We ended the first quarter with $13.7 million in cash, no debt and positive operating cash flow.

We also benefit from strong gross margins, a unique and highly differentiated product line, and a foundation of subscription based accounts. On our last call, I outlined 3 priorities needing attention. The brand, our consumer proposition, and operational excellence and productivity. Over the past 90 days, we have dug deeper and have concluded that we need a comprehensive strategy that reimagines our go-to-market approach our marketing engine, our competitive proposition, and our cost structure if we want to maximize our potential and be prepared to capture the opportunities that lie ahead. The goal is to transform LifeVantage into a brand driven, consumer focused company that leverages digital capabilities to create an expanding community of consumers, and brand advocates.

Our brand, lies at the heart of the transformation. Today, there are thousands of supplement companies essentially selling the same products with the same ingredients and the same benefits to the same consumers. Some offer different forms and features, but beyond their marketing campaigns, many are virtually indistinguishable. LifeVantage, on the other hand, can occupy a much more distinctive space. that is because LifeVantage is built around a fundamentally different proposition. Rather than simply giving the body more ingredients, more products, and more things to take, we develop products designed to work with the body's own biology and activate natural processes that are clinically proven to improve people's health. That distinction lies at the heart of what differentiates LifeVantage.

And it positions the company in a new growing, and ownable white space as the next generation of health and science. Of course, the challenge is to take our differentiated approach to health and science and turn it into a differentiated consumer proposition, and ultimately a differentiated brand. that is the starting point of our strategic roadmap which has 3 major components. The first strategic building block focuses on repositioning the company to change the way people think about LifeVantage and to give consumers a reason to care about the brand. That means repositioning LifeVantage as a next generation nutraceutical company. That positioning builds on our product's unique ability to activate the body's powerful biological systems to improve people's health.

To get started, we are launching a new campaign based on groundbreaking new research that shows how our lead product Protandim NRF2, activates the body's natural defense system to protect the body from environmental toxins like microplastics, pesticides, pollution, and more. For the first time, the new campaign uses before and after images that show the positive impact Protandim has on cells affected by specific environment toxins. it is an exciting new approach designed to create emotional connection with the brand We start with an important consumer outcome which, in this case, is to protect the body from environmental toxins, and we follow-up with simple to understand visuals that provide scientific proof.

Our second strategic building block focuses on reimagining the business proposition. To make it easier to discover, engage with, and share LifeVantage. Our approach is to modernize the business build new capabilities, and align with the way consumers shop and buy today. Followed by a third quarter 2027 launch of a new consumer driven business suite for sellers.

Our third strategic building block focuses on expanding beyond our current scale and scope to more aggressively penetrate key markets expand share in high potential categories, and identify new growth platforms. Starting January 1, 2027, our fiscal year will align with the calendar year.

And the timing is appropriate as January 1st marks the beginning of the next generation of the company that we are building. With that, I would like to turn the call over to Carl so he can walk you through our financial results in more detail. Carl?

Carl A. Aure: Thank you, Terrence, and good afternoon, everyone. Let me walk you through our financial results for the quarter ended 09/30/2026. Please note that I will be discussing our non GAAP adjusted results where applicable. You can refer to the GAAP to non GAAP reconciliation in today's press release for additional details. We delivered net revenue of $37.1 million in the current quarter, which was down 22% compared to $47.6 million in the same period a year ago. The decrease was primarily driven by continued downward pressure in the number of orders from our active consumer base and lower average order size reflecting impacts from the broader macroeconomic environment as well as lower sales from our MindBody GLP-1 System.

These declines were partially offset by sales of the LoveBiome product line which we acquired in October 2025. Foreign currency also negatively impacted revenue by $400 thousand in the quarter or approximately 80 basis points in the quarter. Revenue in the Americas region decreased 22.2% to $29 million and revenue in the Asia Pacific and Europe region decreased 21.2% to $8.2 million including $400 thousand or 3.9% of the negative impact from foreign currency rate fluctuations. Subscription based revenue continues to provide a substantial portion of our revenue in the quarter. Representing more than 75% of total revenue.

We also recognize another quarter of improvement in our retention metrics for both consultants and customers in comparison to the prior year period. We will continue to focus on improving our retention metrics as we work on strengthening the brand and improving the consumer proposition during calendar year 2027. Our gross profit percentage for the quarter was 75.4%, compared to 79.5% in the prior year period, reflecting higher inventory obsolescence expenses along with higher shipping and warehouse expenses. Excluding the additional inventory allowance related to our MindBody product line, adjusted non GAAP gross profit percentage was 78.2%.

Commissions and incentive expense was 41.4% of revenue, compared to 43.5% a year ago primarily due to the timing and magnitude of promotional and incentive programs changes in revenue mix, and changes in the mix of customers and independent consultants. Selling, general, and administrative expenses were 34.3% of revenue, compared to 31.2% in the prior year period, reflecting the overall decrease in net revenue. As Terrence mentioned earlier, we understand the need to reset the economics of the business and are in the process of carefully reviewing all SG&A spend to become more focused and efficient. GAAP operating loss was $100 thousand compared to operating income of $2.3 million in the prior year period.

Adjusted non GAAP operating income was 900 thousand compared to $2.5 million a year ago. GAAP net loss was $200 thousand or $0.02 per diluted share compared to net income of $2.2 million or $0.17 per diluted share in the prior year period. Adjusted non GAAP net income was $600 thousand or $0.05 per diluted share compared to $2.3 million and $0.18 in the prior year period. We recorded income tax expense of $12 thousand for the quarter, We anticipate that our effective tax rate for the 6 month transition period ending 12/31/2026 will be approximately 20% to 25%.

Adjusted EBITDA for the quarter was $1.9 million or 5.2% of revenue compared to $3.9 million or 8.2% of revenue in the same period a year ago. Our financial position remains strong, with $13.7 million of cash and no debt as of September 30, compared to $14.9 million of cash as of 06/30/2026. We had generated $500 thousand of cash from operations during the quarter compared to $2.3 million used in operations in the prior year period, primarily reflecting decreases in accounts receivable and inventory and the timing of payments of accrued expenses. Capital expenditures were $1.2 million during the quarter, compared to $400 thousand in the prior year period, primarily reflecting our continued investment in technology infrastructure including investment in our new e commerce platform. Turning to capital allocation. We did not repurchase any shares during the quarter, and $58.5 million remains under our $60 million share repurchase authorization. We also recently announced a quarterly cash dividend of $05 per share of common stock that will be paid on December 15, 2026, to shareholders of record as of December 1, 2026. We remain committed to our balanced capital allocation strategy in order to maximize shareholder value.

From a reporting standpoint, as Terrence noted, we are changing our fiscal year to align with the calendar year. For the 6 month transition period ending 12/31/2026, in addition to reporting quarterly results, will also file a Form 10-KT including audited financial statements in the first quarter of calendar year 27. Our new 2027 fiscal year will begin on January 1, 2027. But the energy and determination of our team and the groundwork that we have been building coming together, with improvements in our monetization, Infosynthience, and Cutter Studios beginning to take off and Tabulation's launch on the horizon, we are excited to report back with continued updates on our initiatives and progress in our evolution as Pareteum AI. #3033. SIGA (SIGA) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Zero debt and a new Canadian deal stand out, but U.S. contract timing remains unclear.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

SIGA Technologies, Inc. (SIGA +5.16%) reported financial results for the third quarter and nine months ended Sept. 30, 2026, marking the completion of its product delivery obligations under the BARDA 19C contract. Management reported that the company is currently focused on securing a new procurement contract with the U.S. government, though the timing of such an award remains uncertain. The company indicated an expansion of its international customer base through a new five-year agreement with the Canadian Department of National Defence and is in advanced negotiations with another international customer. Strategic updates included a timeline revision for the Post-Exposure Prophylaxis supplemental NDA and the upcoming completion of a Phase I pediatric study.

Operator: Welcome to the SIGA Business Update Call. Before we turn the call over to SIGA management, please note that any forward-looking statements made during this call are based on management's current expectations and observations, and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ from forward-looking statements. SIGA does not undertake any obligation to update publicly any forward-looking statement to reflect events or changed circumstances after this call.

For a discussion of factors that could cause results to differ, please see the company's filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission, including without limitation, the company's annual report on Form 10-K for the year ended December 31st, 2025, and its subsequent reports on Form 10-Q and Form 8-K. With that, I will turn the call over to Diem Nguyen, Chief Executive Officer of SIGA. Diem?

Diem Nguyen: Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining today's call to review our business results. I am joined by Dan Luckshire, our Chief Financial Officer, and we appreciate this opportunity to provide an update on our company. After the update, we will take your questions. Throughout 2026, SIGA has continued to execute on its core mission of working alongside governments to build and sustain long-term preparedness against potential biological threats, namely smallpox. We remain committed to positioning our smallpox therapeutic, TPOXX, for rapid, large-scale deployment should an outbreak occur. As a reminder, in the second quarter, we completed our final product delivery under the BARDA 19C contract, fulfilling all our product obligations under that agreement.

We are proud of this partnership, proud of how we performed, and proud to have played an important role in strengthening the U.S. government's smallpox preparedness. We believe the case for preparedness against biological threats remains strong. Geopolitical tensions and advances in technology, including AI, are reshaping the threat landscape. Mitigating these risks requires proactive, sustained government investment in medical countermeasures stockpiles. In an emergency, ready access to medical countermeasures is essential to protect both civilians and war fighters. At the same time, a compelling case for preparedness does not always translate into predictable procurement.

As we discussed during our last call, the process to secure a new U.S. government contract has progressed more slowly than in the past, and the timing of an award remains uncertain. Even so, we remain confident that TPOXX has an important role in our nation's preparedness plans and that national security for medical countermeasures remain important to the U.S. government. Despite the lack of certainty as to timing and details, based on our discussions with key stakeholders, we continue to believe that a new procurement contract will be awarded. Turning to our international business, I would like to share news of recent contract that advances our efforts to maintain a diverse revenue stream and customer base.

Last month, we signed a contract to supply oral TPOXX to Canada's Department of National Defence, or CDND, over the next five years. This contract is valued up to approximately $15 million. It includes firm commitments about $9 million over the first three years, plus up to $6 million in options exercisable at CDND's discretion. This is CDND's second TPOXX contract. The first, awarded in April of 2020 for the purchase up to approximately $14 million of TPOXX, was completed in 2025. Canada continues to be one of the leaders in smallpox preparedness among our international customers, and we believe this award reflects that commitment. It also highlights another important point.

In a public health emergency, the men and women of the armed forces are often among the first called on to respond, so making sure they have access to smallpox antiviral is a key part of being prepared. Beyond this contract, we are continuing advanced discussions with other international customers, including one which we are in late-stage negotiations. We look forward to providing an update at the appropriate time. Moving to our development activities, I'd like to provide an update on our pediatric formulation and Post-Exposure Prophylaxis, or PEP, programs. We continue to expect results from phase I study of our pediatric formulation by year end, and those results will inform next steps.

If successful, this formulation, together with the oral and IV formulations, would extend TPOXX coverage across the full population, from infants to adults. Children are among the most vulnerable in an outbreak, and an improved pediatric formulation will give governments a more complete solution for their stockpiles. On the PEP program, we continue to work closely with our partners at the Department of War, FDA, and CDC, all of whom remain highly engaged with this program. We recently met with the FDA to review the program, including the immunogenicity sample analysis the CDC plans to conduct.

At that meeting, the FDA has asked us to perform additional validation and related laboratory work to help ensure the accuracy of results from the sample analysis. This work is important and requires time, and as a result, we now expect to file our supplemental NDA in 2028. While this delay is disappointing, it does not change our view on the relevance of this program. In an outbreak, the ability to use TPOXX as a PEP for our military, first responders, and others exposed to smallpox virus can help save lives.

Regarding our financial results, as I said in prior calls, our business is subject to inherent quarter-to-quarter variability, so our results are best viewed over a longer horizon than any single period. Over the first nine months of the year, product revenues totaled approximately $42 million, including sales to the U.S. government and customers in Asia-Pacific region and Europe. That breadth, together with the new CDND contract I talked about earlier, reflects the continued commitment of governments around the world to smallpox preparedness. Before I turn the call over to Dan, I want to recognize Dennis Hruby our Chief Scientific Officer, who is retiring today after three decades with SIGA.

When Dennis joined us in 1996, there was no approved treatment for smallpox. Today, TPOXX is approved in the U.S., Canada, the European Union, the U.K., and Japan. It has been sold to more than 30 countries and is maintained in stockpiles around the world. Dennis's scientific leadership shaped the achievement at every step, from early-stage research through approval. On behalf of everyone at SIGA, I want to thank Dennis for his contributions to our company and to global health security. We're very pleased that he will continue to support us in an advisory role.

In closing, SIGA has always been guided by its mission to ensure governments are prepared to protect their citizens from smallpox, and that mission is unchanged. While procurement processes are not predictable, we stand ready to work with our governments around the world, and we do so with a strong balance sheet, including $116 million in cash and no debt at the end of the quarter. As I said at the start of the call, we believe the case for preparedness remains strong. Smallpox and other high-consequence threats are serious, and emerging technologies have the potential to lower barriers to creating or misusing biologic agents.

With preparation, these threats can be mitigated, and TPOXX has a long history of helping governments meet smallpox threats. With that, I'll turn over to Dan to review our financial results in more detail. Dan?

Dan Luckshire: Thanks, Diem. As noted earlier in the call, the company's product-related revenues are $42 million for the nine months ended September 30th, 2026, with most of the revenues being recorded in the second quarter, reflecting the variable rhythm of SIGA's business model. Year-to-date product revenues include approximately $26 million of IV TPOXX deliveries to the U.S. Strategic National Stockpile and approximately $13 million of international sales to two international customers. For the third quarter, there are no product sales to customers. In addition to product-related revenues for the nine months ended September 30th, 2026, the company also has research and development revenues of approximately $7 million.

Of this total, approximately $1 million of the research and development revenues were earned in the third quarter. Pre-tax operating income for the nine months ended September 30th, 2026, which excludes interest income and taxes, is approximately $2 million. For the quarter, pre-tax operating loss is approximately $7 million. Net income for the nine months ended September 30th, 2026, is approximately $6 million. For the quarter, net loss is approximately $3 million. In turn, fully diluted income per share for the nine months ended September 30th, 2026, is $0.09 per share, while fully diluted loss per share for the quarter is $0.04 per share. The company continues to maintain a strong balance sheet.

At September 30th, 2026, the company had a cash balance of approximately $116 million and no debt. This concludes the financial update. At this point, I will turn the call back to Diem.

Diem Nguyen: Thank you, Dan. With that, we'd like to open the call for questions.

Operator: Thank you. Ladies and gentlemen, we will now begin the question-and-answer session. Should you have a question, please press the star key followed by the number one on your touchtone phone. You will hear a prompt that your hand has been raised. Should you wish to decline from the polling process, please press the star key followed by the number two. One moment, please, while we assemble the queue. Your first question comes from Jyoti Prakash of Edison Group. Please go ahead.

Jyoti Prakash: Hi, good evening. Thank you for taking my questions. First of all, congratulations on the recent contract from the CDND. Just want to understand if this is the international opportunity which was highlighted during the Q2 call, and if there's another order still under discussion, because you did mention that you're in conversations. If there is an order under discussion, can we hear about it during the remainder of the year? Going back to the CDND order, can you provide some color on the delivery schedule, particularly if we can expect anything to be delivered within 2027?

Dan Luckshire: Hi, Jyoti. This is Dan. Thanks for the question. I'll answer this one. On the first part of your question, yes, the October contract is the opportunity that we referenced last quarter. In your question, you asked about, well, is there another order? As noted in our prepared remarks, there is another order. We are in advanced stages for another international contract, and on that, we will provide details at the appropriate time. Toward the end of your question, you're talking about sort of cadence of delivery.

With regard to that, the way the contract is set up is the firm orders are structured, so that SIGA would deliver an equal number of oral TPOXX courses in each of the first three fiscal years of the contract. I want to note that given that the Canadian fiscal year goes from April to March, this could result in two deliveries within one calendar year. I wanted to also highlight that deliveries are expected to start in 2027. The contract has the firm orders I just talked about and also has options.

With respect to the options, courses can be ordered and delivered at any point in time during the five-year contract, and that's at the discretion of the Canadian military.

Jyoti Prakash: Thank you, Dan. That was very useful. My second question relates to recent developments and something which has been on people's minds is the results of the U.S. midterm elections. Do you foresee any implications of the results on biodefense funding priorities and possibly the timing of the U.S. RFP?

Diem Nguyen: Hi, Jyoti. This is Diem. Nice to hear your voice, and thanks for joining the call and this question. I would say historically, there has been bipartisan support for biodefense, and quite frankly, biodefense is not a large or controversial budget line item, which means we don't currently expect a change in direction regarding congressional funding for biodefense. As it relates to the new contract process, we currently do not believe that midterm results will have any material impact on the nature or trajectory of this process beyond the typical transition period that follows any election.

Jyoti Prakash: Great. Thank you, Diem. Just going back to international growth, we noted that Bavarian Nordic recently secured a four-year smallpox vaccine contract with the U.K. government. Are you also seeing broader momentum in European preparedness spending and also greater interest in TPOXX? The reason we're asking this is because recently, the Mpox label was removed in Europe. Do you see any sort of implications of this on your recent discussions with the European authorities?

Diem Nguyen: Thanks, Jyoti. So Europe, like many countries and continents, go through multi-year transformational in terms of national security priorities and spending. In this particular environment, each country has its own dynamics and priorities and is moving at its own pace. Overall, yes, we do believe that there's increased focus on biodefense and smallpox preparedness. This has resulted in the spending like the U.K. contract you just mentioned. I would say historically, though, smallpox preparedness across Europe has largely been vaccine-centric. Part of our work supporting a shift towards a more comprehensive approach that pairs vaccines with antivirals, very much similar to the U.S. model, but we do recognize that changing this paradigm takes time.

Specifically for TPOXX, we are part of evolving conversations on stockpiling, both at the country and regional level. Now, Jyoti, for your second question on our European label, in certain cases, the change does require some additional discussion. While this can affect timing, we do not believe it changes the long-term opportunity in Europe for smallpox stockpiling. Notably, just as a gentle reminder, we recently renewed our TPOXX filings both in Europe as well as in U.K. for the treatment of smallpox, and we really look forward to working with our European counterparts in our preparedness efforts.

Jyoti Prakash: That's very helpful. Thanks, Diem. No further questions from my side.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I will now turn the call back over to Diem Nguyen. Please continue.

Diem Nguyen: Thank you. Today, I'd like to thank everybody for making time to join us on today's call and for your ongoing interest in SIGA. We look forward to speaking with you again next quarter. Have a good evening.

Operator: Ladies and gentlemen, that concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.

Today, we are benefiting from the expanding interest across America as the demand for skilled workers exceeds supply. To meet the demand, we are expanding our programs at existing campuses and developing new campuses. We have focused our strategies on simplifying operations to maximize graduate opportunities in the electrical, HVAC, automotive, welding, and healthcare fields. These careers are in high demand and are expected to remain in high demand for many years despite the effects of artificial intelligence deployment throughout American enterprises.

Our third quarter performance illustrates the success of our established model. We regained our student start growth momentum by generating a 14.2% increase over the prior year period. This growth resulted from our team successfully responding to a rapidly evolving marketing environment, increasing our conversion of leads to starts, examining new channels, benefiting from investments in our high school channel, and consistently exploring ways to increase large language model inclusion of our differentiation and superior outcomes for skilled trades and in-demand career training and education.

Demand for our high return on investment training and education programs remains strong as corporations and organizations throughout America continue to search for ways to close their seemingly chronic employee skills gap, which is inhibiting their growth. We believe the demand for our programs is also benefiting from Americans increasingly turning to the skilled trades to provide stable, rewarding long-term careers. Our strong student starts, as well as the increase in our average student population, led to solid double-digit revenue growth for the quarter.

By continuing to realize operating efficiencies from our Lincoln 10.0 hybrid teaching platform and other initiatives, we generated a substantial increase in cash generated from operating activities, a 22.5% increase in operating income, and more than 30% growth in adjusted EBITDA. And we returned capital to our shareholders through the purchase of approximately 870,000 shares of our common stock during the third quarter. Our decision to repurchase shares and our board's recent decision to increase the authorization to a total of $70 million reflects our confidence in Lincoln Tech's long-term growth prospects and our belief that our stock represents an attractive investment opportunity.

While our Lincoln 10.0 hybrid teaching platform is realizing instructional efficiencies for the company, our instructors, and our students, we are also continuing to invest some of the gains from these efficiencies in programs and processes to continuously drive improved student outcomes, which we believe is positively impacting our student retention rate at our programs open for more than a year. During the quarter, we also continued the development of our Rowlett, Texas campus and initiated the development of our first Arizona campus in Tempe. Our other expansion took place at the Melrose Park, Illinois campus, where we ended our auto collision program, introduced our HVAC program, created our third Tesla training center, expanded our welding program, and bought the facility.

The successful transition means our average student population at Melrose Park has grown to the point where the campus is now the second largest in the Lincoln system, and we have achieved this growth while reducing our facility cost. Some of our recent operating highlights at existing campuses include the teaching out of the collision program at our Grand Prairie campus, where we expect to expand other programs as we've done in Melrose Park, continued strong growth in high school starts throughout our system, consistent graduation and job placement rates, and positive reaccreditation visits at a number of our campuses.

Our efforts to revitalize our healthcare programs continue to generate results as student starts and graduation rates are realizing positive trends. We also made further progress in reducing our bad debt as a percentage of revenues, as well as improving our financial aid processing, which has played a key role in resuming double-digit start growth. As I mentioned at the beginning of my comments, we also improved our lead conversion rate as compared to historical levels, and despite higher lead generation costs, maintained a relatively flat overall student acquisition cost during the third quarter. Our business development team continues to examine underserved markets across the U.S. that would benefit from Lincoln's proven career development programs.

In addition, WorkforceLinc formed a new partnership with the engineering firm ABB, a global leader in electrification and automation, which will support ABB in building a nationwide recurring source of electrical and electronic technician candidates. A major focus of the effort is to develop skilled employees to serve the maintenance needs of the nation's growing number of data centers.

We are continuously working to increase the visibility of our outcomes and differentiation from other less successful training models, and our third quarter performance and outlook for the full year increases our confidence in achieving our 2030 financial objectives of approximately $850 million in revenue and $150 million in EBITDA. Given our strong liquidity, cash flow generation, the board has extended the share repurchase program through May 2028 and increased the authorization by $30 million, bringing the remaining capacity to over $37 million. The timing and amounts of any future repurchase will depend on market conditions, share price, our capital needs, and other factors.

The program does not obligate us to acquire any particular number of shares and may be modified, suspended, or discontinued at any time. In November, we also amended our revolving credit facility to provide greater flexibility, including supporting future share repurchases, which I'll discuss in more detail later in my remarks. Now let's turn to the third quarter financial results. As a reminder, as we have noted in prior earnings calls, there was a shift in our academic calendar last year that resulted in the start class that typically occurs in late June moving to July 1st, 2025.

To provide a meaningful comparison, as in prior quarters, we have adjusted the third quarter 2025 student starts to exclude those July 1st starts and treat them as if they occurred in last year's second quarter. Our discussions today will compare third quarter 2026 starts with those adjusted numbers. We delivered strong financial and operating results in the third quarter, highlighted by solid growth in student starts, revenue, adjusted EBITDA, net income, and continued adjusted EBITDA margin expansion. Demand for our programs remains strong as reflected in our student start growth of 14.2%. Our ending student population grew by approximately 2,100 students, or 11% year-over-year, providing a solid foundation for continued revenue growth.

Organic student starts increased by nearly 5%, reflecting continued demand for our programs. Our measurement of organic growth includes new campuses and programs that were in place for more than one year. The additional start growth over prior year came from our program expansions and our new Houston campus, which continues to grow its student population. As Scott discussed, actions we implemented to improve conversion from leads to enrollment to start gain traction during the third quarter, contributing to student start growth and also benefiting our student acquisition cost. Cost per start for the quarter remained relatively flat despite elevated lead costs, reflecting the benefits of improved lead conversion. This performance exceeded our expectations.

Our strong student start volume and our efforts to improve enrollment conversions offset the higher spend in the quarter, and we are encouraged by this progress. However, we do expect that cost per start will be elevated above prior year levels in the near term as these initiatives continue. Year-to-date, student starts had increased 1,864 or 11%. Based on current enrollment trends, we expect this performance to continue, which supports our outlook for the full year student start growth of 10%-12%. Third quarter revenue increased 12.6% to $159.2 million, driven primarily by a 10.9% increase in our average student population. This marks our 14th consecutive quarter of double-digit year-over-year revenue growth. Turning to profitability.

Operating expenses for the quarter were consistent with our expectations. Corporate expenses were relatively flat, while campus-level expenses increased in line with our revenue growth, supporting our larger student population and continued growth initiatives. This expense growth was primarily offset by favorable bad debt expense, which continues as a percentage of revenue below prior year levels, reflecting our continued focus on collections and managing credit losses. Adjusted EBITDA increased 30.8% to $17.4 million, with our adjusted EBITDA margin expanding by 150 basis points to approximately 11%. This improvement reflects operating leverage from our larger student population. As a reminder, beginning in 2026, our calculation of adjusted EBITDA no longer adds back pre-opening and first-year operating losses from new campuses.

During the quarter, we incurred $2 million in new campus losses compared to $2.7 million the prior year quarter. These costs are fully reflected in our reported adjusted EBITDA, highlighting our ability to deliver strong earnings growth while continuing to invest in our campus expansion strategies. Net income increased 24% to $4.7 million compared to $3.8 million the prior year quarter. Diluted earnings per share were $0.15 based on approximately 31.4 million weighted average diluted shares outstanding. Turning to capital expenditures. We continue to invest in future business opportunities. Year-to-date spending totaled approximately $69.6 million, of which $67.4 million is reflected in our statement of cash flows, with the remainder accrued but not yet paid.

Third quarter capital expenditures of approximately $36.4 million were in line with our expectations, including $17.4 million related to the purchase of our previously leased Melrose Park campus. We continue to expect full-year capital expenditures of $95 million-$100 million, consistent with our previously communicated outlook. Turning now to our balance sheet and financing activities. We continue to generate strong operating cash flow during the quarter, supported by our growing student population, improved operating performance, and effective management of cash collections. Cash flow from operations totaled $34.9 million in the third quarter, an increase of $11 million compared to the prior year quarter.

Year-to-date operating cash flow reached $61.5 million compared to $15.8 million in the prior year, representing an improvement of nearly $46 million. This increase reflects our improved operating performance, continued focus on working capital management. We ended the third quarter with $20.6 million in cash and $115 million available in our revolving credit facility, providing total liquidity of $135.6 million. At quarter end, we had $10 million outstanding under the credit facility. During the quarter, we also completed the purchase of our previously leased Melrose Park campus, financed primarily with a $15 million mortgage loan. This transaction reduced our ongoing facility costs while providing us with a long-term control of the property.

In November, we amended our $125 million revolving credit facility. The amendment expands our flexibility for future share repurchases, provided that we maintain total liquidity of more than $25 million following any repurchase. The amendment also adds a daily borrowing option that can be repaid at any time without penalty. In addition to our existing borrowing options, this lets us manage cash balances and borrowing costs more effectively. Together, these changes enhance our ability to employ capital, supporting our campus expansion initiatives while maintaining the flexibility to return capital to shareholders through our share repurchase program. Turning to our full-year outlook.

Based on our year-to-date results, current trends, we are raising our revenue guidance, narrowing our student start growth range, and reiterating our guidance for adjusted EBITDA, net income, diluted EPS, and capital expenditures. We now expect revenue of $600 million-$605 million, up from $590 million-$600 million, adjusted EBITDA of $76 million-$80 million, net income of $23 million-$26 million, diluted EPS of $0.74-$0.83, capital expenditures of $95 million-$100 million, and student start growth of 10%-12%, narrowed from 10%-14%. As I mentioned earlier, beginning in 2026, our calculation of adjusted EBITDA no longer excludes pre-opening and first-year operating losses from new campuses.

Accordingly, our guidance continues to include approximately $10 million in losses at our new campuses, which remain in line with our expectations. Non-cash stock-based compensation continues to be our only expense add-back to the calculation this year. Growth initiatives represent approximately 75% of our planned capital expenditures, underscoring our continued focus on expanding capacity and supporting future enrollment growth. We'll continue to update our capital expenditure outlook as we announce additional campus locations. In closing, our strong year-to-date performance reinforces our confidence in achieving our long-term financial objectives. I also want to recognize our entire team for their continued dedication to providing a high-quality education and strong outcome to our students. With that, I'll turn the call over to the operator for questions. Operator?

As you mentioned, we have made investments in our high school sales team, and they performed well for us.

The landscape is constantly changing. We're constantly adapting to that landscape, and I'm just really pleased by the performance that our team is achieving.

Alex Paris: I guess that my follow-up would be, since you referred to it, you have a number of channels that you're tapping. Could you break down either total revenue or starts by those various channels, just ballpark at least?

Scott Shaw: Yeah. So, I mean, in aggregate, high school is about 20% of our starts, a little bit higher than that. Obviously, in the third quarters, that's where the bulk of the high school students come in. Military is still small for us. While we reference the fact that we started as 100% military back in 1946, we're only about 6% right now. But we've made investments also in our military channel that we anticipate seeing some benefits from, frankly, in 2027. So, it would be nice to bring that back up to hopefully double digits in the next 24 months.

Then from a corporate standpoint, I still believe that's a huge, really untapped opportunity for us and an area that we are going to put more resources behind. I think that once we tap into that fully, that will really help support our growth beyond just reaching the adults that we do through our existing marketing channels. So, we're just going to continue to find the people where they are, because we know from talking to employers that they have not let up on the need for what we're doing. So, it's really just trying to get our message out there to as many people as possible.
