Eric Wold: Two quick questions, I guess. First off, what are you seeing in terms of the cost per lead increase compared to last year? How is that running? Is it still up 20-ish percent? Then what are you finding is the best way to kind of navigate around that in terms of which channels, like social media, are kind of proving the most effective around that?

Scott Shaw: Sure. Yeah, we're still seeing cost per lead up at that level, Eric, around the 20% level, and that's what we're going to be forecasting going forward. We're hoping that will lessen in time, but as of right now, that's certainly the world we're living in. We're looking then for other channels. One of the great channels that we've had good success is our own students. We just did our student satisfaction surveys.

We got the best results that we've had in years, and we're constantly reaching out to our students and say, "Hey, is there someone else, a friend of yours, a cousin, or someone that could benefit from the Lincoln Education just like you are?" That's a very low-cost, I'll say, source of enrollments and leads. We'll constantly look at where is the best value for us to put our time and energy. As I mentioned earlier, we are putting more into social media.

We've recently ensured that every campus, or at least 95% of our campuses, have someone solely dedicated to be on social media, because we know that's where our students are spending a lot of time, and our campuses really have a lot of rich material that is very attractive to people. Eric Wold: Perfect. Then, follow-up question. Any sense of kind of the number of students or kind of a percentage of students that kind of come looking to enroll and ultimately are unable to because of past financial aid issues?

Scott Shaw: Yeah, I don't have that number, but I can tell you, in general, I mean, it's not something that is of such magnitude that people are viewing that as a headwind for us. I am sure that the number is probably larger than I would like, simply because there's so many people that could benefit from an education. But if they've unfortunately not kept up with their payments, that certainly limits what they can do going forward. But in short, it's not popping up to me at my level as far as being any kind of resistance to our future growth.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Steven Frankel from Rosenblatt Securities. Your question, please.

Steven Frankel: Good morning, and thank you. Scott, could you talk about show rates? That was one of the factors in last quarter's disappointing start rate. Maybe how show rates changed in Q3 and what you're doing going forward to make sure that they're going in the right direction.

Scott Shaw: Yeah. Well, obviously, we were a little bit surprised in Q2. We obviously didn't want to repeat that. So, we stepped up a number of initiatives. One is just more engagement by our admissions folks with students that are enrolled, just to make sure that they remember the value opportunity and why they selected us and why they want to change their life, and just staying in front of those students so that more of them do start. We definitely had more students start who were enrolled with us. Similarly, it's also with financial aid.

The sooner that the students know how much it's going to cost them and how they're going to pay for the education, the more comfortable they are. Last year, I'm sorry, last quarter, we did have more people than the prior year go through financial aid. This quarter, in third quarter, we had even more people. With the admissions folks supporting that initiative and keeping those students engaged in the process seems to have translated into our start rate was up, frankly, a couple of hundred basis points, which is very impactful.

Steven Frankel: That's great. Then on this ABB effort that you're going to be doing around data centers, could you talk to us about what specifically is in this training that's not in your traditional electrical or HVAC training?

Scott Shaw: Sure. So, in this case, we are actually just helping ABB find people who are graduating from our organization to then enroll at ABB and start their program. It's not requiring, frankly, any additional training by us of our students. It's more finding students that are willing and able to move to locations that ABB has. So, it's really a partnership in placement services for ABB.

Steven Frankel: Great. Thank you so much.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Eric Martinuzzi from Lake Street Capital Markets. Your question, please.

Eric Martinuzzi: Yeah. I appreciate the upward revision on the revenue side. We didn't get the flow-through, though, to the adjusted EBITDA. Is that back to your comment, Scott, regarding the increased cost of student acquisition?

Board forms committee to explore strategic alternatives, including a sale.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

WhiteHorse Finance, Inc. (WHF -3.46%) reported the formation of a special committee to explore strategic alternatives, including a potential sale or corporate transaction for the company. Management indicated that current market conditions in the software sector are providing attractive entry points due to lower enterprise valuations and reduced leverage compared to prior years. The company is prioritizing the monetization of equitized assets, specifically citing active sale processes for Chase Products and Playmonster to transition capital into income-producing investments. The board also declared a special distribution to manage undistributed taxable income while maintaining the base quarterly distribution rate.

We are seeing lenders take a more conservative approach to add-backs, synergies and run rate adjustments. Deal structures are generally back below 55% loan-to-value and cash flow coverage is solid and pricing for most of the 2026 vintage has been 50 to 75 basis points higher than in 2025 and 2024.

Because many lenders are overallocated to software and unable to consider new deals in that sector, the software opportunities we are now seeing are unusually attractive with lower enterprise value, lower loan-to-value, much lower leverage and pricing that is 100 to 150 basis points higher than for an equivalent deal outside of the software sector. Robert Dodd: Got it. Got it. One -- a couple of other questions. On one of your comments, I think, was there are some credits that are seeing a little softness. But in most cases, I underline that in my notes, the owners are supporting the credits. I mean, is there any theme for the ones where the owners aren't supporting them? Is it like a one-off or 2-off -- or kind of any themes about in the portfolio or more broadly where sponsors or owners, right, because it might be a nonsponsor deal are still willing to support a deal versus less willing to support a deal?

Stuart Aronson: Robert, the deals that have had covenant defaults have, I believe, all been sponsor deals. And the sponsor or other parties in the deal in all of the situations I can think of have agreed to support the credit with equity injections. That is the beauty of the middle market we serve, where sponsors still inject equity into companies as opposed to the broadly syndicated market, where sponsors generally do LME transactions and jam down their lenders into a more subordinated position. So we are seeing support from owners and we hope that support with money going in underneath our senior debt is an indication that they have confidence that the situations those companies are facing are temporary and/or fixable.

But overall, as I mentioned in the remarks, the general portfolio is stable to improving with only a couple of credits that have had covenant defaults and the need for equity to be injected.

Robert Dodd: Yes. Got it. Got it. One last one, if I can. On -- you could have -- to your point in your remarks, there could be potentially quite relatively large compared to the size of the portfolio amount of equity kind of harvesting over the next, call it, 6 months, right? I mean not everything is going to happen immediately, but over between now and, say, the middle of next year. What would -- and you also mentioned the software deals are starting to look a lot more attractive. And a fair number of the ones out there, certainly the bigger ones, right, have maturities next year.

I mean, is that something you could look to exploit the potential equity realizations and an attractive segment of the software market next year maybe? And is that the kind of redeployment pattern that's realistic? Obviously, if it's lower leverage, lower LTV and higher spreads versus no spread on some of the equity, that could be quite attractive.

Stuart Aronson: Yes. The technology or software deals that we've seen really fit into 2 categories. Category 1 is people trying to fix broken capital structures. And a lot of those deals have companies that have some level of AI risk. In general, so far, we have not been willing to entertain those deals. So broken capital structures and AI risk, we are trying to avoid pretty much entirely so far. And the deals that we've seen in the other category are new money buyouts. And the new money buyouts are happening at enterprise values that are well below where they would have been 1 year, 1.5 years ago, but also leverage levels that are much lower.

On a deal that closed here in Q4 that we did that was a software deal, the leverage on the WhiteHorse EBITDA was 3.8x, which compares to 6, 7, 8, 9x in terms of what you were seeing 1.5 years ago in the market. And the price on that deal was 625 over. So these new money buyouts with fresh equity coming in, where we're able to assess that there is either limited or no AI risk are the types of software situations we're looking for.

And really, for the most part, those are the only types of deals that can get done in today's market because so many of the big players bought a lot of software at the peak of the market, a lot of software loans and don't have room to do any more. So it's an interesting moment in time. We always talk about wanting to not buy high and buy low. That's exactly what we're doing in software where we largely avoided the sector during the peak period and now have an opportunity to selectively add a few credits that have strong underlying credit profile, covenants and low leverage and high spread.

Operator: We'll take our next question from Christopher Nolan with Ladenburg Thalmann.

Christopher Nolan: Stuart, what are the thoughts on share repurchases given the stock price has appreciated a bit since September?

Stuart Aronson: Chris, we're not buying back shares right now. We're working with the special committee to focus on the strategic options that we have indicated are potentially underway. And if those strategic options don't pan out, then we could go back to reconsidering share repurchases. But again, we, as an organization and the Board are more focused on the strategic opportunities that we see in front of us.

Christopher Nolan: Okay. And then should I read into that also that you're going to be less focused on growing the investment portfolio while this process is in process?

Stuart Aronson: No, not at all. We don't know if the strategic options will result in a successful transaction. And not knowing that, we continue to reinvest the portfolio carefully and selectively in a market environment that is really the best market environment here in 2026 that we've seen in about 3 or 4 years, 3 years probably. And we're seeing solid credits, good capital structures, good documents with covenant protection and pricing that on average is 50 to 75 basis points better than it was last year. So the main issue in the market, even though our volumes will be up year-over-year at WhiteHorse is that M&A activity is not that strong.

And Q3, I think, was flat to down from last year in the market. And I expect when the Q4 numbers come out, they'll also show a decrease in M&A activity. That said, we have about 20 originators in 11 physical locations across North America, and that helps us gin up deals outside of the normal sponsor M&A flow. And we hope to get some interesting deals done, hopefully in Q4 and/or early in Q1.

Joyson Thomas: Chris, I was just going to add to that. When we paused the share buyback in Q2, I think it reflects Stuart's comments just now where, again, as we do buybacks, that reduces our equity. And so we need to balance that with putting capital back to work and deploying that into newly originated investments. So it's obviously a fine balance.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Thank you. It does appear that there are no further questions at this time. This brings us to the end of today's meeting. We appreciate your time and participation. You may now disconnect.

#3028. Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

#3026. Over 50? 3 Things You Should Be Doing to Prepare for Retirement Already

At this stage of life, careful planning is crucial.

Just because you're over 50 doesn't mean retirement is right around the corner. You may still have another 10, 15, or 20 years of work ahead of you.

On the other hand, if you're over 50, it's time to get serious about retirement planning. And that means focusing on these three key things.

One big misconception about catch-up contributions in retirement plans is that you need to be "behind" on savings to make them. All you need to do is be 50 or older. That's it. And if you can swing those extra contributions, they might get you closer to your long-term savings goals.

This year, IRAs max out at $7,500 for savers under 50, but you can make a catch-up contribution of up to $1,100. If you have a 401(k), your pre-catch-up limit is $24,500. But this year's catch-up maxes out at $8,000.

Now, if your taxable earnings are $150,000 or higher and you have a 401(k), your catch-up contribution must be made in a Roth account. If your employer's 401(k) doesn't have a Roth component, a catch-up contribution may be off the table. But otherwise, it helps to sneak that extra money into your savings if you can.

A lot of people assume Medicare will cover long-term care, such as home health aides, assisted living, or nursing home stays. Well, here's the bad news -- it won't.

Medicare won't pay for custodial care, which encompasses help with everyday living. If you don't want to have to foot a potentially enormous bill for long-term care without help, it pays to explore your options for long-term care insurance.

The optimal time to apply for long-term care coverage is generally during your 50s. That way, you're not paying those premiums for too many years, but you may also be young enough to lock in affordable costs based on your health.

The earliest age to claim Social Security is 62. At this point, you may not be ready to file for benefits for many years, but it pays to read up on the program's rules and understand how everything works.

It's also smart to develop a Social Security filing strategy, since your claiming age affects the monthly benefit you receive. Waiting until full retirement age, for example, guarantees your monthly benefit without a reduction, while delaying your claim could yield significantly larger benefits.

You don't need to narrow down every specific detail of retirement when you're still years away. But if you're older than 50, it's a good time to look at boosting your savings, research options for long-term care insurance, and learn more about how Social Security works.

#3015. The AI Trade Looks Like It's Falling Apart. AMD's Earnings Delivered a Reality Check.

AMD is still growing and is optimistic about the fourth quarter, despite recent market noise about the AI trade.

Being in the AI trade over the past month has been a battle of grit and determination. It was already a sea of red before U.S. midterm results, but with Democrats winning several key states while campaigning against AI data centers, the sell-off has only gotten worse.

There's a lot of noise about AI stocks, but when it comes to actual results, the thesis looks as strong as ever. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +13.26%) recently reported earnings, and it serves as a valuable reality check amid a sudden bearish wave.

Sales have been marching higher sequentially for most chipmakers, including AMD. Its data center segment's sales almost doubled year over year, with record sales of graphics processing units (GPUs) and central processing units (CPUs) driving the trend. While GPUs have been in the spotlight throughout the AI boom, CPUs are becoming more valuable as the shift toward agentic AI progresses.

AMD generated $13.4 billion in third-quarter revenue, outpacing the high end of its guidance in the process. The company also said that demand for its products is still strengthening while hinting at a stronger fourth quarter.

All this growth also came with rising profit margins. AMD reported 95% year-over-year net income growth. If there's truly an AI bubble, concerns about that scenario didn't show up anywhere in AMD's results. Nvidia delivered similar news when it reported earnings for its fiscal second quarter of 2027, and is expected to do the same in its third-quarter report on Nov. 17. Demand isn't the issue, and profit margins are rising alongside revenue.

GPUs are a key part of AI infrastructure, but a lot of components revolve around each chip. Liquid cooling, AI racks, memory chips, optical cables, and other resources must be accumulated to bring all the GPUs online.

Since AMD and Nvidia both reported stellar earnings and sold more chips, the buyers of those chips will have to invest in the other key components of AI data centers. They also gave solid guidance, suggesting that the momentum is not slowing down.

The tech giants also aren't slowing down on their capital expenditures. As innovations like humanoid robots and self-driving vehicles approach mainstream adoption, every hyperscaler wants to be the winner in these groundbreaking opportunities.

Tech bull Dan Ives anticipates that Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta Platforms will exceed $1 trillion in capital expenditures in 2027. They won't be the only companies boosting spending, especially as demand for AI chips remains resilient and on an uptrend.

AMD's earnings didn't do much to reassure AI investors. Many high-conviction names have been in free fall over the past month. Financing issues and midterm results have concerned many investors.

This negative news cycle makes it hard to be bullish when the majority of market participants are rushing to the sidelines. CNN's Fear and Greed Index projects a "Fear" rating, which highlights prolonged selling pressure.

In the short term, news cycles dominate investors' minds. However, fundamentals prevail in the long run. The AI trade has taken a big hit if you look only at stock prices, but the same opportunity has stronger fundamentals than it did a few months ago.

AMD's earnings served as another reminder that everything is fine. Micron shared that its fiscal 2027 will be even better than its fiscal 2026. It goes to show that AMD's earnings aren't a diamond-in-the-rough scenario. The AI industry is filled with diamonds that are trading like copper at current levels.

"The need for employees trained in the automotive, skilled trades, and healthcare fields continues its significant growth, and Lincoln Tech is providing an established, proven education and training model to help America address its chronic skills gap," Shaw said.

For release at 4:30 p.m. EDT Share

The Federal Reserve Board on Tuesday announced its approval of the application by BancFirst Corporation, of Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, to acquire and merge with Spirit BankCorp, Inc., of Bristow, Oklahoma, and thereby indirectly acquire SpiritBank, of Tulsa, Oklahoma.

The Board also gave its approval for BancFirst, of Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, to merge with SpiritBank and to establish and operate branches at the locations of SpiritBank.
